News.title: Essex explosion live: Inferno after huge blast as 100 firefighters tackle flames
News.content:
Aerial images show the scale of the blaze at a farm in Essex

More than 100 firefighters are tackling a massive fire at a farm off Southend Road between East Hanningfield and Rettendon in Essex

A massive explosion at a farm in Essex has shaken buildings up to 15 miles away, with footage showing an huge fireball erupting from the site.

Essex County Fire and Rescue Service said more than 100 firefighters worked to tackle a blaze involving industrial units at a farm off Southend Road, between East Hanningfield and Rettendon, near Chelmsford, on Friday evening.

The blaze, which is understood to be at Highlands Farm, has been declared a major incident due to its size. Around 50 firefighters will remain at the scene overnight and into the morning. Police have cordoned off a large area around the site.

"If you live or are travelling nearby, please continue to keep your windows and doors closed," the fire service said. "Please avoid the area while we deal with this incident."

News.title: Dad describes hearing screams before diving into sea to help drowning family at West Mersea beach
News.content:
Dad describes hearing screams before diving into sea to help drowning family at West Mersea beach

Craig Bowe was enjoying a family day trip to West Mersea with his wife and daughter when he heard harrowing screams coming from the sea - he has described the moment he decided to step in and help

View 6 Images Craig and Carly helped as best they could during the West Mersea beach tragedy

A dad on a family day trip to West Mersea has reflected on his attempts to save a mother and daughter who drowned off an Essex beach.

‌



Craig Bowe, 42, was on a day trip from Hertfordshire to celebrate his daughter's 10th birthday they arrived at the beach at about 11am and recalled seeing the victims having a "great time" together, until several houts later they heard harrowing screams coming from the water on Wednesday evening.

‌



Without hesitation Craig sprang into action and managed to haul Shally and Samiha Rahman from the waves and also helped a seven-year-old boy onto a lifeboat. However, despite his efforts Shally and Samiha - aged 41 and 15 - sadly died at the scene. While the young boy was airlifted to hospital and remained there in a critical condition on Friday.

‌



View 6 Images Shelina Rahman tragically died alongside her daughter at the scene

Mum shares horror details after robot vacuum explosion left son fighting for life READ MORE :

The tragedy unfolfed at around 5.35pm when Samiha had tried in vain along with her mother Shally to save her seven-year-old cousin from the water . The mother and daughter were reportedly caught in the high tide and, despite the the valiant efforts of teenagers on the beach, were unable to be saved.

Craig, from Northaw, sprang into action after hearing a man screaming in the water and seeing bodies floating. He told the BBC: "When I got there, the first two people I saw were actually face down, so [it was] more serious than I initially thought."

‌



Speaking about how he helped load the seven-year-old boy and another child, who were about 150 yards (137m) out at sea, onto a lifeboat he said: "I helped sort of shoo him onto the boat, because he was face down too... but the seven-year-old was not in a good way."

View 6 Images West Mersea is popular with Essex locals for its beaches (Image: Jamie Lashmar/PA Wire)

Bowe's wife, Carly, was among the group of people trying to resuscitate the mother and daughter on the sand. She told the BBC: "I just wanted them to survive and every bit of me was willing her to breathe."

‌



She added: "Everybody on that beach that day played their part in giving that family the best chance they could to survive. Everyone really stepped up and it was incredible to see."

Essex Police's Detective Chief Inspector Al Pitcher said: "My thoughts, and those of my team, are with the friends and family of the woman and girl who died yesterday. We can now confirm they were a mother and daughter from London and we are supporting their family in what is an unimaginable time.

"Since yesterday we have been working to establish the circumstances which led up to this incident. At this stage we believe they were trying to help a seven year-old boy who had got into difficulties.

‌



View 6 Images A huge emergency response was spotted on the Essex beach (Image: Daniel Rees / Newsquest / SWNS)

"The boy was taken to hospital where he remains in a critical condition but the woman and teenage girl, sadly, died. All the people involved in this incident are related to each other.

"As part of our investigation we are working through speaking to dozens of witnesses and taking their accounts, and we are building a picture of what happened. These enquiries are ongoing and I need anyone who has any information to get in contact.

‌



"Finally, I want to thank the first responders who worked tirelessly to try save their lives and I want to pay tribute to their efforts."

View 6 Images Local people have long called for more warning signs and life-saving equipment along the shoreline. (Image: PA)

Just days after the tragedy Colchester Council said an independent Royal Life Saving Society (RLSS) UK beach risk assessment was carried out on West Mersea Beach four months ago - and found that life-saving equipment was "not recommended" as it was "unlikely to be deployed effectively".

‌



A spokesperson the council said "decisions on water safety measures" are "informed by professional risk assessments and advice from specialist organisations".

A Colchester Council spokesperson said: "We are aware of views that have been expressed regarding additional public rescue equipment. However, decisions on water safety measures are informed by professional risk assessments and advice from specialist organisations.

"As part of our risk assessment process for the site, the council commissioned an independent RLSS UK beach risk assessment in March 2026, which did not recommend the installation of public rescue equipment within the assessed area of West Mersea beach.

‌



"The assessment concluded that, due to factors including the beach profile, tidal range and lateral currents, public rescue equipment would be unlikely to be deployed effectively in an emergency and was therefore not recommended on that stretch of coastline.

"We continue to work closely with partner organisations through the Mersea Water Safety Forum, a multi-agency partnership that brings together organisations with expertise and responsibilities in water safety. Together, the forum assesses local risks and develops and implements measures to help improve safety in and around the water."

View 6 Images The Coastguard at the scene on the beach at West Mersea (Image: BBC)

‌



Cllr David King, Deputy Leader and Portfolio Holder for Local Government Reorganisation, Communities and Public Protection, added: "Everyone at Colchester City Council is deeply saddened by the tragic loss of two people following the incident at West Mersea.

"Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with their families, friends and all those affected by this devastating incident. We would also like to pay tribute to the emergency services and volunteers who responded.

"This tragedy is a stark reminder of the importance of taking care in and around the water. We encourage everyone visiting any coastline this summer to follow water safety advice and take appropriate precautions to help keep themselves and others safe."

Article continues below

Save Lives for Sam - our demands Together, we are all calling for: The Government to launch an urgent public awareness campaign ahead of the summer holidays which targets parents and children on TikTok and other social media platforms. This should include lifesaving techniques and advice such as avoid diving into the water and information on cold water shock. Water companies and those in control of high risk large water bodies, to ‘do the right thing’ by bringing in the correct safety equipment. Compulsory lessons in schools (ahead of the holidays) on how to survive if you get into difficulty in the water, which should include the Water Safety Code, the RNLI ‘Float to Live’ campaign, and Phone-Float-Throw bystander advice. Put in place ‘Sam’s Law’. We urge the Government to make it law that safety equipment should be installed around high risk large bodies of water and make damaging this safety equipment an aggravated criminal offence to damage or steal this safety equipment. Currently it is already a criminal offence under theft or criminal damage but the penalties are low for these very minor offences. And finally the appointment of a Minister for Water Safety, as they have in Wales and Scotland, as drowning must be accepted as a preventable public health issue.

The Mirror has launched the Save Lives For Sam water safety campaign to tackle the UK's growing drowning crisis. Backed by MPs, Olympic champions, national water safety organisations and bereaved families, the campaign is calling for urgent action to make our waters safer.

News.title: Spain and France wildfires live: 200,000 flee as flames scorch tourist areas
News.content:
Firefighters battle a wildfire in the Cebreros area, near Ávila, around 50 miles west of Madrid, on July 24

More than 200,000 people in France and Spain have been evacuated as wildfires continue to tear through vast areas of both countries

Huge wildfires are ravaging parts of south-west France and central Spain, forcing the evacuation of an estimated 200,000 people, including British tourists.

Around 141,000 people have been evacuated from their homes in France's Gironde and Landes departments, the French interior ministry said. Some residents and holidaymakers even fled by boat as flames swept through the popular tourist area of Cap Ferret on France's Atlantic coast.

In Spain, 60,000 have been forced to leave their homes in towns west of Madrid, the Spanish interior ministry said. Wildfires in the Madrid region and the nearby province of Ávila have prompted the government to declare a national emergency over wildfires for the first time.

Meanwhile, Police Scotland has declared a major incident as firefighters battle a huge wildfire in the Cairngorms National Park, with hundreds of people evacuated from homes in its path.

The force said strengthening winds have made the fire more unpredictable and caused it to spread towards Nethy Bridge, a small village in the Strathspey area of the park, prompting the decision to declare a major incident.

News.title: Westminster Bridge: Four police officers seriously injured in horror Thames boat crash
News.content:
A police boat carrying armed cops has crashed near Westminster Bridge in central London, leaving four officers seriously injured after a number plunged into the River Thames.

Emergency services swarmed the scene in central London, with responders from the RNLI seen treating casualties on a boat at the pier.

A large number of police officers, fire crews and ambulances were also at the scene, with the bridge closed to traffic and the Underground also impacted.

Metropolitan Police Commander Nick John said: "Our thoughts are with all those involved, in particular our officers who were injured and those who responded in challenging circumstances.

"The four officers who remain in hospital have serious but non-life-threatening injuries. We will give them all every support as they recover."

News.title: PlayStation Network goes down worldwide as thousands unable to connect servers
News.content:
Video game giant Sony confirmed that all PlayStation services were 'experiencing issues' amid thousands of reports from users around the globe

Gamers around the world, including thousands in the UK, reported issues with the PlayStation Network, with many saying they were unable to connect to servers.

Problems started at around 11.30am on Friday (July 24), with video game giant Sony later confirming all PlayStation services were "experiencing issues". It said it was working to resolve the problem as soon as possible and thanked users for their patience. The company has not yet given a reason for the outage.

Tens of thousands of reports of network issues were logged on outage-tracking website Downdetector.

One frustrated UK user wrote on Downdetector: "Can't load any digital games at all bought or free. Can't connect to servers to verify licences, doesn't matter what I try to load - I get the same message every time."

News.title: Donald Trump defends ‘slave labour’ import tariff against UK amid court challenge
News.content:
Donald Trump defends ‘slave labour’ import tariff against UK amid court challenge

The White House justified the charges in law by claiming the economies targeted had failed to enforce bans on goods produced by slave labour - their imposition coincided with the expiry of a temporary 10% import levy

View 2 Images Mr Trump said: “We put the tariffs on. They’re very standard tariffs" (Image: AP Photo/Rod Lamkey)

Donald Trump has defended slapping fresh taxes on imports from the UK and dozens of other countries as a legal challenge was launched against the move.

‌



The US President slapped duties on 60 countries. They replace a previous set of tariffs that expired on Friday after the US Supreme Court ruled them illegal.

‌



Speaking in the Oval Office, the US president said the new levies were “very standard tariffs” that “follow the line”. The White House justified the charges in law by claiming the economies targeted had failed to enforce bans on goods produced by slave labour.

‌



View 2 Images In 2024, UK exports to the US were worth £66 billion, 17% of all UK goods exports. (Image: Getty Images)

Meghan Markle shares sweet holiday snaps of Archie and Lilibet visiting Diana's childhood home READ MORE :

Their imposition coincided with the expiry of a temporary 10% import levy, already faced by Britain, introduced after the Supreme Court ruled Mr Trump’s initial sweeping global tariffs, which he hailed at the time as “Liberation Day”, were unlawful.

Mr Trump said: “We put the tariffs on. They’re very standard tariffs. The other way was easier. I thought the decision by the Supreme Court was not a good one. But we have many forms of tariffs.”

‌



He was speaking after a legal campaign group brought a case on behalf of two small businesses in the US Court of International Trade in New York, opposing the latest import taxes.

The Liberty Justice Centre, which has successfully challenged Mr Trump’s previous tariffs, is seeking to overturn the replacement levies. Sara Albrecht, the group’s chairman, said: The administration allowed one global tariff to expire and immediately replaced it with another under a different statute.

“Changing the statute doesn’t change the law. Every tariff authority has limits, and every administration must respect them.”

‌



The centre’s senior lawyer Jeffrey Schwab said the legislative provision being relied on by the White House was “a targeted, country-specific and practice-specific remedial authority”.

He added: “It is not a freestanding authorisation to tax substantially all imports from substantially all countries at pre-established rates.”

The UK Government has pointed out there is no change to the tariff rate facing UK businesses as a result of the recent announcement, which would remain at 10%. The UK exports more to the US than to any other single country.

Article continues below

The Economic Prosperity Deal agreed between the two countries last year aimed to mitigate the impact of US tariffs on UK industries and deepen commercial ties.

Meanwhile, US import duties on Scotch whisky has now been lifted. The president announced in April that he would remove the whisky tariff, following the state visit by the King and Queen.

News.title: Twisted schoolboy, 14, who shot classmates and teachers in school rampage laughs as survivor reads statement
News.content:
Twisted schoolboy, 14, who shot classmates and teachers in school rampage laughs as survivor reads statement

Colt Gray was just 14 when he killed four and injured nine people in a horrific gun rampage at his own school - today the teen pleaded guilty in court

View 6 Images Colt Gray in court, in December (Image: AP Photo/Mike Stewart)

A teenager who unleashed a horror gun attack on his school, shooting dead two students and two teachers, laughed as a survivor spoke out to the court.

‌



Colt Gray, 16, killed four people and left nine injured after a gun attack at the Apalachee High School, in Georgia, when he was just 14 years old, in 2024. The trial for the deadly shooting saw survivors and families of victims share their statements to jurors. Survivor Natalie Griffith recalled her horror memories from the shooting but Gray was seen grinning and smiling as she spoke.

‌



On Friday, Gray formally pleaded guilty to all 55 charges against him, in relation to the school massacre. These included murder and aggravated assault.

‌



Calls for UK government to put pressure on Texas cops to re-open case of Brit shot dead by her dad READ MORE :

Coney Island horror mass shooting leaves eight injured including four children as cops swarm READ MORE :

View 6 Images Colt Gray in court on July 24 (Image: AP/YouTube)

Griffith was among the people injured in the school bloodbath and shared the heartbreaking impact the attack has had on her life nearly two years after the September 2024 incident.

The survivor told the court: "I got shot twice, once in my wrist and once in my upper arm. I lost the ability to use my left hand, but on some days it doesn't feel like that is the biggest thing I lost. After the shooting I lost my independence, I could not put on my own clothes or do my own hair, things that were easy for me became a challenge."

‌



View 6 Images Mugshot of Colt Gray after the September 2024 attack (Image: AP)

Griffith shared her story at a fast speed, prompting the judge to ask her to slow down. Several laughs were heard in the courtroom including from twisted Gray who was seen giggling.

Another survivor, Hayden Bowen, also tearfully shared a statement to the court, telling Gray: "I want to start off by saying I forgive you. Not for you, but for me and my peace."

‌



She added: "I have frequent panic attacks. I can't stay in places for too long. I can't go out anywhere. I can't even stay in my own bedroom without feeling fear. I'm not able to be a normal teenager anymore."

View 6 Images The four victims who died in the 2024 shooting (Image: Getty Images)

The four people who were killed in the 2024 shooting were pupils Mason Schermerhorn, 14, and Christian Angulo, 14, as well as two teachers Richard Aspinwall, 39, and Cristina Irimie, 53.

‌



Breanna Schermerhorn, whose 14-year-old son Mason Schermerhorn was shot dead, said her boy was "much more than a victim". She said: "Mason was kind, compassionate, funny and fiercely protective of others.

"As a child with exceptional needs, he understood what it felt like to struggle and be overlooked by others. Instead of becoming bitter, he became an advocate. He made people that were typically unseen feel seen, accepted and safe."

View 6 Images An attorney pointing to a weapon during the trial, in February (Image: AP)

‌



The mum added that Gray "knew that pulling that trigger was wrong, he knew that every choice he made that day would forever alter countless lives".

Gray agreed to a non-negotiated guilty plea, meaning the court will work to decide his sentence. The judge told the court that the minimum sentence is life with parole and the maximum is a life sentence without parole.

View 6 Images Mugshot of the killer teen's dad Colin Gray (Image: Barrow County Jail)

Article continues below

Ismael Angulo, the brother of Christian Angulo, asked the judge to put Gray in prison for life without the chance of parole, as "every day as a nightmare". The brother said: "The defendant's family will still get to see their son, talk to him and know he is breathing. My mother, my father don't get that privilege."

Gray was accused of carrying out the massacre with a rifle that his dad Colin Gray gifted the teen for Christmas. The dad was convicted, in March, of charged including second-degree murder. The court heard audio from Gray's arrest where he asked a police officer to share a message with his dad: "Tell him that it wasn't his fault and that I know he tried his hardest."

News.title: Sarah Ferguson's charity shuts down after scrutiny of links to paedophile Jeffrey Epstein
News.content:
Sarah Ferguson's charity shuts down after scrutiny of links to paedophile Jeffrey Epstein

Sarah's Trust, the charity belonging to Sarah Ferguson, has been shut and 'removed' from the charity regulator's website

View 3 Images Sarah Ferguson pictured in April 2025 (Image: UK Press via Getty Images)

Disgraced Sarah Ferguson has seen her charity wound up after her controversial links to convicted paedophile Jeffrey Epstein emerged.

The former-Duchess's Sarah's Trust charity had introduced philanthropists to good causes in need of funding, but was formally shut last month. It was first registered with the Charity Commission in 2018, but the regulator's website now lists the trust as being "removed", meaning it was no longer a registered charity. Sarah's Trust had also been listed at Companies House as a "charitable incorporated organisation" but its status is now "converted/closed".

Emails released by US officials, as part of the Epstein Files, revealed several emails between Fergie and Epstein and shed new light on their relationship. Ferguson has strongly denied all wrongdoing.

View 3 Images Sarah Ferguson and her ex-husband Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor in September 2025 (Image: UK Press via Getty Images)

The charity back in February said it would close "for the foreseeable future" just days after new revelations emerged after millions of documents were released in the Epstein Files.

At the time, a spokesperson for the charity said: "Our chair Sarah Ferguson and the board of trustees have agreed that with regret the charity will shortly close for the foreseeable future. This has been under discussion and in train for some months."

One of these included an email between Fergie and Epstein where she praised the sex offender and called him the "brother I have always wished for". Appearing in the Epstein Files does not indicate guilt or wrongdoing.

View 3 Images Sarah Ferguson smiling, in April 2025 (Image: Aaron Chown/PA Wire)

In another email, from 2010, the ex-Duchess wrote: "You are a legend. I really don't have the words to describe, my love, gratitude for your generosity and kindness," she writes. "Xx I am at your service . Just marry me."

Other publicly released files also showed that Fergie had invited Epstein to her 50th birthday party at St James's Palace in February 2010. This was after Epstein was released from prison in 2009, for soliciting prostitution of a minor.

Other charities associated with the former duchess also cut ties with Ferguson, including the Teenage Cancer Trust, which dropped her as patron after 35 years, Wiltshire and Dorset-based children’s hospice Julia's House, Prevent Breast Cancer, The Natasha Allergy Research Foundation and the National Foundation for Retired Service Animals.

Fergie's ex-husband Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor was stripped of his royal privileges and titles by the King because of "serious lapses of judgment" over his friendship with the late paedophile. Ferguson also lost her courtesy royal divorcee title and went back to her maiden name.

Article continues below

The Mirror has contacted Sarah Ferguson's representatives for comment.

News.title: Police declare 'major incident' as wind change increases Cairngorms wildfire risk
News.content:
Police Scotland has declared a major incident as emergency services continue to tackle a wildfire which has been burning in the Cairngorms National Park for 10 days.

The force said it followed "a significant change in weather conditions" which has increased the risk of fire spreading towards the village of Nethy Bridge.

All Nethy Bridge residents have been evacuated to allow emergency services to continue their response.

First Minister John Swinney said "all resources that can be deployed are being deployed".

But a local resident of Nethy Bridge told the BBC the wildfire should have been declared a major incident sooner and the lack of communication from authorities had been "pretty poor".

The BBC has contacted the Scottish government and Police Scotland for comment.

Smoke from the wildfire can now be seen 59 miles away in Aberdeen following a change in wind direction.

Supt Judy Hill said weather conditions "experienced within the Cairngorms over the last 24 hours have added further complexities to this situation".

"With evidence suggesting the fire is spreading towards Nethy Bridge, the decision has been taken to declare a major incident and evacuate residents as a precaution."

She said additional police resources were being deployed to help contact those who need to leave their properties.

News.title: Teenage boy dies after stabbing in Luton as police launch murder investigation
News.content:
Police have launched a murder investigation after a teenage boy died following a stabbing in Luton.

Bedfordshire Police said it responded to reports of violent disorder in Kingsway Recreation Ground at about 18:30 on Friday, where a number of teenagers were seen carrying large knives.

A 17-year-old, who has not been identified, was taken to hospital with multiple stab wounds but was pronounced dead shortly after, the force said.

One teenage boy has been arrested on suspicion of violent disorder and is in police custody for questioning. A second teenage boy was arrested but remains in hospital with serious but non-life threatening injuries.

Police are appealing to the public for information.

News.title: Watch moment of explosion as huge fire breaks out in Essex
News.content:
A huge explosion triggered by a fire tore through an industrial unit in Essex on Friday, with more than 100 firefighters sent to tackle the massive fire.

Video posted on social media captured the moment the explosion rattled the surrounding area, with some people seen running from the blaze.

The Essex fire service declared a major incident due to the size of the fire, warning people to stay away from the area and keep doors and windows closed if they live nearby.

In an update on Friday evening, the fire brigade said the blaze was under control and there was no wider risk to the public.

News.title: Horror injury overshadows gymnastics silver for England at Commonwealths
News.content:
A sickening injury to England's Gabriel Langton overshadowed his team's silver medal in the men's team gymnastics final at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

The 19-year-old, from the City of Birmingham Gymnastics Club, needed lengthy treatment on the mat after a horrible fall in the final rotation of the evening at The Arena.

Langton fell head first to the floor after missing his catch on the horizontal metal bar, three metres in the air, leading to a lengthy delay to the action as he was tended to by up to a dozen medical staff.

He was eventually led away on a trolley after being moved on to a stretcher with his head and neck braced and left to huge applause from the packed crowd who had spent much of the previous 10 minutes in hushed silence.

Langton was seen to be conscious and moving his legs and arms before leaving the arena floor, while team officials later said he was moving and speaking to doctors.

In a statement, Team England said: "We are grateful to the medical teams who responded immediately to provide assistance.

"He has been taken to hospital and we will share more information when it is available."

When competition resumed, his England team-mates were unable to overhaul their deficit to Canada who claimed their first gold medal in the event in 20 years, having finished second to England at the past two games.

Langton, a late call-up to Team England in the place of the injured six-time Olympic medallist Max Whitlock, was unable to join his teammates on the podium as England collected their silver medals.

Team-mate Luke Whitehouse, who was first on to the apparatus after the competition restarted and posted a relatively low score of 11.700, said: "When something like that happens, you've just got to forget about it and reset. I just had to focus on my routine one skill at a time."

Whitehouse added: "From what we've heard, he's doing OK. Gymnastics is such a dangerous sport and things like this remind us of that. It's one of those things you have to put out of your mind."

Felix Dolci, who helped Canada to gold and led qualifying for the all-around competition, said: "It's terrible but it goes to show that gymnastics is a very, very difficult and complicated sport. It's dangerous you know sometimes.

"All our thoughts go to Gabriel and the team. Pushing through this is definitely not easy, England stayed focussed, they stayed in the zone, a huge shout out to them because that's not an easy one.

"For any gymnast that was on the field of play, seeing this not only is difficult, but something you never want to see. It goes to show how hard the sport is."

Hamish Carter from Team Scotland - who narrowly missed out on a bronze medal to Australia in the final rotation - said: "I didn't actually see what happened. I'm just so happy that he's alright and, having experienced that, anything could have happened.

"We've walked away with no medal but I'm thinking of Gabe in this moment."

News.title: Heatwave reveals lost archaeological sites across Wales
News.content:
Lost archaeological sites have emerged in grasslands across Wales after a prolonged spell of hot and dry weather.

Wales has seen about 5% of the average rainfall for July, after a series of back-to-back heatwaves and a drier than usual April to June. A drought has also been triggered in parts of Wales.

Experts said these dry conditions have brought to light a range of hidden archaeological remains, including Roman buildings and practice trenches from World War One.

Many are only visible from the air as distinctive marks in crops and grass, with some not being seen for "two or three decades", according to the Royal Commission on the Ancient and Historical Monuments of Wales (RCAHMW).

News.title: Warning shot or publicity stunt - how worried should we be about the OpenAI hack?
News.content:
This week the tech world was gripped by a story that has it all - and which started like a sci-fi thriller.

Hugging Face - a kind of app store for artificial intelligence tools - announced on 16 July it had been hacked by a cyber criminal wielding enormously powerful AI.

The bombshell announcement was full of scary, highly technical terms: "a swarm of sandboxes", "agentic attacker", and "self-migrating command and control".

Hugging Face said the hack was different from anything it had handled before because it was done at superhuman speed by an AI with little or no human guidance.

The AI performed 17,000 actions in less than two days, successfully breaching the large wealthy tech company to steal secrets.

It left the tech world in shock. But who was responsible for this attack?

Hugging Face researchers guessed the mysterious attackers had used one of the big AI models but they had no idea who or where the criminals were.

The perplexed company contacted the police and investigations commenced.

News.title: Law student is charged over intercepted bomb in car
News.content:
A 25-year-old law student has appeared in court charged over a bomb which was discovered in a car in the Republic of Ireland.

Isobella Perrie Sullivan, from Abbeylands Park in Clane, County Kildare, was charged with the possession of explosives.

It was alleged she was driving the car which was intercepted by gardaÃ­ (Irish police) near Carrickmacross, County Monaghan, on Wednesday.

A defence solicitor told the court his client had been asked to take a bag to Northern Ireland and had not been aware what was in it.

Earlier on Friday, gardaÃ­ (Irish police) told reporters their interception was part of an operation targeting dissident republican activity.

The accused, who was arrested on Wednesday, was brought before a special sitting of Trim District Court in County Meath on Friday evening.

A member of the Garda Special Detective Unit told the court the car she was driving was stopped by officers on N2 at Aclint, south of Carrickmacross.

News.title: Heatwave conditions to return for many as UK temperatures to peak at 35C
News.content:
For most of England and Wales the third heatwave of the year ended last weekend when cooler air arrived, dropping maximum temperatures widely to 20-24C.

However, two locations - Usk and Exeter - have continued to just reach their heatwave criteria since then and have now reached 20 consecutive days - the longest run so far this year.

As temperatures drop further over the weekend, and parts of the UK see a little rain, even these local heatwaves are likely to come to an end.

However, it may only be a temporary break.

Next week, high pressure is set to build close to the south of the UK meaning rain-bearing weather fronts will stall.

Any wet weather will become confined to northern and western areas - especially north-west Scotland - and in southern parts of the UK temperatures look set to climb once again.

This could well mean a fourth heatwave is on the cards - although according to the Met Office isolated high temperatures might not be enough.

They say that: "If only one or two stations reach heatwave criteria, that would not be defined as a heatwave."

News.title: Huge explosion and fire rip through Essex industrial site
News.content:
A huge explosion triggered by a fire spreading to a store of fertiliser tore through an industrial unit in Essex on Friday, with more than 100 firefighters sent to tackle a massive fire and a "major incident" declared.

Footage which captured the moment of the explosion showed a ball of flames erupting into the air and people fleeing, while witnesses told BBC News the sound was "like a bomb" and as loud as a "sonic boom".

A number of buildings and vehicles on farmland were gutted by the fire, which was expected to keep burning into Saturday.

People living near the fire - which happened close to the village of Rettendon, south of Chelmsford - were urged to keep their windows closed as smoke spread.

News.title: It's the cocktail taking young drinkers by storm - but the packaging is 'unrecyclable'
News.content:
Cleaning up after pre-drinks, AÃ©dÃ©n Rooney puts his empty BuzzBallz in the recycling.

"It's plastic and metal, so I'd just assume it's recyclable," he said.

The company behind the bright, pre-mixed cocktails that have taken Gen Z by storm said they were recyclable on its website, but experts say this is not true.

BuzzBallz cannot be recycled as the PET plastic ball cannot be separated from the aluminium lid, global environmental action body WRAP said.

"It's greenwashing. I'm shocked," AÃ©dÃ©n said.

BuzzBallz blamed a website error for claiming they were recyclable via Terracycle, a US-only scheme, but did not comment on its now-deleted FAQ that said they were recyclable where UK councils allow.

News.title: Man describes trying to save mother and daughter who drowned off Essex beach
News.content:
A day-tripper has told the BBC how he dived into the sea in an attempt to save a mother and daughter who drowned off an Essex beach.

Craig Bowe, 42, battled the incoming tide at West Mersea, near Colchester, three times after hearing screams on Wednesday evening.

The kitchen fitter, who was on a day trip from Hertfordshire to celebrate his daughter's 10th birthday, managed to haul Shally and Samiha Rahman from the waves and also helped a seven-year-old boy onto a lifeboat.

Despite his efforts, the pair - aged 41 and 15 - died in the desperate attempt to bring the boy to shore.

The boy, who became stranded during a family day out from Barking, east London, was airlifted to hospital and remained there in a critical condition on Friday.

Three others were taken by ambulance to another hospital after the incident unfolded at about 17:35 BST.

News.title: Officers hurt as police boat hits Westminster Bridge
News.content:
Five Metropolitan Police officers have been injured after a police boat struck Westminster Bridge in central London.

The Met said the incident occurred at about 15:40 BST and involved a boat from the Marine Policing Unit which was carrying armed officers.

One officer has since been discharged from hospital and the others have serious but non-life-threatening injuries.

The police confirmed that no members of the public were involved or injured in the crash.

The police boat was responding to a report of a person in the water near Battersea.

The Met said in a statement: "As a result of the collision, three officers were thrown from the boat into the water. They were recovered by those on nearby boats.

"Additional officers responded alongside the London Ambulance Service and London Fire Brigade."

The Met's Cmdr Nick John thanked river users "who came to the aid of the officers, as well as other police and emergency service colleagues who immediately made their way to the scene to assist".

He added: "The quick-thinking and professionalism of all those involved undoubtedly prevented any further injuries."

News.title: Angela Rayner rules out rent controls in England
News.content:
Housing Secretary Angela Rayner has said Prime Minister Andy Burnham is not looking at bringing in rent controls in England.

She told BBC Breakfast that changes made through the Renters' Rights Act, which came into effect in May, were "already having a significant impact on the market".

She added that controls which had been implemented in some areas of the UK over the past few years had not "necessarily brought rents down".

In 2023 when he was the mayor of Greater Manchester, Burnham called for freezes to private sector rents until the cost of living crisis was over.

But Rayner told the BBC on Friday: "I don't think that rent freezes, rent controls, is a way forward at the moment.

"Three years ago, Andy called for that because there was a significant crisis in the rental market.

"We implemented between then the Renters' Rights Act which is giving renters more power and control."

Temporary rent controls were introduced in Scotland in October 2022 but expired last year.

Under new legislation, ministers in Holyrood will be able to designate certain places in Scotland as rent control areas - expected to come in by 2027.

Councils will be able to cap rent increases on some properties at a maximum of 6%.

Green Party leader Zack Polanski has said he wants to see rent controls brought in for all rented property in England.

Responding to Rayner's interview, he described Burnham as "continuity Starmer", posting on X: "The new prime minister talks a lot of about helping with the cost of living crisis. This is the one single measure that would help the most and save billions. All talk."

Jeremy Corbyn, who pledged to bring in rent controls during the 2019 general election when he was the Labour leader, described Rayner's announcement as "extremely disappointing".

"There is no hope of ending homelessness if we do not stand up to vested interests and take action against extortionate private rents.

"We need rent controls, and we need them now."

Sir Sadiq Khan, the mayor of London, has also long called on the government to implement a cap.

But Gareth Bacon, the Conservative's shadow housing minister, said rent controls would be "disastrous" and "intensify the damage done by Labour's agenda that has driven landlords from the market and reduced choice for renters".

"Labour are clearly divided. Burnham's pick for housing secretary has disowned a policy he himself has repeatedly backed," he said.

The term rent controls describes a range of measures a government can implement - from capping price increases to freezing them for a period of time.

Landlord groups say they may exacerbate the housing crisis by putting owners off renting out property.

The Renters' Rights Act was brought in to give more stability and security to the 11 million people who rent from private landlords.

Under the legislation, fixed-term tenancies have been banned and it is now significantly harder for landlords to evict tenants.

Rents can also only be increased once a year to the property's "open market rent".

News.title: Slapping therapist jailed over death 'released early'
News.content:
An alternative healer jailed over the death of a woman at one of his workshops has been released from prison just 18 months into a 10-year sentence, it is understood.

Hongchi Xiao, 63, from California, was convicted and sentenced in 2024 for the manslaughter by gross negligence of 71-year-old Danielle Carr-Gomm in 2016.

Carr-Gomm, who was diabetic, died while taking part in a therapy event in Wiltshire, which involved people being slapped or slapping themselves repeatedly.

On Friday, during a Court of Appeal hearing where an application to overturn his conviction was quashed, it emerged Xiao had been returned to the US and was believed to no longer be in custody.

In his judgment, Lord Justice Dingemans said it seemed Xiao had been returned to the US on 2 July through the Early Removal Scheme.

This enables eligible foreign national offenders to be deported from the UK once they have served the minimum required proportion of their sentence.

However, he added: "Other information suggests he was deported on 30 June 2026. It seems that Mr Xiao is not in custody in the USA."

A government spokesperson said: "Hongchi Xiao's crimes were terrible, and our thoughts remain with his victims.

"This government is deporting foreign national offenders at pace, with more than 5,000 deported last year, and Hongchi Xiao is prohibited from ever returning to the UK."

They added if Xiao were to return to the UK, he will be liable to serve the rest of his sentence from the point he was deported.

News.title: Southport killer Axel Rudakubana appears to be manipulating the system, families' lawyer says
News.content:
A lawyer for the families of the children murdered by Southport killer Axel Rudakubana has said his transfer from prison to a psychiatric hospital may be an attempt to "manipulate the system".

Rudakubana, 19, was given a life sentence for the murder of three children - Alice da Silva Aguiar, 9, Bebe King, 6, and Elsie Dot Stancombe, 7 - and attempted murder of eight other children and two adults.

On Thursday, he was moved from HMP Belmarsh to Broadmoor psychiatric hospital in Berkshire.

Prisoners who are considered to present a risk to staff, inmates or themselves because of mental disorders can be moved to hospital under the Mental Health Act.

Next Wednesday marks two years since Rudakubana carried out the attack at a Taylor Swift-themed dance class on 29 July 2024.

Lawyer Chris Walker, who represents the three bereaved families, said they "don't believe the merits" of the transfer on the basis of a mental health issue and is calling for more information from ministers.

"In my mind this is a new event, this is something which occurred whilst he was at prison, and we at this stage don't believe the merits of it in terms of him because I've seen no evidence at all until today which suggests he has a significant mental health disorder," Walker told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

He added: "We do have an evil person but being evil does not mean that you're suffering with psychosis of some sort.

"We need to know is this a single event, is this a recurring event, is this him playing the system and we need those answers."

The Prison Officers' Association told the BBC that Rudakubana was transferred due to a deterioration in his mental health.

Walker added in a separate statement that the news would "devastate" the families at any time but "the fact that this has occurred as we approach the second anniversary in our view is another move by AR who would appear to be attempting, once again, to manipulate the system".

He continued: "We have been given the barest of details and whilst we are supporting the families through this we are urgently seeking a meeting with the appropriate authorities to understand the situation before commenting further."

A lawyer for the families of the attack's survivors said they did not want to give "notoriety" to Rudakubana and that attention should be focused on supporting the children around the anniversary.

Nicola Ryan-Donnelly of Fletchers Solicitors said: "The focus of public outrage should not be on moves that this perpetrator has made, it should be examining how we are two years on from this attack and some of these girls are still not receiving the proper psychological care and support that they should be to recover from this."

Prior to Rudakubana's sentencing last year, his defence lawyer told the court no psychiatric evidence could suggest a mental disorder contributed to his actions.

The court also heard how Rudakubana presented as having high functioning autism and did not have any associated learning disabilities.

Stan Reiz KC added that his client had appeared to have been a "normal child" until he reached 13, adding: "However, he did make a transition from a normal, well-disciplined child to someone who was capable of committing acts of such shocking and senseless violence."

Rudakubana was deemed mentally fit to be detained, interviewed and stand trial. His late guilty plea meant his mental health was not discussed in detail in court during a trial.

He was given a 52-year prison sentence in January 2025 but the judge was unable to impose a whole life order due to Rudakubana being 17 when he carried out the attack. He will likely never be released.

President Donald Trump stood by awkwardly ahead of his speech on Friday at the White House Correspondents’ Association dinner, as Wall Street Journal reporters won awards for their coverage of the Jeffrey Epstein scandal, reporting which inspired the president to launch a since-dismissed $10 billion defamation lawsuit last year.

Journal reporters were honored multiple times during the Friday dinner. The president often shrugged or smiled as their reporting was described, and he shook some of the winners’ hands.

When it was his time to speak, the president joked that it had “not been an easy evening” reliving those moments.

“All these awards,” he said. “Do I have a say?”

The president also used his remarks to praise freedom of speech and condemn the gunman who stormed the original Correspondents’ Dinner in April, prompting organizers to reschedule.

open image in gallery President Trump spoke Friday at the remounted White House Correspondents’ Association dinner, after April’s original WHCA event was disrupted by a gunman who allegedly sought to kill the president ( Reuters )

”In this country, we believe in freedom of speech,” Trump said. “We settle our differences not with bullets, but with open and vigorous debate, and no deranged loser with a gun will ever change that. We can't let that ever happen.”

Reporters speaking before the president offered a mix of jokes and sincerity.

Weijia Jiang of CBS News, who recently finished her term as president of the Correspondents’ Association, joked that the evening’s entertainment, mentalist Oz Pearlman, didn’t need to guess to president’s phone number.

“Half the reporters in this room already have it,” she said, a reference to Trump’s penchant for taking unexpected calls at all hours from a variety of reporters.

The new WHCA president, Jacqueline Heinrich of FOX News, thanked President Trump for taking part in a celebration of First Amendment freedoms, and she spoke of the importance of journalism in broadening understanding at a time of rising political violence.

“The freedoms we cherish must never be taken for granted,” she said.

Despite the night’s theme of honoring the independent press, the White House has consistently clashed with the media.

Earlier this week, the government withdrew a controversial attempt to compel three New York Times journalists to testify about their sources, after they reported on concerns surrounding the president’s Qatari-gifted Air Force One replacement jet.

Last week, the president called for NBC and ABC to lose their broadcast licenses for not airing his recent, highly speculative primetime address about what he claimed was foreign “election interference.”

Both before and after his election, Trump has repeatedly sued news outlets over coverage he disagrees with.

open image in gallery Cole Tomas Allen has pleaded not guilty to attempting to kill President Trump at the original correspondents’ dinner in April ( Getty )

The Pentagon, meanwhile, has consistently worked to deny journalists the access to defense officials and facilities they enjoyed under previous administrations.

During the dinner on Friday, CBS News’s Jiang gave a special shoutout to the Pentagon reporters in the room.

“Your work is invaluable, especially as our nation is at war,” she said.

Critics have also accused the Trump administration of empowering the president’s political allies to take over important parts of the U.S. media and social media ecosystems and push them in a more conservative direction, including approving a deal for backers to take over the parent company of CBS News and blessing a pending attempt to buy the parent company of CNN.

Cole Thomas Allen has been charged with attempting to assassinate the president in connection with the April 25 attack on the original 2026 correspondents’ dinner.

Allen pleaded not guilty to all four counts against him in May.

The humble blackboard is serving as the canvas, and colorful chalk the paint, for young Japanese artists.

“Kokuban Art Koshien " is an annual national chalk art championship for high school students. Combining the word for “blackboard” ("kokuban") and the famous stadium where high school baseball is contested, the contest attracts artworks, all drawn on blackboards, usually over summer break, from about 300 high schools and junior high schools.

Each work — many dazzling in their artistry and often dreamlike themes — is a collaborative endeavor bringing together anywhere from one or two youngsters to dozens, all delivering a lesson in creativity and teamwork.

The images range from energetic depictions of dinosaurs, dogs and whales; popular manga scenes; Hokusai ’s Mount Fuji or the Mona Lisa, as well as slices of everyday life, except they aren’t all that everyday, such as an underwater classroom.

Some works even show a person writing on a blackboard.

Innovative and experimental art

Kazunari Minamishima, an art teacher at the Saitama Prefectural High School of the Arts, whose students have taken part in the contest, believes it appeals to students because it offers the chance to be more experimental than established forms of art, such as oil painting and sculpture.

“It’s still a work in progress,” he said.

The contest began in 2015 by Nichigaku Co., a Tokyo-based blackboard maker. The annual judging is done by examining the photos of the works, given that the medium, blackboards, can’t be moved easily. The winners will be announced in November.

The use of blackboards for creating artworks existed before in the Japanese school system. It was a stunning replica of Da Vinci’s “Last Supper” by an unknown artist on a school blackboard that caught Nichigaku’s eye.

“Back then, there was graffiti, but there was no genre called blackboard art,” said Nichigaku President Tomohiro Yoshida.

The contest doesn’t really work as a direct marketing tool because schools already have blackboards. But some contestants become professional artists later, Yoshida added proudly.

Chalk powder gets scattered over the blackboard for an almost stardust effect. Smudging with fingers and tissue paper creates shadows and muted tones.

A skilled blackboard artist can depict the shiny translucence of a dragon’s eyeball. One award-winning work used chalk powder mixed in water sprayed a la Jackson Pollock.

‘Better friends while doing it’

All schools in Japan can enter the Kokuban Art Koshien contest, including international schools. Nichigaku hopes the contest can expand overseas some day.

But unlike the paint-on-walls graffiti of the West, blackboards can be erased. The students get permission from the schools to draw on the blackboards in advance, reflective of Japan’s conformist orderly culture.

“The challenge of trying to sort out the conflicting opinions of my two collaborators is the biggest memory about taking part in blackboard Koshien, as opposed to doing your own artwork,” said Kento Misumi, who took part in the contest as a high school student and now works at Nichigaku.

It’s harder than you think, and he and his friends devoted several days to one drawing, Misumi recalled, demonstrating how to draw an apple with chalk on a blackboard.

“I want young people today to go through the experience,” he said.

It was exactly the kind of brainstorming that was going on among a huddle of several students at the Kumagaya Girls' High School, north of Tokyo, in nearby Saitama Prefecture.

They were taking part in the contest for the first time, although their upper grade schoolmates have taken part and won prizes in the past.

“I see it as a chance to deepen my relationships with my schoolmates,” said Chiho Ninomiya, one of the students. “It's our first time so I'm not sure we will be able to do a good job. But even if we don't win, it'd have been worth it as long as we become better friends while doing it.”

Lesson on the impermanence of life

Among the ideas discussed for this year's entries were what they called parodies or spinoffs of well-known artworks like Renoir, juxtaposed with images of high school students in their uniforms, their skirts fluttering.

A blackboard may be a longtime familiar object in classrooms. But drawing art on them with chalk is different from using paints or pencils, Ninomiya said, so they are still learning, drawing, rubbing, wiping.

It can be heartbreaking when the arduously created pieces get erased. But the artists are able to share that heartbreak with their collaborators.

Proponents say it’s a great educational tool to deliver the lesson on the impermanence of life, the fragility of creation and the courage to keep going. For when the work gets erased is the moment that the art is considered to be truly complete.

News.content:

Donald Trump’s administration has admitted that it canceled a block of roughly $7.5 billion in Biden-era clean energy funding “based solely” on the fact the money was flowing to projects in Democratic-led states.

The cuts were not based on “any programmatic, statutory, cost-reduction, or performance-based factor,” the Department of Energy conceded last week as part of early negotiations in a federal lawsuit from University of California researchers.

Instead, the grants were included on a list of cancellations announced in October “based solely on the political identity of the grant recipient’s state, i.e., whether the recipient’s location and/or place of performance was in a Blue State or a non-Blue State.”

The department added that with one exception, 284 terminated grants were slated to fund projects in Democratic-led states or states that voted for Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris in 2024. The roughly 340 grants that survived the chopping block were “in a state that awarded its electoral votes to President Trump in the 2024 election” or had at least one Republican senator, according to court filings.

The admission set off anger on Capitol Hill.

open image in gallery The Trump administration admitted to cutting billions in clean energy funding because projects were located in Democrat-led states ( Getty )

“This Administration has now admitted in court what has long been obvious: it terminated nearly 300 cost-cutting energy projects for no reason other than the fact that the states they were in did not vote for the President in the 2024 election,” Democratic lawmakers wrote in a statement.

“This is an astounding admission that the President and his team corruptly abused their power to kill good jobs and punish hard-working families because of their political views,” they said.

The Independent has contacted the Energy Department for comment.

The striking admission follows the Trump administration’s previous claims that the cuts were not influenced by politics and were instead aimed at ensuring federal funds flowed to effective and reliable energy projects.

“President Trump promised to protect taxpayer dollars and expand America’s supply of affordable, reliable, and secure energy,” Energy Secretary Chris Wright said in a statement in October.

The Department of Energy added at the time that its review sought to “identify waste” and “safeguard taxpayer dollars.”

open image in gallery The White House has pushed to give political appointees more influence over awarding federal funding, a move critics warn would undermine the process and expose it to partisanship ( AP )

Elsewhere in the lawsuit, which was filed last year, the Trump administration admitted to using keywords related to diversity, gender, vaccine hesitancy, and COVID-19 to guide cuts that canceled nearly $2 billion in grants to the University of California.

Around the time the energy grants were canceled, top Trump administration figures used highly partisan language to describe the effort, which was announced the same day as a government shutdown began.

Russell Vought, director of the White House Office of Management and Budget, wrote on social media that “nearly $8 billion in Green New Scam funding to fuel the Left's climate agenda is being cancelled.”

The following day, Trump, who moved to slash billions in funding for projects in Democratic states during the shutdown, shared a video on Truth Social depicting Vought as the Grim Reaper, soundtracked by a song that warned Democrats the administration was “gonna tie your hands.”

Secretary Wright has denied partisan politics influenced the funding review.

open image in gallery Republicans gutted the Biden administration’s signature clean energy law, even though investment and incentives largely flowed to red states ( Getty )

“No decisions were made on politics,” he testified to members of Congress last month. “I keep hearing that charge. It’s bull****. We’re going to say it a million times.”

A spokesperson for the department told The New York Times on Friday that the initial review of grants, which was later submitted to the White House for further consideration, was apolitical, and that the secretary’s testimony remained accurate.

The allegations of political favoritism in the federal funding process are somewhat ironic, given that the Biden administration’s landmark climate funding law steered investments and incentives towards largely Republican-held districts, a move that advocates hoped would ensure the Inflation Reduction Act proved politically durable.

Instead, Republicans in Congress have gutted the law.

Renewed scrutiny into the grant process comes as the Trump administration is pushing to give political appointees more authority to award federal grants, rather than the current expert-led, peer-review system used in many science- and defense-related opportunities.

“This proposed rule would essentially undermine that process by adding a layer of political review that could undo scientific recommendations for reasons that have nothing to do with science,” Heather Pierce. senior director of science policy at the Association of American Medical Colleges, recently told NPR of the proposal.

Refugees and activists are alarmed about a reported effort by the federal government to begin interviewing hundreds of Afghans in the U.S., fearing sensitive information gathered by immigration officials will be used to fuel future deportations.

The Office of Refugee Resettlement is reportedly seeking to interview roughly 800 Afghans brought to the U.S. for what the agency called a “wellbeing initiative” focused on assessing “common challenges” among Afghan refugees who may be in “vulnerable situations.”

The alleged effort, according to a July 14 email to ORR staff obtained by The Washington Post, includes asking respondents about their identities, assimilation into American culture and the immigration status of each member of their household. The questionnaire also reportedly includes a notice that answers are not anonymous and information shared with interviewers could be retained for 15 years.

The survey calls have likely already begun, one activist group told The Independent.

The interviews may have started as early as this Thursday, according to Shawn VanDiver, founder of the advocacy group #AfghanEvac. It remains unclear how the information would be used, prompting concern among advocacy groups given the vulnerable status of Afghan immigrants in the U.S.

open image in gallery The Trump administration is reportedly launching an effort to interview hundreds of Afghan refugees living in the U.S., in what community members fear is an attempt to power future deportations ( via REUTERS )

“There’s no good reason for them to be doing this,” VanDiver told The Independent. “They don’t care about the welfare of Afghans. ... Everything that this administration has done with them has been to cause harm, has been to throw them out of the country.”

“This is a group that has seen nearly every pathway closed to them, and holds dwindling hope for reuniting with their families,” Beth Oppenheim, CEO of the refugee advocacy group HIAS, told The Independent in a statement.

“Every moment for them is fraught with uncertainty, and the potential for even more fear as a result,” she added. “We want everyone we welcome into this country to feel safe, and we need to remember the distrust that closed doors and blocked pathways create for people when we ask them to be vulnerable again and again.”

VanDiver added that he has been hearing from sources within the administration that the interview program has “nefarious” intentions.

ORR, which operates under Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., “is strengthening its efforts to ensure that the populations it serves receive the services funded by American taxpayers,” the Administration for Children and Families told The Independent in a statement.

“The agency is actively conducting outreach to connect eligible individuals with ORR-funded services and will continue those efforts for the duration of their eligibility,” the agency said.

The agency added that ORR “works closely with its federal law enforcement partners” and is required by law to share information “regarding individuals involved in suspected criminal activity.”

The Independent has contacted the Department of Homeland Security for comment.

open image in gallery Critics accuse the Trump administration of mistreating Afghans in the U.S., pointing to the death of Mohammad Nazeer Paktiawal in ICE detention and the decision to strip away emergency protections from Afghan refugees ( Courtesy of #AfghanEvac )

Advocates have repeatedly voiced concern about Donald Trump’s record towards Afghans so far.

Over the last year-and-a-half, the administration has frozen refugee resettlement from most countries, stripped Afghan refugees in the U.S. of emergency protected status, paused new visas for Afghans and banned travel from Afghanistan to the U.S.

The White House has also left more than 1,000 people in limbo at a refugee center in Qatar. The group was originally taken there under the Biden administration after the fall of Kabul in 2021 as part of his effort to resettle Afghans who partnered with U.S. forces.

The administration has floated a plan to send the people there to the Democratic Republic of Congo.

“Kinshasa won’t kill him on Day One, but the State Department knows there’s no community for him there, no legal status, and no real protection for him or for the children traveling with these families,” retired U.S. Marine Corps Gunnery Sgt. Sean Jamshid, whose brother was being held at the center, told reporters in April. “They know they are offering him an option they know will be refused, just so they can say they tried. This is not a real choice. This is not policy. This is theater.”

Advocates have also accused the Trump administration of mistreating those already in detention.

In March, Mohammad Nazeer Paktiawal, who fought alongside U.S special forces, died within one day of entering Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention. The death was caused by an adverse drug reaction to an unidentified substance, according to his death certificate.

“We do not understand. What kind of accident takes a healthy 41-year-old man who was in the care of the United States government? We have so many questions, and almost no answers,” his family said in a statement after the death. “Nazeer was a person. He was loved. He still is. He deserved more than a single word.”

Late last year, reports emerged that the Trump administration was planning to re-interview and potentially revoke the status of hundreds of thousands of refugees admitted to the U.S. during the Biden administration.

A November memo signed by Joseph Edlow, director of U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, orders the agency to review and re-interview all of the roughly 233,000 refugees who were admitted to the country between January 20, 2021, and February 20, 2025, and blocks processing of green card applications from refugees admitted during that time period.

This story was updated on July 24, 2026, to feature the correct spelling of #AfghanEvac founder Shawn VanDiver’s name.

Volodymyr Zelensky has denied taking cocaine with French president Emmanuel Macron in a bizarre interview with an American far-right MAGA influencer.

Laura Loomer, a close ally of Donald Trump and an ardent conspiracy theorist, travelled to meet the Ukrainian president and witness the impact of the war in Kyiv, after spending the last three years downplaying Russia’s invasion.

Ms Loomer, who has two million followers on X, had previously labelled Ukraine a “country full of Nazi apologists” and had claimed that they were being led “by a Jihadi apologist”.

However, the hardline right-wing activist has changed her stance in recent months and met with Mr Zelensky at the Marrinsky Palace, telling him: “I’ve come to realise that I was bamboozled by Russian propaganda and I came to believe a lot of untrue things about Ukraine.”

open image in gallery MAGA far-right influencer Laura Loomer interviewed Zelensky in Kyiv ( AP )

Rumours about Mr Zelensky taking Class A drugs with Mr Macron were amplified by Tucker Carlson, a fellow figure on America’s right who carried out a sit-down interview with Russian president Vladimir Putin in 2024.

When asked about the story, the Ukrainian leader laughed and replied: “Of course not”.

Ms Loomer’s shifting position on the war in Europe reflects the growing impatience among the Trump administration and Washington over Moscow’s actions and their lack of readiness to negotiate a peace deal.

In response to Russian propaganda of Nazism in his country, Mr Zelensky explained the history of Soviet persecution of Judaism in Ukraine and stressed: “We are not Nazis”.

He also said that he is due to visit Washington next week for the funeral of Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, and is expecting to see Mr Trump.

The relationship between the two leaders has been fraught with tension over the years, resulting in a shouting match in the Oval Office where Mr Zelensky was criticised for not wearing a suit.

However, he told Ms Loomer that now the relationship is “better and really good” since they met in the Vatican last year.

The pair spoke for around 15 minutes inside St Peter’s Basilica ahead of the funeral of Pope Francis.

open image in gallery Mr Zelensky said his relationship improved with the US president after their meeting at the Vatican ( Ukraine Foreign Affair Ministry )

“The tone has changed, absolutely,” he told Ms Loomer in response to a question about the shift in dynamic. “We had [a] first changing moment in Rome. It was not a long meeting but I always said it was this historic moment because we changed the relations during 15 to 20 minutes.

“Nobody was around us and I was very happy to hear the president. Let it be between the two of us but it was very good when we calmed down. I was very happy because a lot of life depends on relations.”

As well as speaking to Mr Zelensky, the MAGA influencer also travelled around the city, which included visiting a McDonald’s scarred by shrapnel from a Russian missile strike.

In a video recorded from inside a church, Loomer accused Mr Putin of hypocrisy by portraying Russia as pro-Christian.

“I just don’t think that you should be allowed to say that you’re protecting Christianity if you’re trying to drone strike Jesus Christ," she said.

Andy Burnham has ruled out a snap general election, saying it would “postpone that essential work” of implementing his own version of Labour’s 2024 manifesto.

On Friday, the prime minister opened a new headquarters for the centre of Government in Manchester, which has been named ‘No 10 North’.

Mr Burnham is expected to work at No 10 North, at Heron House in Manchester, once each week during his premiership, as part of his move to push power out of Westminster.

During an interview with Manchester Evening News, the former mayor insisted he would not call an election, having entered Downing Street on Monday after a rapid climb to power.

He said: “No I’m not. I don’t think that is right.

“We live in a parliamentary democracy. There was a manifesto in 2024. I’m sticking to that manifesto. I’m bringing forward my version but it is still within that manifesto. I just think that we need to focus on making the country work.

open image in gallery The prime minister opened the new No 10 North in Manchester ( Getty )

“That is the biggest priority right now. A general election would postpone that essential work. I’m also trying to do politics differently, as I did when I was mayor of Greater Manchester.”

He added that although he was relishing his new role as PM, he missed being the mayor of Greater Manchester, which famously earned him the moniker ‘King of the North’.

During a speech to his team and members of the media, Mr Burnham said he wants to “get Britain hoping again” and described opening the new base as the “best day of my life”.

He said it was a “full circle” experience for him, as he had to leave the North West to start his career.

Mr Burnham added: “And it’s true of places all over the country to get on in life, you had to leave where you where you were because things weren’t here.

“The country has always been a little like that, hasn’t it?

“That opportunity has not been evenly spread around the country, and not all places have felt that they are part of the national story, and that is what this Government is going to work every single day to change.

open image in gallery Mr Burnham (centre) is set on splitting his time between London and Manchester ( PA )

“And that is what No 10 North is all about: putting power in every postcode so that people can turn things around for themselves and make changes, just as this great city has done, and the other English cities are doing through devolution, turning things round because of that ability to be able to do more for themselves.”

The prime minister insisted No 10 North was key to getting “good growth going in every part of the country”.

Mr Burnham also spoke about wanting to create a “one-team feeling” across the whole of the UK, and insisted No 10 North was “as much for Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland, as it is for the regions of England”.

The new Prime Minister met face-to-face for the first time on Thursday with Scottish first minister John Swinney, and told him that another independence referendum is “off limits”.

He also met with Wales’s first minister Rhun ap Iorwerth in Glasgow, who pushed for the Welsh Government to be given the same devolved powers as those available to Scotland, including over rail, policing, justice and the Crown Estate.

Concluding his speech at No 10 North, Mr Burnham railed against critics – “often London based” – who he claimed will see the project as a “gimmick”.

The Metropolitan Police are intensifying their efforts against illegal e-bikes and e-scooters by deploying new testing kits across London.

It comes as the force reports a record number of seizures in 2026.

The crackdown aims to curb their use in criminal activities, particularly phone theft.

As part of Operation Lexand, officers seized 29 e-bikes and seven e-scooters near Tottenham Court Road Station on Friday.

This targeted action forms part of a broader Metropolitan Police initiative to tackle phone theft and neighbourhood crime, marking the seventh such operation this year, with five more planned throughout the summer.

So far in 2026, the project has led to the seizure of over 2,500 illegal electric two-wheelers, surpassing the 2,241 impounded in the entirety of 2025.

open image in gallery As part of Operation Lexand, officers seized 29 e-bikes and seven e-scooters near Tottenham Court Road Station on Friday ( Ben Whitley/PA Wire )

The force is utilising innovative "rolling roads" technology to efficiently identify non-compliant vehicles. These portable Dynostar and Wenger test kits act as treadmills, quickly measuring whether e-bikes or e-scooters can propel themselves faster than the legal limit of 15.5mph through electrically assisted pedals, batteries, or throttles. The Met and Nottinghamshire Police are currently the only forces in the country to deploy this advanced equipment.

During the operation, officers stationed at two stop sites near Tottenham Court Road – an area identified for its disproportionately high e-bike traffic and associated crime rates – used plain-clothed colleagues to assist in pulling over users. Each test took approximately one minute, with drivers typically held for no more than 15 minutes.

If a vehicle was found to be too fast, or if drivers lacked proper licensing or insurance, the bikes were impounded. Owners are given 14 days to provide the correct documentation before the vehicles are stripped for recyclable parts and destroyed.

open image in gallery Police are using portable Dynostar and Wenger test kits that act as treadmills, quickly measuring whether e-bikes or e-scooters can propel themselves faster than the legal limit of 15.5mph ( Ben Whitley/PA Wire )

Commander Neerav Patel, overseeing the operation, highlighted the public's frustration. He told the Press Association: "We’ve heard loud and clear that Londoners are fed up of the criminal and antisocial use of e-bikes. We recognise that the use of e-bikes [can be] perfectly legitimate, but there are a vast number of people intent on using e-bikes for criminal and anti-social uses. We know that e-bikes are used in phone snatches, particularly in this part of London."

Two arrests were made during the Friday operation, one for assaulting an emergency worker and another for public order offences, theft, and recall to prison.

The Met claims the crackdown is yielding significant results, both statistically and in public perception. Commander Patel added: "What we are doing is clearly working. Phone theft in the West End, increasingly perpetrated by thieves riding illegal e-bikes, has nearly halved. We’ll continue to do everything we can to make London an even safer city for everyone to enjoy."

Superintendent Luke Baldock, second-in-command, noted a marked difference in public reaction. He said: "Usually we get a lot of grief when we’re out like this but it’s been night and day. Just speaking to the members of the public passing by, everyone is saying thank goodness you’re doing something about this."

open image in gallery This targeted action forms part of a broader Metropolitan Police initiative to tackle phone theft and neighbourhood crime, marking the seventh such operation this year, with five more planned throughout the summer ( Ben Whitley/PA Wire )

He explained that public consultations consistently identified "speed bikes" as a major concern due to their danger and role in enabling other crimes like robbery.

"We’re using the ‘rolling road’ solution. That means we’re detecting more illegal e-bikes [and it’s] allowing us to seize many more," he added.

Some seized bikes, from brands including Engwe, Fiido, Hitway, and Super73, were found to be capable of speeds exceeding 27 miles per hour. The Met attributes a reduction in local crime to these seizures, reporting a 14% decrease in neighbourhood offences in London over the 12 months to June compared to the previous year, equating to 35,000 fewer reported offences.

This includes 23,311 fewer thefts from person (down 23%) and 2,943 fewer personal robberies (11% lower). Looking ahead, Mr Baldock revealed discussions with charities and prisons to involve young people in disassembling seized bikes, while Mr Patel mentioned ongoing educational work with the gig economy.

News.content:
