Jorge David Núñez Aguilar, 31, known as “Coco Pastilla,” is considered the head of a group linked to the intellectual authorship of the killing of Geiner Zamora Hidalgo, the deputy chief of the OIJ’s Guápiles delegation, who was shot outside a restaurant in January 2025 and died days later. Núñez, a native of Pococí with a registered address in Guácimo, had been sought by the Judicial Police since that killing. A fourth suspect, identified by the surnames Ríos Oconitrillo and the alias “Coco Guácimo,” died during the operation after being shot by tactical officers, Soto said.

Agents seized five high-caliber rifles at the scene, including weapons of the AK-47 type, along with three pistols. Investigators also recovered drone equipment that the group is believed to have used to monitor the approaches to the property and complicate any police advance. Infobae reported that a FAL rifle was among the weapons recovered, a detail not carried by other outlets.

Arias Monge walked out of prison on October 28, 2016, after completing a period of preventive detention as a suspect in two homicide cases. He was subsequently declared in rebellion after failing to appear for trial, and his whereabouts remained unknown until Friday. Over the intervening years, authorities came to attribute to him as many as 100 killings, along with attempted homicides, drug trafficking, cattle theft and money laundering. The OIJ has also said he issued threats against police officers, including recordings in which he offered payment for the killing of agents. None of these allegations has been tested at trial, and the cases against him remain at the pre-trial stage.

Investigators had long placed him in the Guápiles area of Pococí, moving through rural terrain toward the northern border. Soto said in earlier interviews that Arias Monge relied on a small circle of people loyal to him to move undetected, and that the Judicial Police made more than ten attempts to detain him during 2024 alone. The Drug Enforcement Administration and Costa Rican authorities have identified cells operated by his network across all seven of the country’s provinces, with recent reporting placing its activity in the Caribbean, Sarapiquí, the northern zone, Pococí and Turrialba.

Soto has also cautioned that the figure of “Diablo” grew larger than the man. He has described the name functioning as a kind of franchise within criminal networks, used by others to frighten or extort victims, and has said a degree of mythology built up around him.

The case drew unusual attention from Washington. On April 30, 2025, the State Department’s Bureau of International Narcotics and Law Enforcement Affairs announced a reward of up to $500,000, roughly ₡250 million, under its Transnational Organized Crime Rewards Program, for information leading to the arrest or conviction of Arias Monge in any country. The offer, coordinated with the DEA, followed a series of meetings between the agency and Costa Rica’s Attorney General’s Office and OIJ. It is the largest reward the United States has offered for a Costa Rican national.

The State Department described him as the head of a violent transnational criminal organization and Costa Rica’s most wanted fugitive, wanted on multiple Costa Rican warrants for drug trafficking, robbery, aggravated homicide and money laundering. The DEA has said he conspired with traffickers to move multi-hundred-kilogram loads, or several hundred pounds, of cocaine from Colombia through Central America and Mexico toward the United States.

Speaking after the operation, Soto used the capture to argue for stronger funding for the judiciary, noting that his officers confronted an increasingly well-armed organization. The government of Laura Fernández announced in June a proposed reduction of ₡3.053 billion to the Judicial Branch’s 2026 budget, a cut the OIJ has said would constrain its capacity to carry out raids, conduct criminal analysis and protect victims.

Friday’s operation follows a sustained push against the network in recent weeks, including the July 9 detention of an alleged principal operator known as “Guato” in a mountainous area of Valle La Estrella. The OIJ said it would release further details in the coming hours on the circumstances of the detention and the condition of the wounded officers.

World.title: Costa Rica Betting Operation Lands California Man in Federal Prison
World.content:
A California man who survived an assassination attempt outside an Escazú café more than a decade ago has been sentenced to federal prison for running an illegal gambling and money laundering operation out of Costa Rica. Jason Noah Feinman, 52, of Calabasas, received 27 months on June 9 in federal court in Los Angeles after pleading guilty in January to one count each of tax evasion, operating an illegal gambling business, and money laundering. A federal judge also ordered him to pay more than $1.3 million (about ₡589 million) in restitution and a $150,000 (₡68 million) fine, plus interest.

According to the Justice Department, Feinman operated a Costa Rica–based business that ran a website unlicensed bookmakers used to take wagers, including from bettors living in California, in violation of both state and federal law. The platform was a service layer for other operators rather than a consumer-facing sportsbook, and court filings do not name the business. Prosecutors say Feinman then laundered the cash the operation generated by converting it into checks made out to himself or his companies.

The mechanics were straightforward and repetitive. Between May 18, 2018 and January 2, 2024, the Justice Department says, Feinman handed a single customer more than $1.5 million (₡680 million) in cash and received 18 checks payable to him or his businesses for the equivalent amount, one of them for $200,000. Court filings identify that customer only by the initials C.K. and describe checks whose memo lines frequently referenced loans. Across the life of the operation, prosecutors say Feinman exchanged between $1.5 million and $3.5 million (₡680 million to ₡1.59 billion) in cash for checks.

The tax case ran alongside it. Feinman reported no taxable income to the Internal Revenue Service on his 2020 return and paid nothing that year, despite earning roughly $1.8 million (₡815 million), according to the Justice Department. Between 2018 and 2022 he evaded taxes on approximately $4.2 million (₡1.9 billion) in income, a loss to the United States that prosecutors put at about $1.52 million (₡689 million).

Assistant Attorney General Colin McDonald of the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division and First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bilal A. Essayli for the Central District of California announced the sentence. IRS Criminal Investigation and Homeland Security Investigations conducted the investigation, and Trial Attorneys John C. Gerardi and Charles A. O’Reilly of the Criminal Division’s Tax Section prosecuted the case. The Fraud Division was created on April 7 and counts the case among its early results.

Feinman’s history in Costa Rica predates the gambling charges and includes a considerably more violent episode. In 2015 he was ambushed by gunmen on a motorcycle as he left a parking lot in Escazú, struck by nine rounds, and survived. Two men, Ricardo Francisco Solís Méndez and Steven Javier Calvo Sánchez, were tried at the Pavas courts for attempted homicide in a case that rested heavily on Feinman’s own identification of his attackers, which his attorney Miguel Jiménez Cerros said the American made on three separate occasions.

During the trial, two parking attendants who witnessed the shooting testified they had heard gunfire but could offer nothing further, with one telling the court he had a family. Jiménez Cerros said at the time that his client’s next objective was helping investigators identify whoever ordered the attack, a question the proceedings never resolved.

The case is not an outlier. In October 2025, Christopher Scott King, 51, of Santa Monica was sentenced to 21 months after admitting he ran an unlicensed bookmaking operation from Los Angeles County using a Costa Rica–based sports betting website to take wagers from California bettors. Prosecutors said King concealed $13.6 million (₡6.16 billion) in income from the IRS between 2019 and 2022 and laundered proceeds through real estate development and gold purchases.

He was ordered to forfeit $10 million (₡4.53 billion) and pay $3.8 million (₡1.72 billion) in restitution. A year earlier, Matthew Bowyer of Orange County pleaded guilty to running a betting ring that moved wagers through Costa Rican websites and casino agents, an operation whose clients included Ippei Mizuhara, the former interpreter for Los Angeles Dodgers star Shohei Ohtani, who placed roughly 19,000 bets through it.

The pattern that emerges from these prosecutions is consistent enough to be a template. American operators establish the technical and administrative side of a bookmaking business in Costa Rica, where offering online betting services to customers abroad occupies a permissive regulatory space and has supported a substantial data-processing sector for years, then use that infrastructure to reach bettors in states where the activity is plainly illegal.

What repeatedly ends these operations is not the betting itself but what happens to the cash afterward. In Feinman’s case it was checks. In King’s it was property and gold. In each, the proceeds eventually had to enter a banking system, and that is where IRS Criminal Investigation found them.

For the thousands of foreign residents working in or around Costa Rica’s online gaming and call center industry, the distinction that matters is jurisdictional rather than technical. Costa Rica does not license offshore sportsbooks in the way Curaçao or Malta do, and companies here have historically operated under ordinary commercial registration on the understanding that no bets are accepted from within the country.

That arrangement offers no protection whatsoever from United States law when American customers are on the other end of the transaction, and the last three years of federal sentencings suggest prosecutors have become considerably more systematic about following the money back to its source.

World.title: October court date set for Elvira Mulholland; accused of attempting to murder her husband
World.content:
October court date set for Elvira Mulholland; accused of attempting to murder her husband

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A tentative October 2, 2026 court date has been set in the attempted murder case against Elvira Mulholland, who is accused of shooting her husband during a domestic dispute in 2024.

Mulholland appeared before Justice Candace Nanton in the High Court on Friday, represented by attorney Dr. Lynden Jones. She remains out on High Court bail.

The defence informed the court that Mulholland is also currently on trial in the Magistrate’s Court for an alleged robbery arising from the same incident. That trial, which began in April, is scheduled to continue on August 3.

Justice Nanton adjourned the attempted murder matter until October 2 for a case management conference, by which time the lower court proceedings are expected to have concluded. A firm trial date could then be determined.

Police allege that on October 25, 2024, Mulholland followed her husband, Jeffrey Mulholland, along the Coastal Road, ran his pickup truck off the road and shot him with his own licensed firearm following a struggle.

She was committed to stand trial in the High Court after a preliminary inquiry concluded in July 2025.

World.title: Collin Francis found stable to stand trial for murder of Nestor Vasquez Jr. but Court says it won’t accept just one evaluation
World.content:
Collin Francis found stable to stand trial for murder of Nestor Vasquez Jr. but Court says it won’t accept just one evaluation

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The murder case against Collin Francis Jr. could take a significant turn when it returns to the High Court on Tuesday, July 28, 2026.

Francis had previously been found unfit to enter a plea and was ordered to undergo psychiatric evaluations every six months for two years. However, Justice Nigel Pilgrim was informed on Friday that only one evaluation had been completed.

The June 29, 2026 report, prepared by psychiatrist Dr. Denethia Usher, found that Francis is now stable, taking his medication and considered fit to enter a plea. The report also noted that his condition had improved while he was away from marijuana.

The prosecution indicated that the Director of Public Prosecutions’ office was prepared to proceed to trial. Justice Pilgrim, however, said he would not allow the case to proceed to trial based solely on the single evaluation.

The judge asked whether the prosecution would consider accepting a guilty plea, but the Crown said instructions would first have to be obtained from the DPP.

Francis is charged with the 2019 murder of 60-year-old Nestor Vasquez Jr., who was fatally injured while the two men were detained in a cell at the Queen Street Police Station.

The matter was adjourned until Tuesday for the prosecution to indicate how it intends to proceed.

World.title: BDF volunteer soldier Mark Nolberto sentenced to nearly 18 Years for raping 17-year-old girl and videoing it; Says his sentence is ‘unjust’
World.content:
BDF volunteer soldier Mark Nolberto sentenced to nearly 18 Years for raping 17-year-old girl and videoing it; Says his sentence is ‘unjust’

By Breaking Belize News Staff: High Court Justice Candace Nanton today sentenced 31-year-old Belize Defence Force (BDF) volunteer soldier Mark Anthony Nolberto to 17 years, 10 months, and 3 weeks in prison following his conviction on two counts of rape against a 17-year-old girl.

Justice Nanton ordered that the sentences for both counts run concurrently. In addition to his prison term, Nolberto must undergo counseling as well as medical and psychiatric treatment while incarcerated. Upon his release, he will be legally required to report his residential address to the Commissioner of Police and the Department of Human Development.

The convictions stem from an incident where Nolberto struck the minor with a metal cup, forced her into his residence, subjected her to physical and sexual assault, and recorded the act on his mobile phone—video footage that was later extracted by police and presented as evidence in court.

In delivering the sentence, Justice Nanton classified the harm as severe and noted the high degree of offender culpability, pointing to the victim’s age, the violent nature of the attack, and Nolberto’s lack of remorse throughout the trial. Starting from a 19-year baseline, the judge deducted two years for Nolberto’s prior lack of a criminal record and community service, added one year to reflect the overall severity of the crime, and credited 40 days for time served on remand.

Defense attorney Orson “OJ” Elrington had requested a suspended sentence, but Justice Nanton rejected the plea, citing statutory laws that restrict suspended sentences to offenses carrying maximum terms of three years or less. Under Belizean law, rape carries a mandatory minimum sentence of eight years in prison up to life imprisonment. The prosecution was led by Crown Counsel Joseph Perez.

Following the sentencing, Nolberto maintained his innocence as he was escorted from the High Court, telling reporters that he refused to cover his face because he believed the conviction was “unjust.”

World.title: What is your child doing this Summer? Making memories, Learning new skills or scrolling social media?
World.content:
What is your child doing this Summer? Making memories, Learning new skills or scrolling social media?

By Zoila Palma: With schools closed for the summer break, children and teenagers across Belize have more free time on their hands.

For parents, this can be a valuable opportunity to encourage their children to explore new interests, develop practical skills and build meaningful relationships.

But it also raises an important question: How are our children spending their summer vacation?

Across the country, organizations, churches, schools and community groups offer summer camps and activities designed to keep young people engaged and learning.

From Youth in Agriculture Summer Camps that introduce children to farming, livestock and food production, to Vacation Bible Schools that focus on faith, values and fellowship, there are opportunities for children to learn outside the traditional classroom.

Sports camps, arts programs and other youth activities also allow children to discover talents and interests they may not have had the chance to explore during the school year.

Summer is also a chance for children to gain experiences that cannot always be taught in a classroom.

A child who participates in an agriculture camp may learn how to care for animals, grow food and understand where the food on their plate comes from.

Another child attending a Bible school may strengthen their faith and develop important values, while sports and creative programs can teach teamwork, discipline and confidence.

These experiences can help shape a child’s character and expose them to possibilities that could influence their future.

Parents can also use this time to consider how much time their children are spending on social media, video games and their phones.

Technology has its benefits, but unlimited screen time can quickly consume an entire summer if there are no boundaries.

Instead of allowing children to spend hours scrolling through TikTok, Instagram or other platforms, parents can encourage a healthier balance that includes reading, learning, helping at home, spending time outdoors and participating in activities that challenge them.

Summer vacation should not mean that learning comes to a complete stop.

Are our children taking advantage of every opportunity to learn something new, make friends and develop skills, or are they spending most of their days online?

A summer filled with new experiences, learning and positive activities can create memories that last a lifetime—and perhaps even inspire a child to discover a passion that shapes their future.

World.title: International News: Western Europe records hottest June ever as extreme heat fuels wildfires
World.content:
International News: Western Europe records hottest June ever as extreme heat fuels wildfires

By Zoila Palma: Western Europe experienced its hottest June on record in 2026, with extreme temperatures affecting large parts of the region and contributing to wildfires, drought and serious health risks.

According to the Copernicus Climate Change Service, the region recorded an average temperature of 20.74°C, which was 3.05°C above the 1991–2020 average and surpassed the previous record set in June 2025.

The heatwave continued into July, with Spain’s Fabra Observatory in Barcelona recording 40.5°C on July 8, the highest temperature recorded there in more than a century. France also issued widespread heat alerts amid high fire danger caused by drought, extreme temperatures and low humidity, while devastating wildfires affected parts of France and the Iberian Peninsula.

Temperature records were broken across several European countries during June.

Germany recorded 41.7°C in Coschen on June 28, while Hungary reached 40.7°C, Austria 40°C and the United Kingdom recorded 37.3°C in southern England. France experienced its hottest day on record on June 24, with temperatures reaching 43.8°C in Palluau, while Spain’s Bilbao reached a record 42.7°C for June.

Health officials warned that prolonged extreme heat, particularly when nighttime temperatures remain high, can place severe stress on the body. Older adults, young children, pregnant women, outdoor workers, people experiencing homelessness and those living with chronic illnesses are among those most at risk.

The extreme heat was also accompanied by widespread dryness, worsening drought conditions and increased wildfire activity across parts of Europe.

World.title: International News: Former President Hernández to return to Honduras after Trump pardon, challenge local charges
World.content:
International News: Former President Hernández to return to Honduras after Trump pardon, challenge local charges

By Zoila Palma: Former Honduran President Juan Orlando Hernández is set to return to Honduras on Sunday and seek the dismissal of separate fraud and money-laundering charges that were not covered by the pardon he received from U.S. President Donald Trump.

Hernández, who was released after Trump pardoned his 45-year prison sentence for cocaine trafficking in the United States, said he expects to begin legal proceedings in Honduras in early August.

He maintains his innocence and has argued that the local case was politically motivated, adding that he has already requested that the arrest warrant against him be dropped, Reuters report.

The former president faces the Honduran charges in connection with the Pandora II case, which investigated alleged corruption and the misuse of state funds.

Hernández, who governed Honduras from 2014 to 2022, was extradited to the United States in 2022 and convicted in 2024 after prosecutors accused him of facilitating the trafficking of hundreds of tons of cocaine.

He served less than two years of his sentence before Trump’s pardon.

World.title: International News: More than 21,000 Venezuelans displaced 1 month after earthquakes
World.content:
International News: More than 21,000 Venezuelans displaced 1 month after earthquakes

By Zoila Palma: One month after twin earthquakes devastated northern Venezuela, more than 21,000 people remain displaced and living in temporary shelters, while families continue searching for missing loved ones.

Humanitarian organizations warn that the disaster is quickly becoming a long-term recovery crisis that could take years to overcome.

More than 5,200 people have died and nearly 17,000 others have been injured, while the World Bank estimates the earthquakes caused $19.6 billion in direct physical damage.

Entire neighborhoods remain in ruins, with schools, hospitals, roads and businesses struggling to reopen.

Nearly 18,000 homes were reportedly destroyed or left uninhabitable, forcing thousands of families into shelters, schools, sports facilities and temporary camps, Latin Times reports.

Although formal search-and-rescue operations ended weeks ago, families in the hardest-hit areas, including La Guaira and neighboring states, continue to search for answers about missing relatives.

Aid workers say survivors are also facing shortages of housing, clean water, medical care and essential services, while overcrowded shelters and damaged infrastructure raise concerns about public health risks.

World.title: Ministry of Health and Wellness and Pan American Health Organization discuss Tobacco Control Bill
World.content:
Ministry of Health and Wellness and Pan American Health Organization discuss Tobacco Control Bill

By Zoila Palma: This week, the Ministry of Health & Wellness continued discussions with the visiting Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) country mission team on the next steps toward advancing the Tobacco Control Bill in Belize.

On July 20, 2026, a meeting was held by Minister of Health & Wellness, Kevin Bernard, along with the Ministry’s management team.

Discussions focused on public sensitization of the Tobacco Control Bill, tobacco taxation, and strengthening national capacity to support its implementation.

The Ministry says that it remains committed to working closely with PAHO and other partners to identify the support needed and determine the next steps toward the successful adaptation and implementation of the Tobacco Control Bill in Belize.

World.title: Market Bag: Soup vendor Bulbie shops for staples as prices fluctuate
World.content:
KINGSTON, Jamaica — Shoppers at the Coronation Market will encounter a mixed basket in terms of prices this week.

Persistent dry conditions continue to impact farming, pushing up the prices of some produce including tomatoes at $150 per pound, Scotch bonnet peppers at $350 per pound, sweet peppers at $400 per pound, bananas at $1,400 a dozen and lettuce at $700 per head.

Plantains ($700 for three) also continue to be a pricey commodity.

Still, other food items held steady or declined, including onions at $200 per pound.

In this week’s episode of Market Bag, popular soup vendor Nicardo “Bulbie” Sayer joins host Carlysia Ramdeen as he shops for the fresh ingredients behind his signature Bulbie Soups, a favourite among soup lovers.

Catch the latest episode of Market Bag on all Jamaica Observer digital platforms.

World.title: Rajindra Campbell signs with Nike
World.content:
Rajindra Campbell signs with Nike

KINGSTON, Jamaica — Jamaica’s 2024 Olympic shot put bronze medallist Rajindra Campbell has signed a contract with Nike.

The 30-year-old Campbell, who has always highlighted the plight of non-track athletes in surviving financially, made the revelation via social media earlier this week.

“The work behind the scenes is paying off, and I’m still building. The season isn’t over yet; the best is still to come. Happy to announce I will be continuing my journey as part of the Nike family, Nike Athlete,” Campbell posted on Instagram.

“From the indoor season to now, 2026 has been all about growth, consistency and progress. Every competition has been another opportunity to improve and compete with the best in the world,” he added.

Campbell was one of four Jamaicans who tried to switch allegiance to Turkey in 2025, citing the lack of financial support from Jamaican athletics administrators.

However, world governing body World Athletics rejected their applications.

In announcing the decision, the panel said approving the applications would undermine the intent of World Athletics’ eligibility and transfer-of-allegiance rules.

It found the requests were part of a coordinated recruitment effort by the Turkish Government, operating through a state-funded club, offering lucrative contracts to attract foreign athletes and enable them to compete for Turkey at major events, including the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics.

In 2024, Campbell accused the Jamaica Athletics Administrative Association (JAAA) of not caring about athletes, pointing to an eight-year US$40 million ($6.4 billion) Adidas contract which was turned down when the JAAA extended its contract with longtime sponsors Puma.

“I don’t believe that they really understand that it is challenging. For one, track and field, we are not sprinters, obviously, and as you can see, I am still unsponsored,” he said at the time.

World.title: $1.5-b pothole rescue
World.content:
Water has settled in this pothole on Fairdene Avenue in St Andrew on Thursday.

AS motorists across the island continue to face gaping potholes, minister with responsibility for works Robert Morgan has told the Jamaica Observer that the Cabinet on Monday approved a further $1.5-billion spend for patching and sheeting work on main roads across the island to bring some well-needed relief to drivers.

This brings the money allocated to tackle the persistent pothole problem to $3.1 billion for this fiscal year.

According to Morgan, the additional allocation was necessary based on the scope of the problem. He told the Observer that the money initially allocated for the pothole patching programme is already being spent.

“We are engaged in a $1.6-billion programme patching the roads. It’s really sheeting in many cases. Cabinet just approved another $1.5 billion to do more roads. We are doing the $1.6 billion now and then, before the end of the year, we are going to spend another $1.5 billion on road rehabilitation,” said Morgan.

But even as the minister promised relief, motorists across the Corporate Area were pointing the Observer to several roads where potholes are making driving almost impossible.

In downtown Kingston, where many large potholes pockmark the streets, motorists pointed to one on Orange Street, close to its intersection with Heywood Street, which they said is a source of frustration for many.

While an Observer news team was in the area on Thursday, motorists and pedestrians urged the team to take as many pictures and videos as possible to expose the failure of authorities to maintain roads.

In response, Morgan said that area could be fixed as early as next week as it is schduled for priority repairs.

He underscored that his ministry is responsible for fixing main roads through the National Works Agency, and not streets or lanes.

“Not all the roads are mine. I am strictly responsible for main roads; I am not responsible for avenues, lanes, and I am not responsible for crescents. I am not responsible for any of those community roads. None at all. My roads are roads like Washington Boulevard, Constant Spring and Barbican Road.

“Roads like Liguanea Avenue, Paddington Terrace, roads in Cherry Garden, and a lot of the community roads in downtown Kingston are not mine — they belong to the Kingston and St Andrew Municipal Corporation — but I have been getting blamed. Parish councils get a billion dollars a year and they need to fix those roads,” argued Morgan.

However residents of several Corporate Area communities only want their roads fixed, with no concern over which agency will do it.

On Fairdene Avenue in Ackee Walk, St Andrew, residents and passing motorists expressed their displeasure at the state of the road, which is littered with very deep and wide potholes..

“It is treacherous. It is dread. When the rain falls, pedestrians get splashed easily all the time. They need to fix the roads properly and done,” said one motorist.

He was supported by another motorist, who charged that the condition of the roads in Corporate Area forces drivers to make detours into areas where they would rather not drive.

In the meantime, one motorist complained about damage to his vehicle by the potholes.

“The road stay very bad, man. The road need to fix. It a mash up mi front end and we have to drive on the roads every day,” lamented the motorist.

World.title: Grief turns to protest in Troy
World.content:
Placard-bearing residents in Troy, Trelawny, on Thursday protesting againt the arrest of a man in connection with fatal mobbing following murder of 10-year-old Shani Coke.

TROY, Trelawny — Still mourning the murder of 10-year-old Shani “Kaidra” Coke on Tuesday residents of the usually quiet district took to the streets on Thursday after one of their own was reportedly arrested by the police in connection with the mob killing of the man believed to have attacked her.

According to residents the man was taken into custody by the police who are probing the death of Shani and the fatal attack on the suspected child killer Delroy Coke, and the brutal beating of his father.

The placard-bearing residents used debris to block the Troy main road — which links part of south Trelawny to northern Manchester — as they charged that the police had no reason to arrest the man, whose identity has not been released.

The residents also expressed their anger at the murder of Shani.

“We want justice. Protect our children. Children are the future. Let us protect them. The justice system failed us. We want justice for the brutal murder of Shani,” some of the placards read, while other called for the freeing of the man they said had been taken into custody.

Some of the protesters also took to social media platform TikTok to express their frustration and disgust.

“We a protest, because the police lock up a man and we want him to be freed…. We want justice,” one of the protesting residents told the Jamaica Observer.

Shani partially nude body was found with her throat slashed in bushes on Tuesday. Police said following the discovery of the child’s body, there was a mob attack on the father and son in the community.

Residents told the Observer that the two men are Shani’s relatives. They accused the son of raping and killing the child. He was beaten, chopped and stoned to death, while his father was left with major wounds.

When contacted head of the police Area One Assistant Commissioner Glenford Miller said the investigators are seeking those involved in the mob attack.

“I know we are investigating to know who were the persons involved in that mob killing. I cannot say at this time if we have made any arrests,” Miller said mid-morning on Thursday. Subsequent efforts to get a further update were unsuccessful up to press time.

A heavy pall of gloom and anger clouded over Troy on Thursday with one resident telling the

Observer that the community remains grief-stricken.

“The whole of Troy is in mourning. We can’t stop thinking about the little girl and how she died so awful,” said the resident who requested anonymity.

According to a police report, as well as the account of residents, mid-afternoon Tuesday, Shani was walking home from a shop along a roadway near her home when she was abducted.

Later, a farmer, who had gone in search of his cow after hearing strange sounds from bushes, made the grisly discovery and raised an alarm.

On Wednesday relatives remembered the child for her brilliance and radiant smile.

“All last week she got her certificate to show her brilliance. When you look at her you see the next doctor, lawyer, and they just took her life, just cut her off. Right now we are devastated. Right now we don’t know our head from our feet. Last night [Tuesday] we nuh sleep. This is traumatising. Maybe Kaidra was going to come and take her mother out of poverty and they cut her life short and kill her,” her aunt Shawna Williams-Stevens said before breaking down in tears.

World.title: ‘The best yet’
World.content:
Kevin Downswell.

Award-winning Jamaican gospel artiste Kevin Downswell says his upcoming album is the most personal project of his career, describing it as his “the best yet” and the most vulnerable he has ever allowed himself to be in his music.

Speaking with the Jamaica Observer’s Spalsh ahead of his Pre-Album Launch Worship Experience on Sunday, July 19 at Victory Tabernacle, Bayside, Port Henderson Road, Portmore, Downswell revealed that the unnamed album was largely written during the COVID-19 pandemic, with its songs inspired by seasons of uncertainty, disappointment, perseverance, and renewed faith.

“I wrote most of these songs in the pandemic, when we were feeling all the pressure and the battles, the tears, the pain and the disappointment,” he said. “Wherever you are in your process, one song will connect with you.”

Asked to describe the album in three words, the gospel minister replied simply: “The best yet.”

Downswell said listeners can expect what he considers his strongest songwriting to date.

“I think this is the realest I’ve ever been in my songs,” he said. “This is the most vulnerable I’ve ever been with my tracks… and I think this is the best I’ve ever written.”

He added that fans will hear pieces of his own testimony throughout the album: “You’ll hear my story in every song. You’ll know that I couldn’t write like this if I hadn’t been through something like this.”

The first taste of the project came with the release of Higher (From the Fire) on Tuesday, July 14, an Afro-soca anthem centred on overcoming life’s trials.

“Sometimes what was meant to destroy you actually lifts you higher,” Downswell explained, pointing to the biblical story of Joseph as one of the inspirations behind the song.

The singer also disclosed that the album moves beyond traditional gospel, blending worship music with reggae, Afro-soca and calypso influences.

“I’ve always tried to stay away from limitations,” he said. “It’s a beautiful mixture.”

The event, which formed part of the Portmore New Testament Church of God’s 50th anniversary celebrations, served as an opportunity for fans to hear songs from the upcoming album before its official release.

“There’s nothing like live performances,” he said. “I’ve worked all my life to make the live experience better than the recordings.”

Beyond the music, Downswell said his greatest hope is that listeners encounter God in a fresh way.

“I’ve fallen in love with God all over again,” he said. “I just want people to experience His presence and His love. I want God to meet people wherever they’re at.”

World.title: BPO’S US$220-M SLIDE
World.content:
Key points:

Local spending fell 22 per cent from about US$1 billion to US$780 million as another 5,000 jobs disappeared.

Government data put employment at 50,000, while the GSAJ estimates about 40,000.

A working group is pursuing new investment, better skills and a shift towards higher-value KPO services.

JAMAICA’S global digital services (GDS) sector spent an estimated US$780 million in the local economy in the fiscal year ended March 2026, down US$220 million from about US$1 billion a year earlier as the industry lost another 5,000 jobs.

The estimate — which measures spending in Jamaica rather than export earnings — was higher than the US$612 million earned from bauxite and alumina exports in 2025 and was equivalent to about 47 per cent of the country’s US$1.65 billion in total merchandise exports.

The spending covered wages, office-space leases, utilities and other operating expenses.

Employment in the sector fell to approximately 50,000 in March 2026 from 62,000 two years earlier, while the number of companies declined from more than 90 to about 70.

The sector had already missed Government’s March 2025 target of 70,400 jobs by 15,400. By March 2026, the gap had widened to 20,400 jobs.

“This decrease in employment is attributed to a variety of factors which include: Onshoring/reshoring, geopolitical considerations, technological advancements, the impact of Hurricane Melissa and the local challenges of cost of doing business,” the Government of Jamaica stated in its annual report on Form 18-K for the fiscal year ended March 31, 2026, filed with the United States Securities and Exchange Commission.

The report said Hurricane Melissa compounded those pressures.

“Hurricane Melissa, in particular, had a disruptive impact on Jamaica’s GDS sector, primarily through damage to critical infrastructure and interruptions to essential utilities. Widespread outages in electricity and telecommunications networks constrained business continuity across BPO (business process outsourcing) and other digitally enabled services, limiting firms’ ability to meet international client demands and maintain service-level agreements. In addition, damage to transportation networks and displacement of workers further affected operational capacity and productivity,” the annual report added.

However, Global Services Association of Jamaica President-elect Yoni Epstein has placed employment in the sector at about 40,000 for two consecutive years. The

Jamaica Observer reported on August 1, 2025, that Epstein said the sector employed about 40,000 people, a figure he repeated to the

Financial Gleaner earlier this month. The Government, by comparison, reported approximately 55,000 jobs in March 2025 and 50,000 in March 2026, leaving differences of 15,000 and 10,000, respectively. It was not immediately clear whether the discrepancies reflected different reporting periods, industry coverage or methods of counting workers. Epstein is the founder and CEO of Outsourcing Management Limited, trading as itel.

Since 2012, the Development Bank of Jamaica Limited (DBJ) has committed US$92.66 million in financing to the GDS sector and disbursed US$90.01 million to 20 BPO ventures covering approximately 1.18 million square feet of operating space. The ventures had a combined capacity for 27,513 jobs.

The report said DBJ financing also facilitated US$152.72 million in private-sector investment. However, the Government’s latest report gives a different account of the occupancy of the DBJ-funded projects.

The 2025 annual report said all 20 projects had been completed, leased and occupied and had reported total employment of 22,598. However, the 2026 report said only 19 projects were leased and occupied and had provided 22,598 jobs at their peak. It said the remaining project had been completed with capacity for another 1,200 jobs, but the developer was still seeking an operator. The reports do not explain the change in the stated occupancy of the projects.

The sector’s contraction has also affected the Port Authority of Jamaica (PAJ), which recently postponed plans to monetise its BPO real estate assets through an initial public offering on the Jamaica Stock Exchange.

A CariCRIS report on the PAJ noted, “The authority decided that prevailing market conditions were not conducive to achieving favourable valuation outcomes and therefore postponed the transaction.”

The Government has responded by establishing a working group comprising representatives of the GDS sector, the PAJ, Jamaica Promotions Corporation (Jampro) and the Jamaica Special Economic Zone Authority (JSEZA) to develop and implement an action plan aimed at growing the industry.

The working group’s mandate was limited to three areas in the Government’s 2025 annual report. The latest report expands the mandate to six areas. One of the six areas is changing the industry’s mix of BPO and KPO (knowledge process outsourcing) jobs from 80:20 to 60:40. This would reduce the sector’s concentration in basic queries and routine tasks while expanding its participation in more advanced, higher-value activities.

Other focus areas include enhancing job-readiness and digital-skills curricula, optimising processes, institutions, regulations and the incentives framework, strengthening the sector’s value proposition, and developing incubator and accelerator programmes for small and medium-sized enterprises. These initiatives build on work being done with the HEART/NSTA Trust, the United Kingdom Trade Partnerships Programme and the Inter-American Development Bank to better prepare GDS firms and their staff to take on new global opportunities.

“Jamaica, through Jampro (the government agency responsible for the promotion of business opportunities in export and investment), has actively engaged international KPO operators to get them to expand their business to Jamaica. Additionally, Jampro continues to work with local universities and key stakeholders, sharing opportunities for employment as well as establishing partnerships for training in the KPO and ITO (information technology outsourcing) space,” the annual report stated.

World.title: CASH SQUEEZE
World.content:
Jamaica Football Federation headquarters in New Kingston (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

JAMAICA Football Federation (JFF) President Michael Ricketts has outlined what he considers a harsh financial reality facing the body, which is managing a tight cash-flow situation after putting significant resources into national team programmes that ultimately missed out on major qualification payouts.

International football is a high-stakes business, and Ricketts says the JFF is counting the cost of an aggressive push for global recognition that fell short on the pitch.

Failing to qualify for the 2026 FIFA World Cup cost the JFF a guaranteed minimum payout of at least US$10.5 million to US$12.5 million (under J$2 billion) — a windfall tied to FIFA participation and preparation fees.

For a federation historically hampered by tight budgets, a capital injection of that size could have cleared existing debt, reduced reliance on government subventions, and fully funded grassroots facilities, coaching development, and youth travel across all age groups.

“Right now, it’s challenging,” Ricketts told the Jamaica Observer. “We would’ve invested heavily in so many of the World Cup qualifiers. The U-20s leave [today] to participate in the last round. The ladies will play their last game against Costa Rica in November, and of course the senior men’s team didn’t do as well as we would’ve thought; hence, we did not get the returns based on the investment.”

The immediate strain comes as national squads continue to compete. While the senior men missed their target, the federation must still fund ongoing campaigns, including the departure of the national Under-20 team and the senior women’s team’s crucial November fixture.

Should the Reggae Girlz win that Concacaf W Championship game against Costa Rica, they qualify not only for the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028, but also for the 2027 FIFA Women’s World Cup in Brazil. At the latter, they would receive a financial payout for competing in the group stage at the very minimum. FIFA has however not yet shared an exact breakdown of monetary prizes for this tournament.

Ricketts defended the heavy spending as a necessary cost of doing business in modern football, where federations must spend aggressively across all age groups just to remain competitive on the world stage.

“There were so many teams vying for global recognition that it cost us a lot of money,” Ricketts said. “So, we are struggling right now financially, simply because we would’ve invested heavily in these programmes and the senior men’s team didn’t qualify.”

Despite the short-term financial challenge, Ricketts says staying visible on the global stage remains the JFF’s best path forward. Mentioning long-term commercial goals, such as Jamaica’s interest in hosting the 2031 FIFA Women’s World Cup, Ricketts says the high cost of international football is a necessary investment in the country’s social and technical future.

He believes the star power of players like Khadija “Bunny” Shaw and Jody Brown demonstrates the return on investment that numbers alone cannot capture.

“This is to ensure that we impact the lives of every Jamaican,” Ricketts said. “Everybody wants to be like Bunny Shaw, everybody wants to be like a Jody Brown, everybody wants to be like a Jamaican player. So, we’re very hopeful, we’re optimistic that this will, from a commercial standpoint, from a technical standpoint, from a social standpoint, certainly help our country.”

World.title: Addison adds up victory
World.content:
Chris-John Addison celebrates his second win in the Drift Ruption series at Falmouth Cruise Ship Pier on July 19.(Photo: Rory Daley)

Chris-John Addison was the winner of the second round of Drift Ruption, which was held on Sunday, July 19, at the Falmouth Cruise Ship Pier, Trelawny.

“This victory is a great feeling, because we were leading the competition from round one, and nevertheless we came out today to execute, and that’s what we did,” Addison told the Jamaica Observer’s weekly Auto magazine.

Addison worked his way through a field stacked with major drift talent from across the island.

In the Drift Ruption format, entrants are whittled down to the highest-scoring eight, and then the highest-scoring four to determine the winner.

It is not a timed event, but a pure drift event in which the drivers have to display maximum slip angle while navigating and interacting with various obstacles for points.

So tough was the competition that several drivers posted perfect runs, leading to multiple ties. When it came to the final four Addison was tied with Sheldon Johnson at the very end. It was his consistently high scores throughout the event that eventually gained him the win.

“This round we didn’t do anything different, because we have an engine being built for high-speed drifting, so we decided to use the stock motor for this, the last car park event. Other than that, no major upgrades. That happens next event,” explained Addison.

Following Addison and Johnson were Cleve Ottey and Nicholas Barnes.

The current standings put Addison at the top of the leaderboard with 200 points. Johnson sits in second with 176 points. Barnes is third on 128 points, while Ottey is fourth on 124 points.

“The event went very well for me and my team,” said Kingsley Scott, event organiser and conceptualiser.

This event marks a change for Drift Ruption as it shifts to high-speed tandem drifting and a move to circuit venues, such as Dover Raceway in St Ann and JamWest Speedway in Westmoreland. The Drift Ruption finale is for a to-be-determined date in December.

World.title: We’ve fallen in love with drones, but they’re not the sole answer
World.content:
They are not. But nor are they mere bit players.

The enthusiasm for drones is understandable. According to the Kyiv Post, on July 9 alone “Ukraine said it struck 14 Russian vessels overnight in the Sea of Azov, including 12 tankers allegedly belonging to Moscow’s sanctioned ‘shadow fleet.’ Ukraine’s drone commander said a total of 35 ships had been hit over the previous 96 hours, while Ukrainian forces also targeted 45 military sites in occupied Crimea and southern Ukraine.”

It’s as if Ukrainian drones are everywhere. And not only is Ukraine using them to hit Russian targets without causing devastating losses to human life the way, say, missiles would; it’s also able to do so at enormous distances.

Drones hit Russian shadow vessels in the Black Sea. They hit Russian shadow vessels in the Mediterranean. They hit Russia’s oil refineries. They hit Russia’s Baltic Sea oil terminals. They’re causing constant problems for the Russian military, and have hit Russia itself. Earlier this month they even struck an oil refinery in Siberia.

In fact, Ukraine’s drones have become such a success that they’re triggering increasingly loud demands for NATO’s European members to shift their focus to these mostly small and cheap weapons. Look at how drones have helped Ukraine shift the course of the war! Look at how much you can achieve at relatively small expense! Drones are the future! Our governments are behind the curve! That’s how the argument goes.

But while drones are indisputably part of the future of warfare, they’re also still experimental and lack clear rules of engagement.

World.title: Trump administration rejects UN farm declaration over gender references
World.content:
The plan, which is completely voluntary, was finally adopted by delegates on Friday. It advises countries to address issues such as biodiversity, animal welfare, emissions and how to prevent the spread of disease.

The word gender only appears once, to explain the numerous mentions of women and equality throughout the document. The goal is to promote equal opportunities for women farmers as well as their nutrition.

“The cross-cutting themes of gender, youth and inclusion are considered essential to ensure that the transformation leaves no one behind,” the agreement states.

But for Washington, the word is too ambiguous. The U.S. administration made its stance clear back in March, when a working group drafted the plan, and again in June, explaining its red lines in a statement.

“It is the policy of the United States to recognize two sexes, male and female. To achieve this, we will use clear and accurate language,” the statement said. For the U.S., focusing on inclusion comes “at the loss of recognizing hard work, excellence, and individual achievement.”

On climate change, the U.S. does not accept the term but prefers to narrow the focus to “specific environmental threats” facing livestock, it said.

World.title: Governments criticize EU’s cash-for-reforms model in new budget
World.content:
It’s yet another thorny issue to solve for the EU's 27 countries racing to reach a deal before the start of 2027, when national elections are due in France, Italy, Poland and Spain, which could make discussions even more difficult.

Major contributors to the budget including Italy, France and Spain, and net recipients of EU funds such as Hungary, Malta and Poland, spoke out against the cash-for-reforms model during Wednesday's meeting. Critics say that the approach could increase the power of national governments at the expense of regions, and result in the EU imposing reforms with no political backing.

“We don’t want [the Commission’s] recommendations to become impositions,” said an EU diplomat who, like others quoted in this article, was granted anonymity to speak freely.

On the other hand, Netherlands defended the plan during the meeting, according to the diplomats. Other fiscally conservative states, such as Sweden and Denmark, have long argued that conditionality could help poorer EU countries become economically more efficient

But two EU diplomats from the rival camp argued that their real motivation is to slow down payments to less affluent regions.

The RRF model

The cash-for-reforms model was tested in the EU’s post-Covid recovery fund, the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF), where payouts were linked to judicial and pensions reforms among others.

World.title: World chess chief steps aside after EU sanctions
World.content:
Arkady Dvorkovich, president of the International Chess Federation (FIDE), talks to media during the pre-tournament press conference on June 16, 2026. | Yu Chun Christopher Wong/Eurasia Sport Images/Getty Images

Arkady Dvorkovich stepped aside temporarily after the EU accused him of supporting policies that threaten Ukraine’s sovereignty.

Arkady Dvorkovich, Russia’s former deputy prime minister and president of the International Chess Federation (FIDE), suspended his duties Thursday evening after the European Union sanctioned him.

In its latest sanctions package, the EU accused Dvorkovich of “supporting actions or policies which undermine or threaten the territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence of Ukraine.” The FIDE chief pushed back, stating “unequivocally” that he considers the decision “unlawful and unfair.” “I am confident that justice will prevail,” he added.

Dvorkovich became FIDE’s president in 2018, drawing criticism over his closeness to Vladimir Putin’s regime. The Russian president appointed him as deputy prime minister from 2012 to 2018.

Dvorkovich said the decision would remain in effect for as long as he is subject to EU and Swiss sanctions. FIDE Deputy President Viswanathan Anand, a former world champion, will take over his duties. In 2022, Anand told AFP that Dvorkovich had “clearly demonstrated that he is independent of Kremlin influence.”

Under Dvorkovich’s leadership, FIDE’s Ethics and Disciplinary Commission largely overturned a 2024 ruling that had temporarily suspended the Chess Federation of Russia and reprimanded him for “improper association” with an organization or person whose activities conflicted with FIDE’s objectives or interests. The reprimand against Dvorkovich was rescinded.

World.title: China strikes back at EU sanctions targeting defense, tech firms
World.content:
A Bundeswehr truck with the logo Rheinmetall is seen in Unna on July 21, 2026. | Ina Fassbender/AFP via Getty Images

The announcement came a day after the EU added 14 Chinese and Hong Kong entities to its sanctions list, barring European companies from doing business with them.

BRUSSELS — China announced it will add export restrictions on 14 EU defense and technology companies after the EU added 14 Chinese businesses to its Russia sanctions lists.

This marks Beijing’s most direct and forceful response yet to EU sanctions listings, which it denounced as “egregious.” Recent studies estimate that up to 90 percent of sanctioned goods still reaching Russia transit through China.

Germany’s rapidly expanding defense company Rheinmetall is among 14 firms that Chinese exporters are now barred from supplying with dual-use goods — products that have both civilian and military applications — China’s Ministry of Commerce said Friday. The list also includes Czech truckmaker Tatra, Dutch naval engineering firm IHC Merwede, and several optics and laser companies.

Exporters may apply for licenses permitting certain shipments when they are deemed “truly necessary.”

The announcement came a day after the EU added 14 Chinese and Hong Kong entities to its sanctions list, barring European companies from doing business with them. Most are not high-tech defense firms, but logistics companies that help Russian importers obtain Western technology.

World.title: Polish conservatives split ahead of 2027 election
World.content:
That clash at the top boiled over on Friday when Kaczyński expelled Morawiecki and some three dozen MPs for refusing to abandon an internal grouping in PiS that has been widely seen as Morawiecki’s attempt to build his own splinter party.

Kaczyński announced the expulsion after a midnight deadline he had given Morawiecki and his group to sign loyalty declarations.

“Everyone knew what they were supposed to sign and at the same time everyone knew what the consequences of not signing were. And so they made the decision they made,” Kaczyński told a press briefing at PiS’s headquarters in Warsaw.

Morawiecki’s allies are now expected to establish a separate caucus in the Polish parliament, the 460-seat Sejm.

The departure of Morawiecki’s followers is going to reduce its parliamentary contingent to 140-145 seats, making it the second-biggest caucus after Tusk’s Civic Coalition.

While PiS was ahead of Civic Coalition in polls last fall, support has now dropped to 26 percent, according to POLITICO’s Poll of Polls, behind the Civic Coalition on 32 percent.

World.title: EU signals relief over new US tariffs as Trump respects transatlantic truce
World.content:
“The EU notes positively the fact that this outcome is in line with the U.S. tariff commitments agreed under the EU-U.S. Joint Statement,” said Olof Gill, deputy chief spokesperson for the European Commission.

While Brussels cautiously welcomed these new tariffs, it is still conscious that more investigations — looking at alleged industrial overcapacity in Europe and pharmaceutical pricing policies — are under way, meaning cumulative duties could ultimately breach the 15 percent cap. Those probes are conducted under Section 301 of the U.S. Trade Act of 1974, a tool used by Washington to take action against unfair trade practices by other countries.

“Looking ahead, the EU expects the U.S. to continue abiding by the terms of the EU-U.S. Joint Statement, including as regards any remedies under additional Section 301 investigations,” Gill added.

The new U.S. tariffs follow a five-month investigation into efforts to crack down on imports of goods made with forced labor — a measure specifically combating manufacturing from America's trade rivals in Asia.

The EU’s own forced labor regulation will only apply from Dec. 2027. This is the justification cited by the U.S. Trade Representative for applying a 10 percent tariff on goods coming from the bloc.

The EU’s foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas struck a less diplomatic note, pushing back against Washington’s reasoning to impose the tariffs.

“We had a deal with America and we have kept to that deal, that side of the deal. That's why this is a negative surprise that this agreement is not kept,” she told Reuters on the sidelines of a meeting with ASEAN countries in the Philippines.

“If you compare our labor laws to the ones of the United States, I mean, we have paid vacations, we have very good labor conditions for our employees, so it's not really grounded.”

World.title: Merz seeks to revive political fortunes with cabinet reshuffle
World.content:
“These personnel changes follow a clear guiding principle,” he added. “We want a government that works with the greatest enthusiasm and joy, while also reflecting the diversity of our society and political landscape. We are a reform-oriented government, and we intend to continue demonstrating that.”

Merz has often been publicly criticized for surrounding himself with men at top adviser level. With the appointment of Nina Warken, the current health minister, as chancellery chief he is putting a woman in charge of the chancellery’s inner workings for the first time in Germany’s postwar history. The position is of strategic importance as it is key to behind-the-scenes brokerage work, for example when mediating between the chancellery and ministries as well as with lawmakers and at state level.

“She is assertive, and she is also well-versed in security policy issues, which are, after all, coordinated here in this house,” Merz said of Warken. “She will therefore be one of the most important — if not the most important— pillars of support for me in the day-to-day work of the government, as well as my primary point of contact.”

The cabinet reshuffle allows Merz to make a political reset before crucial regional elections in September. Polls show that the AfD has a chance of winning an outright majority in Saxony-Anhalt on Sept. 6 and is poised to perform well in Mecklenburg–Western Pomerania and Berlin later that month.

To fend off the rise of the far right, Merz has promised to bring much-needed reforms, for example to the pension system, through parliament this fall. In doing so, he would show voters that the political center is indeed the only viable option to get things done, or at least that’s how the thinking goes in the government.

The current general secretary of Merz’s CDU, Carsten Linnemann, is set to take over as health minister from Warken. He will be tasked with bringing one of the key reforms, the health reform, through parliament later this year.

World.title: Iran military says it targeted US bases in Bahrain, Jordan and Kuwait
World.content:
Iran's military said on Friday that it had targeted US military bases in Bahrain, Jordan and Kuwait in retaliation for Washington's latest strikes on the country.

 

"This morning, the fuel tanks, large equipment warehouses and silos, and the barracks of the US terrorist army forces at the Isa Air Base in Bahrain were targeted by Arash kamikaze drones," the Iranian army said in a statement carried by state TV.

The US has not confirmed that any of its facilities or personnel were targeted.

Meanwhile, Iran's Revolutionary Guards also claimed they had targeted an Amazon data centre in Bahrain, according to state media. Neither the US tech giant nor Bahraini authorities have commented on the claim.

An explosion and warning sirens were reported in Bahrain on Friday, although it was not immediately clear whether the two incidents were connected.

Bahrain later said it intercepted and destroyed "a number of Iranian aerial aggressions", accusing Tehran of targeting civilians.

The Iranian army also claimed it had carried out drone attacks against Jordan, targeting "aircraft hangars, aviation maintenance hangars and a barracks" at Al-Azraq base.

Jordan's military said it had intercepted seven missiles and six drones fired by Iran on Friday, saying the operation "resulted in no casualties or material damage".

In a separate statement, the Iranian army said it had also launched drones targeting US equipment warehouses at Camp Udairi, as well as American military personnel stationed at Camp Doha and Camp Arifjan in Kuwait.

Iran's Revolutionary Guards, the military's ideological arm, separately claimed they had targeted Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait, saying they destroyed an ammunition depot and inflicted casualties among US personnel.

They also said they had struck equipment storage silos at Camp Udairi in Kuwait and a US Fifth Fleet watchtower in Bahrain.

Ali Abdollahi, head of Iran's Khatam al-Anbiya central military command, warned US personnel in the region on Friday that Iran had "prepared free, one-way tickets to hell for you".

"For every proud citizen of the Islamic Republic of Iran who is martyred, one American service member will be sent to hell," he was quoted as saying by the state broadcaster.

World.title: ICC chief prosecutor removed from post over sexual misconduct allegations
World.content:
Member states of the International Criminal Court (ICC) removed chief prosecutor Karim Khan from office on Friday, diplomats told the Associated Press, marking the first dismissal of a chief prosecutor in the court’s history.

 

The ICC's 125 member states voted by a large majority to remove Khan from office following allegations of sexual misconduct, which he has repeatedly denied.

The move marks the first-ever removal of an ICC chief prosecutor. Khan had been temporarily suspended in June while the allegations were reviewed after an internal report found he had committed serious misconduct, a finding he strongly rejects.

According to documents seen by the Associated Press, Khan had a sexual relationship with the woman and allegedly tried to discourage her from pursuing her complaint.

An independent oversight report found that he had committed "serious misconduct", though Khan denies the allegations.

Related ICC chief prosecutor suspended pending proceedings on sexual misconduct allegations

Khan's removal comes as the ICC faces mounting pressure from US President Donald Trump administration, which has already imposed sanctions on him and a dozen other ICC employees.

The sanctions were imposed in response to the ICC's arrest warrants for senior Israeli officials, including Israel Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, over the war in Gaza, as well as the court's investigations into US personnel in Afghanistan.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said last week that the United States was launching a “comprehensive campaign to crush the threat that the International Criminal Court poses to US sovereignty”.

Rubio said the US would pressure member states to withdraw from the institution, sanction organisations that cooperate with the court and deny its employees entry to the United States. Countries that “benefit from the US security umbrella” are to be urged to reject the court’s jurisdiction over US citizens.

Khan’s removal has no immediate impact on the arrest warrants already issued. Decisions on whether they remain in force are made solely by ICC judges.

World.title: Trump and Zelenskyy to meet in Washington next week
World.content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy will meet US President Donald Trump in Washington on Tuesday, a White House official said, amid renewed efforts to end the war with Russia.

 

"President Zelensky is slated to meet with President Trump at the White House on Tuesday," the White House official told AFP on condition of anonymity on Friday.

Zelenskyy said this week he had spoken with Trump's envoy Steve Witkoff and the US president's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, as part of efforts to revive stalled talks aimed at ending the four-year war.

US-led efforts to end the war have stalled as Washington shifted its focus to the conflict with Iran.

Trump and Zelenskyy have had a tense relationship, ranging from a heated Oval Office clash in February 2025 to warmer ties in recent months.

This week, the Ukrainian president met right-wing US influencer and Trump ally Laura Loomer, in another sign of improving relations.

The 33-year-old conservative commentator, who has millions of social media followers, has recently softened her stance on Ukraine.

"This is everyday for every Ukrainian, I feel like such an a**hole for minimizing the struggle of Ukrainians for the last five years," she said of the experience.

Trump reposted one of Loomer's social media posts about her Zelensky meeting on Thursday with the caption: "Very good!!

Zelenskyy is due to meet Trump on the same day as a memorial service in Washington for US Senator Lindsey Graham, a longtime supporter of Ukraine who died earlier this month at the age of 71.

Trump is due to meet Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on the same day as Zelenskyy.

World.title: Wildfires trigger mass evacuations across France and Spain
World.content:
Large forest fires continue to burn out of control across south-western France and central Spain, forcing massive evacuations and prompting military intervention in both nations.

 

In France, a massive wildfire has reached the outskirts of Bordeaux, raising the total number of people evacuated across surrounding areas to 110,000. Earlier, tens of thousands of residents already fled as wildfires swept through the tourist peninsula of Cap Ferret on the Atlantic coast.

The French Prime Minister has requested army support to assist firefighters on the ground.

The main blaze, active since Wednesday near Cap Ferret (60 kilometres from Bordeaux), has consumed 125 square kilometres. Around 1,500 people escaped the peninsula by sea, arriving in Arcachon aboard water taxis and ferries.

In total, 44,000 people were evacuated in the Gironde department, where 53 homes and a campsite were destroyed and 42 firefighters injured, while 23,000 were evacuated in the neighbouring Landes department due to an uncontained 25-square-kilometre blaze further south.

"It’s quite impressive and even frightening," said Laurent Moretti, a resident of Arès. "An evacuation on this scale has never happened before. All we really hope is that the firefighters can quickly get it under control."

French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez stated that France has 32 active wildfires, with over 50,000 hectares burned since January, nearly triple last year's total.

Military Emergency Unit in charge of operations in Spain

In Spain, the government declared a national emergency for wildfires for the first time. The Minister of the Interior has assumed direct coordination of all firefighting resources, with the Military Emergency Unit taking charge of operations on the ground as a heatwave brings temperatures above 39°C and high winds have fanned multiple blazes.

Two major fires west of Madrid merged into a single blaze, charring 30 square kilometres and prompting the evacuation of 18,000 people. Nearby in Ávila, a blaze consumed 90 square kilometres, forcing 1,500 people to flee

Authorities later ordered the evacuation of 7,000 more people from two new localities west of Madrid. In total, around 60,000 people in the Madrid and Ávila areas have been evacuated or told to remain indoors.

Meanwhile, the La Mierla fire in Guadalajara—the largest in Spain, which has scorched 32,000 hectares—has finally begun to subside. However, the national toll remains severe: the total burned area across Spain has doubled in just two weeks, approaching 120,000 hectares so far this year.

Spanish police arrested one man in Castilla y León for starting a fire using farm machinery during a ban, with a second person under investigation.

Wildfire analyst Raúl Quílez noted that climate change and rural land abandonment have left villages exposed, creating a "perfect cocktail" for severe blazes.

International assistance and broader impact

Both nations have requested European Union assistance. France will receive aerial reinforcements from Croatia, Portugal, the Czech Republic, and Slovakia. Spain is receiving four water-dumping aircraft deployed by Italy and Greece, along with support from the Copernicus satellite system.

Wildfires also continue to affect Sicily, where temperatures over 40°C resulted in scattered evacuations and claimed the life of a firefighter in Caltanissetta.

Wildfires are becoming more frequent and intense in Europe, WHO Europe said on Friday. Portugal and Spain have each reported a 100% increase in wildfires this year compared with the same period in 2025. Since 2022, the number of wildfires has risen by 57% across the WHO European Region.

Last year alone, around 2.2 million hectares burned, while 254,388 hectares had already been destroyed by 22 July this year, according to the European Forest Fire Information System (EFFIS).

World.title: Boycotts and apologies: Argentina row over Rosalía and Patti Smith after World Cup
World.content:
The fallout from the World Cup final between Spain and Argentina has spilled over into music. In just a few days, the singer Rosalía has seen a tribute concert to her work cancelled in Argentina and calls grow for a boycott of her upcoming concerts in Buenos Aires. American artist Patti Smith has also ended up backtracking on a post about the match after receiving a wave of criticism.

 

The controversy broke out against a backdrop of high tension after the World Cup final. The match and the days that followed were marked by clashes between fans on social media, traded insults, harassment campaigns against public figures and several rows over the behaviour of some Argentine players and supporters, which sparked a wide debate beyond the country.

Both artists ended up apologising after some Argentine fans interpreted their messages as making fun of the national team. But what exactly did they post, and why has it caused such an uproar?

"My bad": What did Rosalía post and why did she apologise?

The controversy began shortly after the World Cup final, when Rosalía shared on TikTok a video originally posted by influencer Mia Khalifa celebrating Spain's victory. The clip featured "La Perla", one of the songs on the album "LUX", with the caption: "How life sounds now that the pearls have been defeated".

Many Argentine users understood the phrase "the pearls" as a reference to the Albiceleste national team and took the post as mocking their defeat. The video spread quickly on social media before the singer deleted it.

In the face of an avalanche of criticism, Rosalía posted an apology in her Instagram stories. "I hit share because 'La Perla' was playing and I didn't even read what it said, my bad. Sorry," she wrote next to an Argentine flag. In another post she added: "I only have love x Argentina", insisting she had not meant to offend the country.

Messages from Rosalía posted on Instagram. @rosalia.vt/Instagram

What consequences has this had for the singer?

The backlash did not stay confined to social media. Some Argentine fans began to promote campaigns to sell on or return tickets for the four concerts Rosalía is due to play in Buenos Aires at the beginning of August, while others called for seats to be left empty as a form of protest.

The most immediate consequence, however, came in Córdoba. A symphonic tribute concert to Rosalía, organised by an independent production company with no connection to the artist, was cancelled after receiving "numerous messages of hate and anger", the organisers said.

Those behind the show stressed that the project had been in preparation for months and that its aim was purely artistic. In a statement released on social media they said they understood the anger after the final because "football is not just a sport, it is part of our identity, our history and our culture", but lamented that the tension had ultimately forced them to call off the event to protect the musicians taking part.

For now, Rosalía's four official concerts in Buenos Aires are still scheduled as announced by the promoter.

What happened with Patti Smith?

American singer and poet Patti Smith also found herself caught up in the row over a post she made after the final. In it she celebrated Spain's victory and described Spain as "the good guys", a phrase many Argentine users interpreted as putting the opposing team on the wrong side.

The criticism multiplied within a few hours and the artist ended up deleting the post. She later shared an image of Lionel Messi and posted a new message saying she had never intended to belittle Argentina or its national team.

Smith also recalled the ties she has maintained with the South American country over many years, expressed her admiration for Messi and said she deeply regretted that her words had been interpreted as a lack of respect towards the Argentine people.

Why has a football final ended up triggering a cultural row?

Although the posts by Rosalía and Patti Smith were different, both ended up forming part of a wider phenomenon that has shaped the conversation after the World Cup final. Argentina's defeat generated huge activity on social media, where celebrations, mockery, nationalist messages and boycott campaigns against various public figures who openly backed Spain all became intertwined.

In that climate, posts that at another time would probably have gone unnoticed took on a much greater political and emotional significance. The rapid spread of screenshots and videos meant the messages circulated far beyond the artists' usual followers.

Both Rosalía and Patti Smith chose to delete their posts and offer explanations, but their apologies have not managed to end the debate; days after the final whistle, the artists' posts are still attracting both criticism and expressions of support.

World.title: Church reshapes Spain's history: did Moors and Christians ever live in peace?
World.content:
A hill in the northwest of Murcia is forcing historians to rethink some of the most established ideas about the early centuries of Al-Andalus. Excavations at Cerro de la Virgen de Calasparra have brought to light an early Christian church that not only survived the Muslim conquest of 713, but remained in use for almost two more centuries.

 

The study (source in Spanish), published in the scientific journal "Salduie" by researchers David Martínez and Rubén Fernández, documents the existence of a church founded around the first half of the 5th century that would have preserved its religious function at least until the 9th century. If this chronology is fully confirmed, it would amount to one of the strongest pieces of evidence for the continuity of Christian worship in the Iberian Peninsula during the first years of Moorish occupation.

The church was identified thanks to various prospecting and excavation campaigns carried out in the area since 2021. Archaeologists describe it as a single-nave building with a tripartite chancel, a layout they see as characteristic of certain "late antique" churches.

"This represents an architectural model with notable parallels in Visigothic churches such as Santa Cristina de Lena", the authors of the study note, referring to this church in Asturias. They also point out that the sacristies and apses show similarities with some "parochial and episcopal" churches in Syria, a connection that reflects the use of similar architectural models across the Mediterranean in late antiquity.

Much more than a question of timing

Radiocarbon dating places the construction of the building between the years 410 and 440 AD. This is backed up by ceramic and stratigraphic analyses that support the hypothesis of prolonged occupation of the site. The site had already attracted researchers’ attention in previous campaigns, when a striking early Christian bronze lamp was unearthed, shaped like a eucharistic dove and considered at the time an exceptional piece in the European context.

However, the most significant aspect of the new study is not the age of the church, but its survival as such after the Muslim conquest of the Peninsula. Traditionally, many historical accounts have presented the arrival of Moorish troops in the early 8th century as a relatively sharp break with Visigothic traditions. The Calasparra finds, however, sketch a more complex reality.

The researchers argue that there is no evidence that the church was converted into a mosque, nor that it immediately lost its religious function. In fact, they state that "the record, with the presence of containers and cooking pottery, should not be understood as evidence of the desacralisation of the church or its conversion into Islamic dwellings", the study reads.

The typological and stratigraphic study of the ceramics points to the liturgical character of the church enduring well into the 9th century David Martínez y Rubén Fernández Authors of the study

"On the contrary, such materials should be analysed as indicators of continued use of the space for community practices that encompassed both worship and resource management", they argue.
