World.title: Are you this kind of traveler? Here are 5 traveling habits in 2026
World.content:
AirAsia MOVE's insights from travel bookings set between July and December point to travelers now prioritizing value, convenience, and deliberate planning over volume alone

Traveling has become increasingly common. People from older generations have often told me that, back in their day, traveling was never really something that crossed their minds. Today, however, as economic and global conditions evolve, travel has become a priority for many consumers across Southeast Asia.

You may be thinking: Traveling? In this economy? This is exactly why people are becoming increasingly mindful of how they book their trips, spend their money and choose their destinations.

According to AirAsia MOVE’s insights from the 2026 bookings for travel between July 1 to December 31, 2026, travelers now prioritize value, convenience, and deliberate planning over volume alone. In short, they are becoming smarter and more intentional with their trips, ensuring that they consider budget without compromising experience.

Here are some of the habits that shape traveling in 2026:

Spending smarter, not less

Traveling does not go easy on the pockets. That is no secret. Flight rates today are around 35% higher than the average accommodation rates. Because of this, booking luxury and five-star hotels is no longer the first thing people do.

Data from hotels across AirAsia MOVE shows that travelers have increasingly prioritized value over luxury in recent years, as convenience, comfort, and affordability have become top considerations.

The mindset? People travel to explore the place—not stay in their hotel rooms the entire trip.

Turning plans into bookings during payday

Booking during payday? That sounds about right!

Data from AirAsia MOVE also shows that about 40% of flight bookings are made for travel taking place between the 25th and 5th of each month, aligning with the usual salary cycles across many ASEAN markets.

Many use this strategy to enjoy travel with less spending guilt because they have payday to look forward to!

Choosing convenience above all

What’s more convenient than visiting a country that’s just a short flight away while still getting your money’s worth?

Nowadays, distance, time, and reach are huge deciding factors when it comes to picking travel destinations, and most choose the ones that are no more than four hours away. In fact, bookings for international flights under four hours have increased by 14% in the second half of 2026 compared to the same period in 2025.

It’s not about how far it is, but about making the most out of the experience.

Going international… and planning way beforehand

Cramming is no longer an option. Yes, I hear it in my mom’s voice whenever I tell her about a trip: “Book now. That might become even more expensive later. Do it now so you have more time to lay things out.” The same is apparently true for most people today.

Bookings are now made more than 120 days before departure. Again, traveling has become more intentional, so many prefer having longer booking windows.

Millennials and Gen Z driving travel demand

Millennials are the largest traveling generation on MOVE, accounting for 43% of all bookings on the platform, followed by Gen Zs who account for 23%.

This highlights what was said earlier: traveling today has increasingly become a priority — especially for young people who want to see the world while they can.

As travel becomes part of more people’s lives, habits have changed, making traveling more possible than ever.

Traveling today isn’t just about the destination now. It is about what you are able to do, the places you get to see, the food you get to eat, and the culture you experience. Staying within budget is important, but getting the best worry- and guilt-free experience is just as important too. – Rappler.com

World.title: Kiyapo rapidly intensifies into typhoon, leaves PAR
World.content:
KIYAPO. Satellite image of Typhoon Kiyapo (Noul) as of July 25, 2026, 4 am.

Typhoon Kiyapo (Noul) can still trigger heavy rain and strong winds in portions of Northern Luzon on Saturday, July 25, even though it is already outside the Philippine Area of Responsibility

MANILA, Philippines – Kiyapo (Noul) rapidly intensified from a severe tropical storm into a typhoon and left the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR) at 2 am on Saturday, July 25. However, due to its intensity, it is still affecting Northern Luzon.

As of 4 am, Kiyapo was already 320 kilometers west of Basco, Batanes, moving west northwest toward China at 25 kilometers per hour (km/h).

Its maximum sustained winds are now at 120 km/h, with gustiness of up to 150 km/h.

In a bulletin released at 5 am on Saturday, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) said Kiyapo is likely to strengthen further in the next 12 hours, ahead of its expected landfall in China. But it may weaken quickly once it moves further inland there.

In the Philippines, Kiyapo made landfall as a tropical storm in Camiguin Island, Calayan, Cagayan, at 2:10 pm on Friday, July 24.

While Kiyapo is now outside PAR, it can still trigger moderate to heavy rain (50-100 millimeters) in Ilocos Norte, Ilocos Sur, Apayao, and Abra on Saturday. The rest of the Ilocos Region, the rest of the Cordillera Administrative Region, and Cagayan Valley may also have scattered rain and thunderstorms due to the trough or extension of the typhoon.

The southwest monsoon or habagat also continues to affect Central Luzon, Southern Luzon, the Visayas, and Mindanao, causing scattered rain and thunderstorms in many areas. But fewer provinces are seen to have significant rainfall during the weekend, based on PAGASA’s separate 5 am advisory on Saturday.

Saturday, July 25

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 mm): Zambales, Bataan, Occidental Mindoro

Sunday, July 26

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 mm): Pangasinan, Zambales

PAGASA advised areas affected by Kiyapo and the southwest monsoon to remain on alert for floods and landslides.

Also as of 5 am on Saturday, strong winds from Kiyapo are still reaching some Northern Luzon provinces, so Signal No. 1 remains raised for them:

Batanes

western part of Babuyan Islands (Calayan Island, Dalupiri Island, Fuga Island)

northwestern part of mainland Cagayan (Pamplona, Sanchez-Mira, Claveria, Santa Praxedes)

northern part of Apayao (Luna, Calanasan)

Ilocos Norte

The highest tropical cyclone wind signal raised due to Kiyapo was Signal No. 3.

The southwest monsoon and the typhoon’s periphery or outer bands are also bringing strong to gale-force gusts to these areas:

Saturday, July 25

most of Luzon, Western Visayas, Negros Island Region, Northern Samar, Zamboanga del Norte, Davao Oriental

Sunday, July 26

Batanes, Cagayan, Ilocos Region, Zambales, Bataan, Quezon, Mimaropa

Monday, July 27

La Union, Pangasinan, Zambales, Lubang Islands, Kalayaan Islands

Moderate to very rough sea conditions persist on Saturday, too.

Up to very rough seas (travel is risky for all vessels)

Seaboards of Batanes and Babuyan Islands; northern seaboard of Ilocos Norte – waves up to 4.5 meters high

Up to rough seas (small vessels should not venture out to sea)

Northeastern seaboard of Cagayan – waves up to 3.5 meters high

Rremaining seaboards of Ilocos Norte and Cagayan – waves up to 3 meters high

Up to moderate to rough seas (small vessels should take precautionary measures or avoid sailing, if possible)

Seaboards of Isabela and Ilocos Sur; northern seaboards of La Union and Pangasinan – waves up to 2.5 meters high

Northern seaboard of Aurora; western seaboards of Pangasinan, Lubang Islands, Calamian Islands, and mainland Palawan; seaboards of Zambales and Bataan; eastern seaboards of Catanduanes, Siargao-Bucas Grande Islands, Surigao del Sur, and Davao Oriental – waves up to 2 meters high

Kiyapo was the Philippines’ 11th tropical cyclone for 2026, and the fourth for July alone. – Rappler.com

World.title: [Vantage Point] Oil’s false prophets
World.content:
The Economist mocked investors in late April for predicting Brent crude oil to reach roughly US$88 per barrel by the end of the year.

Brent Crude—a light, sweet crude oil originally extracted from the North Sea—is widely used as the primary international benchmark for pricing oil globally because its properties make it easy to refine into high-demand products like gasoline and diesel. On July 2, however, the publication issued a retraction as spot Brent prices plummeted to slightly over $70.

That mea culpa looked sincere, but it committed a new forecasting mistake. It compared oil for delivery at year-end with a single day’s price in July, erroneously treating the difference as a verdict on a war and a timeline that have yet to conclude.

A December futures contract and a July spot Brent answer different questions. While spot measures an immediately available barrel, a year-end contract reflects expected supply, demand, inventories, storage costs, interest rates, and geopolitical risk months ahead.

The valid test was not whether spot stood below $88 on July 2, but how that December contract had moved since April and where it eventually settled. Brent surged toward $100 as attacks against tankers and threats to the Strait of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb returned, making the apology another attempt to call the ending before the final act.

The two maritime straits are the world’s most critical chokepoints, handling a combined total of over 20 million barrels of oil daily and a significant percentage of global container trade. Recent blockades due to the ongoing conflict between the United States and Iran have severely disrupted these global energy and commercial shipping corridors.

Oil forecasting in wartime fails because analysts confuse three quantities: gross supply disruption, net market deficit, and quoted price. During March, April and May, flows averaged only 2.7 million, implying a 17.3-million-barrel reduction in daily traffic.

Global production fell 10.1 million barrels a day in March. By May, it stood 13.6 million below its prewar level. The International Energy Agency (IEA) was not exaggerating when it called this the largest physical oil disruption in history.

Losing 13.6 million barrels of production, however, does not create an equal market deficit. The balance is production plus inventory releases, minus consumption and stockbuilding.

In the second quarter, global demand fell by almost 5 million barrels a day year on year. IEA countries authorized 400 million barrels from emergency reserves, while observed inventories declined at an average 3.8 million barrels daily after hostilities began. Atlantic Basin exports redirected toward Asia rose by 3.5 million barrels a day. These responses did not erase the loss; they prevented its full force from appearing in spot Brent.

China ‘saves the world’?

Although China supplied a separate adjustment, saying that Beijing “saved the world” confuses a drop in demand with actual production. Chinese imports dropped from a five-year average of 11.5 million barrels a day to about 8 million during the crisis, then plunged to 7.12 million in June—the lowest since 2016.

China and Japan together cut imports by nearly 6 million barrels daily as refinery runs and industrial consumption weakened. Those absent Chinese bids released cargoes for other buyers, but no additional oil was manufactured.

This is where linear forecasts collapse. Analysts estimate how much supply is lost and apply an assumed price response, but neither side remains stable. A closure may stop tankers without destroying production; producers store oil until tanks fill, after which output must be shut. Consumers drive less, delay flights, switch fuels, or accept slower growth.

Governments release reserves, suspend taxes, and subsidize transport. Every price increase alters the demand it measures, making oil a feedback system rather than static arithmetic.

Opacity compounds the problem. Nobody outside Beijing can measure China’s strategic stocks or predict when officials will replenish them. Spare production is counted even when the barrels sit behind a blocked strait. Announced pipeline capacity is confused with usable capacity: Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates had about 2.6 million barrels a day of spare bypass capacity before the crisis, which is a fraction of normal Hormuz traffic. Politics is less tractable still. A ceasefire can remove $20 of risk premium; one tanker attack can restore it overnight.

Brent can give false comfort. Motorists buy refined fuel, not crude, and their bill includes refinery margins, freight, war-risk insurance, currencies, taxes, and inventory timing. During the crisis, crude weakened, while diesel and gasoline remained scarce. Refining margins exceeded $60 a barrel, while Asian refined-product imports remained below prewar levels.

Moderate Brent could thus coexist with punishing Philippine diesel prices. Anyone watching crude alone was measuring the input, while missing the damaged machinery converting it into fuel.

The honest method is scenario analysis, not theatrical precision. A durable reopening of Hormuz may return Brent toward $70 to $80; intermittent disruption combined with Chinese restocking can support $90 to $110; simultaneous restrictions at Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb can make $120 plausible.

These are conditional ranges, not prophecies. These are conditional figures that must be adjusted as key factors shift. These factors include transit volumes, inventory releases, Chinese import levels, consumer demand drop-offs, and overall geopolitical conflict duration.

The Economist deserves credit for admitting error, but its deeper mistake was believing that one price snapshot could settle the argument. The shock was real: more than 1.3 billion barrels of cumulative Middle East supply were lost, while inventories and emergency reserves absorbed the damage.

The world was not rescued from scarcity; it borrowed barrels from the past, suppressed present demand, and reduced its insurance against the future. Forecasting fails when analysts mistake temporary resilience for abundance—and forget that in wartime, the crucial number is not today’s price, but how many cushions remain when tomorrow’s disruption arrives. – Rappler.com

This analysis draws on oil-market data from the International Energy Agency, including its March, April, and June 2026 reports and its assessment of the Strait of Hormuz disruption; the US Energy Information Administration’s estimates of normal Hormuz traffic and available Saudi and UAE bypass capacity; and Reuters reports on Brent prices, China’s crude imports, global refining margins, and Asia’s refined-product shortage.

The projected Brent ranges of $70–$80, $90–$110 and $120 or higher are my own scenario estimates, not forecasts issued by these institutions, and depend on the duration of the conflict, Hormuz transit volumes, Chinese restocking, inventory depletion, and any simultaneous disruption at Bab el-Mandeb.

World.title: LeBron James to join 76ers for record-extending 24th NBA season
World.content:
'I still want to compete, to win, and to have a chance at the feeling of winning another championship,' says LeBron James as he teams up with Joel Embiid, Tyrese Maxey, and Jaylen Brown in a stacked 76ers crew

LeBron James has decided to join the Philadelphia 76ers for the final chapter of his NBA career, he said on Friday, July 24, forgoing bigger paydays for one more shot at a championship with a franchise that has not won a title in 43 years.

The league’s all-time leading scorer, who had the basketball world on tenterhooks for weeks awaiting his decision on what team he would join for his record-extending 24th NBA season, delivered the news in a series of social media posts.

James spent the last eight seasons of his glittering career with the Los Angeles Lakers, leading them to a title in 2020 after two separate stints with the Cleveland Cavaliers and four years with the Miami Heat.

“This is my last decision. I’m not going for money. I’m not going for family. What am I really playing for at this point? I still want to sacrifice. I still want to work. I still want to grind. I still want to compete, to win, and to have a chance at the feeling of winning another championship,” James wrote on social media.

“I believe I can help make the Philadelphia 76ers a championship team and I am so excited to energize a new fan base and start this incredible journey one last time. Thank you LA. Miami I’ll forever love and Northeast Ohio will always be home!”

James did not disclose terms of the deal but ESPN reported that the four-time champion signed a two-year, $8 million contract with a player option.

The four-time NBA Most Valuable Player will join forces with Joel Embiid, Tyrese Maxey, and recently acquired Jaylen Brown in a 76ers team that moved from 20-1 odds to win the NBA title to 10-1 after his announcement.

The Sixers made the 2026 NBA playoffs by securing the Eastern Conference’s seventh seed through a play-in tournament before falling to the eventual champion New York Knicks in the second round.

James considered retirement

A number of teams had been pursuing James, with Cleveland, Miami, the Golden State Warriors, and Minnesota Timberwolves all believed to have been interested in the high-profile free agent.

The 41-year-old James, who last March surpassed Robert Parish’s record for most career regular-season games played, has continued to perform at an elite level despite his age.

He earned a league-record 22nd consecutive All-Star selection last February during a season in which he averaged 20.9 points, 6.1 rebounds, and 7.2 assists over 60 games. His season ended when the Lakers were swept from the second round of the playoffs in May and he initially thought about retiring.

“I thought I was done when the season ended. I wasn’t ready to announce it, and I knew I needed some time to really decide, but I was pretty sure I played my last game. I was honest at that last press conference when I said I needed to look at myself and decide if I still love this game. I still truly love this game, and I have more to give,” James said.

“The last few weeks have really been special. I’ve never been able to have no clue what to do and take real time to just think. I’ve had an incredible few months with all the people I love trying to figure it all out.”

In a testament to his durability, James and his son Bronny became the first father-son duo to play together in a regular-season NBA game in October 2024, fulfilling what he had long said was one of his remaining basketball goals.

Longest NBA career

James, a four-time NBA Finals Most Valuable Player, joined the Lakers in 2018. He set the league record for the longest career in NBA history last year when he surpassed Vince Carter’s mark of 22 seasons.

He was selected with the first pick in the 2003 NBA Draft by his hometown Cavaliers, where he spent seven seasons before announcing during a live TV special titled “The Decision” that he was leaving for Miami.

The announcement damaged James’ public image and led to many people burning his replica No. 23 jerseys on Cleveland’s streets that night.

In Miami, James teamed up with Dwyane Wade and Chris Bosh to create an instant powerhouse that won two NBA titles during their four seasons together in South Beach.

James returned to Cleveland and in 2016 rallied the team from a 3-1 series deficit in the NBA Finals to stun the Golden State Warriors and make good on his promise to deliver the Cavaliers their first championship.

Two years later, James again left his hometown team, where he remains the franchise leader in nearly every major statistical category, to join the Lakers, where for the first time he played in the NBA’s Western Conference. – Rappler.com

World.title: Signal No. 3 up as Kiyapo now a severe tropical storm
World.content:
KIYAPO. Satellite image of Severe Tropical Storm Kiyapo (Noul) as of July 24, 2026, 7 pm.

Three islands in the Babuyan group are placed under Signal No. 3 at 8 pm on Friday, July 24, due to Severe Tropical Storm Kiyapo (Noul)

MANILA, Philippines – Kiyapo (Noul) strengthened from a tropical storm into a severe tropical storm on Friday, July 24, prompting the raising of Signal No. 3 for some islands in the Babuyan group early evening.

The Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) said in a bulletin issued at 8 pm on Friday that Kiyapo now has maximum sustained winds of 95 kilometers per hour from the previous 85 km/h. Its gustiness is now up to 130 km/h from 115 km/h.

As of 7 pm, the severe tropical storm was still over the coastal waters of Calayan Island, which belongs to the Babuyan group and is part of the municipality of Calayan in Cagayan province.

It is moving west northwest at a slightly slower 25 km/h from 30 km/h. Generally, however, it has been relatively fast in its passage through extreme Northern Luzon.

Earlier at 2:10 pm, Kiyapo made landfall as a tropical storm in Camiguin Island — also belonging to the Babuyan group.

It is projected to leave the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR) by late Friday evening or early Saturday morning, July 25.

World.title: Mount Maculot in Batangas remains closed to trekkers – LGU
World.content:
Mount Maculot in Cuenca, Batangas is temporarily closed to hikers as local authorities implement rehabilitation efforts and new tourism management measures to ensure sustainability and visitor safety. — Photo courtesy of MENRO LGU-Cuenca

LUCENA CITY — Climbing activities at Mount Maculot in Cuenca, Batangas, remain strictly prohibited, the local tourism office reiterated on Friday, July 24.

In a public advisory, the Cuenca Tourism Office (CTO) clarified that the climbing ban covers all areas of Mount Maculot, all hiking and climbing activities, and any purpose or reason for attempting to ascend the mountain.

“This prohibition applies to all areas of Mount Maculot, all types of climbing activities, and any reason or purpose for attempting to climb the mountain,” the advisory stated.

Article continues after this 

The CTO also denied claims that climbing is allowed in other parts of the mountain or that only the Rockies and Summit areas remain closed.

READ: Mount Maculot closed for rehabilitation, tourism planning

“If there are reports claiming that climbing is allowed in other parts of the mountain or that only the Rockies and Summit areas are closed, our office strongly denies such statements,” the tourism office said.

It added that such claims were neither coordinated with nor reported to the barangay, the municipal government, or the CTO.

The continued closure is being enforced under Executive Order No. 1, Series of 2020.

Article continues after this 

During Holy Week in March, the Cuenca local government reiterated that hiking activities at the 3,107-foot Mount Maculot would remain suspended “for the foreseeable future” as part of efforts to promote responsible and sustainable tourism.

Authorities are assessing the mountain’s carrying capacity to determine the safe number of visitors it can accommodate while protecting its natural environment and ensuring sustainable tourism management.

Article continues after this 

A comprehensive tourism master plan is also being finalized to guide the site’s long-term development and management.

The temporary closure will allow the local government to implement several measures, including introducing environmental user fees, retraining and re-accrediting local guides, rehabilitating and properly managing existing trails, and deploying additional personnel.

Mount Maculot is among the most popular hiking destinations in the Calabarzon region, known for its scenic views of Taal Lake.

The mountain attracts day hikers, campers, and outdoor enthusiasts, particularly during Holy Week and the summer season.

World.title: Leyte heritage advocates push to save Carigara landmarks
World.content:
Photo courtesy of Carigara Heritage Society

MANILA, Philippines — Heritage advocates in Leyte have renewed calls to preserve Carigara’s historic buildings, ancestral houses, monuments, and other cultural landmarks, warning that neglect and rapid modernization threaten to erase the town’s centuries-old cultural legacy.

The Carigara Heritage Society (CHS) urged the restoration and protection of the municipality’s heritage structures, saying they embody the town’s collective memory and should be safeguarded for future generations.

Council Member Myla Aguilar, who also serves as CHS president, said preserving these landmarks would help younger generations appreciate their cultural roots while strengthening the town’s identity.

Article continues after this 

READ: Magnitude 6.9 earthquake kills 61, damages heritage churches in Cebu

“Preserving heritage structures strengthens local identity and promotes pride among residents while creating opportunities to boost cultural tourism and local economic development,” Aguilar said.

Aguilar authored Municipal Ordinance 2025-016, which identifies local cultural properties, establishes a heritage zone in Carigara, and creates the Carigara Council on Culture and the Arts. The council is envisioned as the municipality’s counterpart to the National Commission for Culture and the Arts, tasked with protecting and promoting local cultural heritage and the arts.

Since its establishment in August 2025, the CHS has intensified efforts to encourage residents, particularly young people, to rediscover Carigara’s history. Among its initiatives is the “Heritage Spokes” tour, which features the town’s historic buildings and ancestral homes while highlighting Carigara’s role in Leyte’s history and its well-preserved architectural heritage.

“Every old building tells a story. When we lose these structures, we lose a part of who we are,” Aguilar said.

Article continues after this 

Carigara is considered the first town established in Eastern Visayas, possibly predating 1571. It once served as the province’s first capital and housed the cabecera of the Jesuit mission, making it the center of Christian evangelization in Leyte. Its historic district remains home to structures that reflect centuries of religious, commercial, governmental, and family life.

The CHS said preserving historic structures is not only about protecting old buildings but also about safeguarding the stories, traditions, and collective memory that define Carigara as one of Leyte’s oldest towns.

Article continues after this 

READ: Search on for shipwrecks in San Bernardino Strait

Heritage advocates also said conserving the town’s historic core could spur local economic development. They noted that heritage conservation efforts in other parts of the Philippines have attracted tourists, researchers, pilgrims, and entrepreneurs, creating jobs while strengthening community pride.

According to the group, every restored ancestral home, maintained monument, preserved historical marker, and shared story helps ensure that Carigara’s history remains a living legacy rather than a fading memory.

For the CHS, protecting the town’s cultural landmarks is ultimately about preserving the spirit of Carigara so that future generations can experience its history through the places and traditions that have shaped the municipality for centuries. /das

World.title: Seaweed processors in Pangasinan get BFAR livelihood aid
World.content:
Cato Calipi Association president Hilda Espinosa proudly displays seaweed-based buchi following the group’s receipt of BFAR livelihood assistance to expand its food processing enterprise. — Photo by Yolanda Sotelo

ALAMINOS CITY, Pangasinan — Two fisherfolk organizations in this province received livelihood assistance packages worth P600,000 each from the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR) in the Ilocos Region to strengthen their seaweed-based food processing enterprises.

The beneficiaries are the Cato Calipi Association (CCA) of Infanta and the Ilio-Ilio Farmers and Fisherfolk Agricultural Cooperative of Burgos, two coastal towns facing the West Philippine Sea.

In a recent interview, BFAR Regional Director Remely Lachica said each package includes a food cart, portable solar generator, refrigerator, cooking and food processing equipment, utensils, and raw materials needed to launch and sustain the livelihood project. The assistance was turned over to the groups last week.

Article continues after this 

READ: BFAR opens P5-M seaweed laboratory in Pangasinan

Before the distribution last week, BFAR also provided business capability-building training to help the beneficiaries manage and operate their enterprises.

“The project is essential for facilitating the efficient and sustainable storage and marketing of seaweed products, ensuring proper storage conditions, and supporting the growth of the seaweed industry,” Lachica said.

CCA president Hilda Espinosa said the association’s 38 members — mostly fishermen and their wives — are grateful for the support, which will enable them to produce buchi, pastillas, and other kakanin enriched with Eucheuma seaweed.

She said the group’s food cart has been set up at the Cato Fish Port, where it serves residents and fishing boat workers.

Article continues after this 

According to Espinosa, their seaweed-based snacks have become popular among customers because they are both nutritious and filling.

The project is part of BFAR’s Enhanced Philippine Seaweed Development Program (EPSDP), under a memorandum of agreement signed with the two organizations.

Article continues after this 

The EPSDP is one of BFAR’s flagship livelihood programs aimed at reducing poverty by increasing seaweed production and providing fisherfolk organizations with appropriate technologies and livelihood support for seaweed farming and processing. /das

World.title: Oriental Mindoro power coop defends high rates, welcomes probe
World.content:
INQUIRER FILES

CALAPAN CITY, Oriental Mindoro — The Oriental Mindoro Electric Cooperative (Ormeco) has defended the province’s high electricity rates, saying it did not pass on the full cost of power to consumers and expressing support for an investigation into issues surrounding electricity charges.

In a statement released Friday, July 24, Ormeco said it recognized the burden of higher electricity bills on Mindoreño households and acknowledged consumers’ right to seek answers.

The statement came a day before a planned protest by the Mindoro Consumer Coalition, which is demanding lower electricity rates and an investigation into the cooperative and the National Electrification Administration (NEA) over alleged irregularities in the Competitive Selection Process (CSP) for power supply contracts.

Article continues after this 

READ: Consumer group seeks probe into Oriental Mindoro’s power situation

Ormeco clarified that while the actual cost of purchased electricity in May 2026 reached P18.2907 per kilowatt-hour (kWh), consumers were billed only P14.9177 per kWh, with the cooperative initially absorbing the P97.71 million difference.

It said the recovery of the deferred amount is subject to a formal petition before the Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC), which evaluated six recovery scenarios to minimize the impact on consumers.

The cooperative also disputed claims that electricity rates had already reached P21 per kWh, saying the figure was merely an estimate and not the actual rate charged. It said the official electricity rate for July 2026 is P17.2278 per kWh, as reflected in its monthly rate publication.

Ormeco stressed that it does not profit from higher generation charges, explaining that it operates as a non-stock, non-profit electric cooperative and that generation charges are pass-through costs paid directly to power suppliers.

Article continues after this 

READ: Lightning strike triggers province-wide blackout in Oriental Mindoro

According to the cooperative, the spike in electricity costs was primarily caused by its reliance on a temporary Emergency Power Supply (EPS), which carries higher generation costs and is not covered by the Universal Charge for Missionary Electrification (UCME) subsidy. It said the emergency arrangement was necessary while new suppliers under the province’s 57-megawatt Competitive Selection Process await provisional authority to operate from the ERC.

Article continues after this 

The cooperative also cited higher global fuel prices triggered by the Middle East crisis and the national government’s declaration of a State of National Energy Emergency in March 2026 as contributing factors.

Ormeco further noted that the ERC’s approval in October 2025 of the National Power Corp.’s petition increasing the Subsidized Approved Generation Rate (SAGR) from P7.39 to P9.2464 per kWh also affected electricity prices, describing it as a nationwide policy beyond the cooperative’s control.

The electric cooperative said it expects generation costs to decline once new power plants with a combined 105.5 MW contracted capacity become fully operational. It added that it has issued demand letters and implemented plant performance monitoring protocols for suppliers that have yet to commence operations.

As a consumer relief measure, Ormeco said the ERC has suspended electricity disconnections for unpaid bills until October 2026. Consumers using 200 kWh or less per month may also pay their bills in installments for at least three months.

Addressing calls for an investigation, the cooperative said it welcomes transparency and will fully cooperate with any inquiry by the Department of Energy and the ERC. It noted that Rep. Alfonso Umali Jr. has already requested a comprehensive review by the two agencies.

Ormeco also said it regularly publishes its monthly electricity rates and remains open to dialogue with consumer organizations through its Member Consumer Owners Organization (MCOO) councils across Oriental Mindoro’s 14 municipalities and Calapan City.

The cooperative said it shares the public’s goal of achieving “more affordable, reliable and transparent electricity service” for all Mindoreños. /das

World.title: First tranche of P85 daily wage hike in NCR takes effect
World.content:
INQUIRER FILES

MANILA, Philippines — The first tranche of the P85 daily wage hike in the National Capital Region took effect on Saturday, July 25.

Under the first tranche of the Wage Order No. NCR-27, Metro Manila minimum wage earners will get a P60 increase in their daily salary.

READ: Inflation, jobs, corruption, WPS: Questions hanging over Sona 2026

Article continues after this 

This effectively adjusts the income of those in the non-agricultural sector from P695 to P755, while those in the agriculture sector, service and retail shops with 15 or fewer employees, and manufacturing firms with fewer than 10 employees will have salary increases from P658 to P718.

Meanwhile, the second tranche which will guarantee a P25 wage increase will take effect on January 20, 2027. This will bring the daily minimum salary for the non-agriculture sector to P780, and P743 for those in the agriculture sector, service and retail shops with 15 or fewer employees, and manufacturing firms with fewer than 10 employees.

With this, the Department of Labor and Employment (Dole) said that this wage hike is the “largest in Metro Manila to date,” where 1.1 million workers are expected to benefit from.

READ: NCR workers to get 1st tranche of P85 wage hike on July 25, not July 19

“In line with the implementation, the labor chief continues to remind employers to follow the wage adjustment, as non-compliance will result in penalties set by law. He also urged resolving wage distortion, or the adjustment of salaries above the minimum wage, through collective bargaining agreements between labor and management,” the Dole said in a press release.

Article continues after this 

Despite the call of a non-government organization Foundation for Economic Freedom to the government to suspend the implementation of the wage order, the Palace earlier said that it will not defer the wage hike.

The group said that it should be suspended until the spirit of tripartism is upheld and a consensus among employers, labor, and government is reached.” /das

World.title: Kiyapo intensifies as it exits PAR; Signal No. 1 in 5 N. Luzon areas
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines – Severe Tropical Storm Kiyapo (international name: Noul) has intensified into a typhoon as it exited the Philippine area of responsibility (PAR) early Saturday morning, according to the state weather bureau.

In its early morning bulletin, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (Pagasa) reported that Kiyapo exited PAR at around 3 a.m.

It was last spotted some 320 kilometers (km.) west of Basco, Batanes, with a maximum wind speed of 120 kilometers per hour (kph) near the center and gusts of iup to 150 kph while moving west-northwest at 25 kph.

Tropical cyclone wind signal number 1 is still up over Batanes, western portion of Babuyan Islands (Calayan, Dalupiri, Fuga Islands) northwestern part of mainland Cagayan (Pamplona, Sanchez-Mira, Claveria, Santa Praxedes, northern part of Apayao (Luna, Calanasan) and Ilocos Norte.

World.title: Lacson: More ‘damning evidence’ in Taguig projects
World.content:
Sen. Panfilo “Ping” Lacson on Friday hinted at uncovering more “damning evidence” in his investigation into alleged anomalous infrastructure projects in Taguig City, declaring that the “list lengthens” and the “case strengthens.”

Lacson had begun his inquiry into infrastructure projects in Taguig, the bailiwick of Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano, amid an escalating feud between the two senators.

Article continues after this 

Cayetano, whose wife Lani is Taguig Mayor, has denied the existence of ghost projects in the city and challenged Lacson to produce evidence.

Lacson has also been posting further findings on X (formerly Twitter) but did not provide details.

‘Double appropriation’

His remarks came amid renewed scrutiny over the controversial cauldron-like structure built for the Philippines’ hosting of the 2019 Southeast Asian (SEA) Games, after the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) said it would revisit issues that hounded the SEA Games organizing body then headed by Cayetano.

Lacson had also earlier flagged a possible “double appropriation” involving two P100-million allocations that appeared to cover the same slope protection project in Taguig City.

“One of the two must be ghost,” he said in an earlier post.

Article continues after this 

Lacson said his team had found three additional P100-million slope protection projects under the 2025 General Appropriations Act, raising the total value of the Taguig projects being scrutinized from P2.085 billion to P2.385 billion.

He said his team had documented at least two case studies involving suspected ghost projects in Taguig.

Article continues after this 

The Inquirer has sought Cayetano’s reaction but he has yet to respond as of press time.

World.title: Marcos teases new chapter in corruption fight
World.content:
“Abangan ang susunod na kabanata” (Wait till the next episode)—as the popular saying goes.

This was President Marcos’ cryptic response on Friday when asked if he would again tackle corruption issues in his penultimate State of the Nation Address (Sona) on Monday, as he did in his Sona last year.

Article continues after this 

In his 2025 presidential address, Mr. Marcos delivered a fiery rebuke against widespread corruption in flood control projects.

But critics have belittled his catchphrase in that speech “Mahiya naman kayo (Have some shame)!” since no one among his close allies have been charged in connection with the flood works scandal.

The President, however, hinted at renewed campaign against corruption when he spoke to reporters on Friday.

A survey by Pulse Asia conducted June 28 to July 3 and July 6 showed that 29.8 percent of Filipinos want Mr. Marcos to discuss the government’s fight against corruption in his upcoming speech.

Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial (1.2 percent) and the recent leadership crisis in the Senate (1 percent) were among the least concerns, according to the Stratbase Group-commissioned survey among 2,400 respondents.

Article continues after this 

What biz groups want

Meanwhile, business groups representing the country’s leading manufacturers and exporters said they want Mr. Marcos to lay out concrete plans to reduce the cost of doing business.

In a statement by her group, Federation of Philippine Industries (FPI) chairperson Elizabeth Lee said “Cutting power costs is a key factor to putting Philippine manufacturing on equal footing across” the region.

Article continues after this 

FPI said lower power costs remain critical to energy-intensive industries, such as steel, cement, chemicals and food processing. It said reforms in the energy sector—including renewable energy expansion, grid modernization and policy reviews—should be accelerated.

The group also called for measures to reduce logistics costs, which it said are driven not only by fuel prices but also by port congestion, redundant local government pass-through fees and other operational bottlenecks.

World.title: Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan Expand Strategic Partnership Through Trade, Transport and Regional Agreements
World.content:
101462

ALMATY – Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan signed regional and commercial agreements worth more than 80 billion tenge (US$146 million) on July 24 as the two countries advanced cooperation in trade, transport, industry and cross-border development during a series of meetings in Aktau.

The agreements were concluded following the 23rd meeting of the Kazakhstan-Uzbekistan Joint Intergovernmental Commission and the inaugural Council of Regional Leaders, co-chaired by Kazakh Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov and Uzbek Prime Minister Abdulla Aripov.

The leaders reviewed implementation of agreements reached by Presidents Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and Shavkat Mirziyoyev. They discussed priorities for expanding cooperation in trade, investment, industrial production, transport, regional development and cultural ties.

“Thanks to the joint efforts of our heads of state, multifaceted cooperation between our countries continues to develop dynamically and today serves as a successful example of partnership for the entire Central Asian region,” Bektenov said.

Aripov said the governments remain committed to implementing the tasks set by both presidents during their meetings in Bukhara, Astana and Turkistan this year.

“I am ready to take all necessary measures to fulfill these instructions. I am confident that today’s negotiations will contribute to the further development of trade, investment, industrial, transport, interregional and cultural cooperation,” he said.

Transport and logistics

Transport connectivity featured prominently in the discussions as both countries seek to strengthen regional trade corridors. According to Bektenov, rail freight between Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan increased 16% in 2025, reaching 32.3 million tons. The two governments have adopted a joint action plan to increase railway corridor capacity from 35 million to 60 million tons.

The prime ministers also visited the Aktau International Sea Trade Port, Kazakhstan’s largest maritime hub and a key component of the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (TITR). Covering 44 hectares, the port can handle nearly 12 million tons of cargo annually and provides year-round connections to the Caucasus, Central Asia and the Caspian region.

According to Bektenov, Kazakhstan completed dredging works at the Kuryk Port in 2025, becoming the first Caspian state to do so. Similar dredging at Aktau is expected to finish by the end of this year, allowing fully loaded vessels to enter the port safely while increasing cargo capacity.

According to Kazakhstan Temir Zholy Chairman Yelzhas Otynshiyev, the combined capacity of the Aktau and Kuryk ports now stands at 22 million tons annually.

He highlighted that container transit through Kazakhstan’s Caspian ports along the TITR has increased 3.8 times between 2022 and 2025. To support further growth, Kazakhstan has launched the first phase of a new container hub at Aktau with an annual capacity of 140,000 TEU, which is expected to expand to 240,000 TEU after completion of the second phase in 2027-2028.

The country has also ordered six new container vessels, four scheduled for delivery in 2027 and two in 2028, while modernization continues on the Shalkar-Beyneu and Beyneu-Mangystau railway sections to improve cargo access to Aktau and Kuryk.

Cargo handled through Aktau and Kuryk on behalf of Uzbekistan increased by more than 60% in 2025, supported by favorable tariffs and improved transport infrastructure.

“Our task is to provide Central Asian cargo with fast and reliable access to the markets of the Caucasus, Türkiye and Europe. Kazakhstan is ready to expand transit of Uzbekistan’s export cargo through the ports of Aktau and Kuryk,” Bektenov said.

Trade and investment cooperation

Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan continue to deepen economic integration, with bilateral trade reaching $4.8 billion in 2025. During the first five months of 2026, trade increased 37% year-on-year to $2.3 billion.

Bektenov highlighted Kazakhstan’s export potential in metallurgy, mechanical engineering, petrochemicals, chemicals, pharmaceuticals, transport equipment and construction materials, while emphasizing implementation of a $7.8 billion investment and trade roadmap designed to diversify bilateral trade and attract new investment.

Industrial cooperation remains one of the partnership’s fastest-growing areas. The two countries are jointly implementing 80 projects worth more than $1.8 billion. Fifteen projects valued at $227 million have already been launched, creating nearly 5,000 jobs, while six additional projects worth $102 million are under active implementation. Authorities are also developing 59 new initiatives totaling approximately $1.5 billion.

World.title: Kazakh FM Urges More Practical SCO as Global Turbulence Reshapes Regional Priorities
World.content:
118693

ALMATY – The Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) is increasingly shifting from a platform centered on political dialogue and regional security toward one that places greater emphasis on economic resilience, trade connectivity and practical cooperation, as member states respond to growing geopolitical and supply-chain disruptions.

That transformation was at the center of discussions during the July 24 meeting of the SCO Council of Foreign Ministers in Cholpon-Ata, the Kyrgyz Republic, where Kazakhstan called for stronger coordination on trade security, transport connectivity, climate resilience and water management ahead of the organization’s summit in Bishkek on Sept. 1.

Speaking at the meeting, Kazakh Foreign Minister Yermek Kosherbayev said that the rapidly changing geopolitical environment is making economic resilience an urgent priority for the region.

“Geopolitical turbulence, increasingly spilling over into the military sphere, is seriously affecting the stability of international trade relations. Today, the security of supply chains is becoming an ever more pressing issue, including for Kazakhstan,” he said.

Kosherbayev cited attacks by unidentified unmanned systems on energy infrastructure and tankers chartered by Kazakhstan to transport oil as an illustration of growing vulnerabilities affecting international logistics. He said that these risks underscore the need for the SCO to make the protection of regional trade routes one of its strategic priorities.

The emphasis on supply-chain security reflects a broader shift in Kazakhstan’s regional diplomacy. As global trade routes face growing disruption from geopolitical tensions and attacks on critical infrastructure, Astana is increasingly framing transport connectivity not only as an economic objective but also as a strategic security issue.

Analysts say Kazakhstan’s priorities reflect broader changes taking place within the SCO itself. According to Manarbek Kabaziyev, deputy chairman of the board of the Foreign Policy Research Institute under Kazakhstan’s Foreign Ministry, the organization itself is undergoing a broader transformation.

“The SCO is indeed going through a stage of qualitative transformation. While its primary task in the early years was strengthening trust and ensuring regional security, today its agenda has become much broader. The focus now includes trade and economic cooperation, transport and logistics connectivity, digitalization, energy, food security and technological cooperation,” he said.

That assessment closely aligns with Kazakhstan’s own priorities within the organization. Alongside transport security, Kosherbayev called for deeper cooperation on climate adaptation and sustainable water management, reiterating Kazakhstan’s proposal to establish an International Water Organization under the auspices of the United Nations and an SCO Water Issues Analysis Center.

The minister also emphasized that the SCO should continue adapting its institutions to contemporary challenges, reflecting Kazakhstan’s broader push to make regional organizations more responsive to economic and technological change.

For Kazakhstan, Kabaziyev said, the shift toward project-oriented cooperation carries particular strategic significance.

“Kazakhstan’s geographic position and its role as one of Eurasia’s key transit hubs objectively make the country one of the main beneficiaries of projects aimed at developing transport connectivity, digital logistics and regional value chains,” he said.

According to him, whether the SCO succeeds in making that transition will likely become one of the defining questions for the organization over the coming years.

Attention will now shift to the Sept. 1 SCO summit in Bishkek, where the organization’s heads of state are expected to define the bloc’s strategic priorities. The extent to which leaders embrace Kazakhstan’s calls for stronger economic coordination and practical cooperation may offer an early test of whether the SCO is indeed evolving beyond its traditional security agenda.

World.title: Kazakhstan Rises to 53rd in Updated Global Investment Risk and Resilience Index
World.content:
100803

ASTANA – Kazakhstan ranked 53rd out of 150 countries in the May 2026 Special Edition of the Global Investment Risk and Resilience Index (GIRRI), improving from 70th place in the original 2025 ranking, as the updated index reflects the impact of recent geopolitical and economic developments on global investment risk.

The updated ranking was released by Henley & Partners in cooperation with AlphaGeo and incorporates Country Risk Premium (CRP) data as of April 1, allowing the index to combine long-term structural resilience with real-time market assessments of sovereign risk.

The Global Investment Risk and Resilience Index evaluates countries using two core dimensions: structural resilience, which measures long-term economic, institutional and environmental strengths, and sovereign risk, reflecting exposure to political, financial and external shocks, according to Henley & Partners.

The May 2026 Special Edition does not revise the original methodology or resilience scores. Instead, it serves as a stress test of the existing framework by keeping structural resilience unchanged while updating the risk component with current market data.

According to the report, the revised rankings provide a risk-adjusted view of the global investment environment, showing how geopolitical and economic developments have reshaped investor perceptions.

The report notes that changes in country rankings reflect relative shifts in position compared with other countries rather than absolute improvements or deterioration in risk or resilience. The update is intended to illustrate how the global investment landscape is evolving as markets respond to current geopolitical and economic conditions.
