The Commonwealth Games said they won’t provide an update on the injury to England’s Gabriel Langton who lay motionless after falling from the high bar during the men’s all-around team final.

In a statement to the Telegraph, London, a spokesperson for the Games said, “We are aware of an injury to one of the athletes at the gymnastics session this evening. The welfare of athletes at the Games is our absolute priority. Medical teams at the venue responded quickly to the incident. We will not be providing any further update.”

Gabriel Langton competing on the rings earlier in the competition. Getty Images

Three-time Olympic gold medallist Max Whitlock (who was named to England’s Commonwealth Games squad but withdrew because of an injury and was replaced by Langton) watched the 19-year-old fall and told the Telegraph: “It’s not official yet but we saw he was moving his arms and moving his legs. It was a horrible fall on the high bar.

“Both hands came off the bar, which is unusual on a skill like that, and then coming down onto his head from that height. It wasn’t nice to watch, it wasn’t nice to be in the arena, the atmosphere you could feel a big drop in it. It’s one of those things that when it happens in any kind of competition or sport, the whole atmosphere changes. It puts a lot into perspective.”

World.title: Odysseus didn’t rest on his laurels. But like the rest of us, maybe he should have
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsWork/life balance Opinion Odysseus didn’t rest on his laurels. But like the rest of us, maybe he should have Julia Baird Journalist, broadcaster, historian and author July 25, 2026 — 9:30am

July 25, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The phrase “resting on your laurels” hasn’t always been a criticism; once it was a point of praise. Instead of suggesting complacency and laziness, it was a public recognition of achievement. In Ancient Greece, athletes were awarded wreaths of laurel leaves – also known as bay leaves, the kind you pop into a soup or stock. The term had arisen from mythology and the age-old phenomenon of spurned men really not picking up the vibe. In short, the god Apollo had the hots for the beautiful river nymph Daphne, and pursued her doggedly despite her lack of interest. One day, when he was chasing her and had just caught her, she begged her father, the river god, to save her. Naturally, he turned her into a laurel tree. (To be fair, Cupid, annoyed with Apollo, had shot him with a gold-tipped arrow of love and Daphne with a lead-tipped arrow of repulsion, so this was never going to go well.) Matt Damon as Odysseus and Zendaya as Athena in The Odyssey. Apollo tried to salvage this turn of events by kissing the tree, whispering: “Since you cannot be my bride, you must be my tree!” He hacked off some branches to make a wreath for his head. Laurels became crowns of victory. From the 6th century BC, bay leaves were placed on the head of every winner at the Pythian Games in Delphi. Now, with the broad public dissection of The Odyssey, a rare box-office triumph, including talk of Odysseus’ relentless drive, I’d like to suggest we revert to the original, Grecian meaning of this long-misused term. Tell people to rest on their laurels for a bit! Stick it to the “rise and grind” of hustle culture, and celebrate a time to pause, regroup, be satisfied after something you’ve accomplished, instead of maniacally thundering towards the next hurdle.



When Chaucer wrote The Knight’s Tale in the late 1300s, he wrote that when someone is crowned with laurels, he is “crowned a conqueror [who] lived in joy and honour”. This, in my view, is what the phrase should mean: joy and honour. You’ve achieved something? Rest up, relax, marinate in that joy and honour. Related Article Cinema Confused by the gods, monsters and mortals of The Odyssey? This is your cheat sheet Then, as with so many traditions, things took a dark turn in Regency and Victorian times. In 1825, The Literary Chronicle and Weekly Review told novelist Maria Edgeworth that despite her literary success, she must not rest: “We do not affect to wish she should repose on her laurels and rest satisfied; on the contrary, we believe that genius is inexhaustible … For Miss Edgeworth there must be no rest on this side the grave.” This is so daft. As though it’s a bad thing to “rest satisfied”. The fact that the meaning of laurel-resting has flipped so firmly since its inception is surely a sign of the ushering-in of hustle culture following both the industrial and technological revolutions. (Note that the hustle is always assumed to occur in jobs outside the home, despite the considerable hustle within.) And anyway, why is Odysseus, a man who left his wife and son for decades to carry on in other countries, now being heralded simply as a hero without the observation that he is also the central figure in a cautionary tale?



Ryan Holiday, a bestselling author and advocate for stoicism, says that those who find Odysseus inspiring miss the fact that when he arrives home after a 20-year journey, he quickly turns on his heels and goes out raiding in an attempt to build wealth. He is restless, unsated, discontent. Related Article Cinema 17 kilometres of film, $47 a ticket: How The Odyssey is resurrecting film Holiday cites a poem I was obsessed with as a teenager, and stuffed into my backpack when I travelled: Ulysses by Tennyson. (Read it here.) The old king is pondering his life and future, his unquiet soul and inability to stop wandering the earth: “I cannot rest from travel: I will drink/Life to the lees … always roaming with a hungry heart”. He continues: “I am a part of all that I have met;/Yet all experience is an arch wherethro’/Gleams that untravell’d world whose margin fades/For ever and forever when I move./How dull it is to pause …” When I was a teenager, stomping around Europe with backpack and boots, this hunger for adventure mirrored my own. But now I can better see that perhaps the man needed to relax for a bit, spend time with his wife and son. Stoics generally recognised Odysseus’ good qualities, such as a capacity to endure and resist temptation. However, as Holiday points out, Stoics like Seneca objected to the romanticising of Odysseus and considered his insatiable appetites for motion more curse than blessing. Sometimes we forget the beauty of the pause, especially after a period of struggle. In the same way we tell people to “move on”, to rush past relationships or grief or the pain of giving birth, we need to have words and respect for a period when a kite lands, having sliced through clouds. To stop, to look in wonder. This doesn’t mean never trying again, not working hard in the future – nor sitting around gloating – just that, for a period, you should allow yourself to be content without punishing yourself with the next goal, or measuring your distance from various heights that others may have reached.



Surely we can accept that exhaustion does not equate to accomplishment? The automatic response to “how have you been?” shouldn’t be “yeah, crazy-busy, hectic, flat out”. Related Article Opinion

Film Hey Elon Musk, The Odyssey doesn’t fail because it’s woke. It’s not woke enough Bill Wyman Contributor As Angie Dixon wrote in digital magazine OnlySky after being forced into retirement by disability: “The reward for productivity is the expectation of more productivity. You finish one project and receive another. You hit one goal and create a bigger one. There is no finish line. Nobody appears with a certificate declaring that you have finally done enough and may now rest without guilt.” Well, if you’d like a certificate, please accept this column as one. Pin a bay leaf in your hair, or slip it into your wallet as a reminder that you’ve worked hard, you’ve cared immensely and that, when the time is right, you really should go and have some sweet rest on those laurels. Julia Baird is a journalist, author and regular columnist. Her latest book is Bright Shining: how grace changes everything. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: New blow for LIV Golf as Asian Tour partners with rivals
World.content:
SportGolfLIV Golf Series New blow for LIV Golf as Asian Tour partners with rivals Evin Priest July 25, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Professional golf’s four-year turf war appears close to being over after LIV Golf was dealt hammer blows by America’s PGA Tour and the DP World Tour this week as the rebel league’s tournament was being held in the Midlands of England. LIV was already reeling from the withdrawal of financier Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, but now the hopes it can continue into 2027 have taken a fresh hit. LIV Golf star Cameron Smith. Getty Images On Tuesday, while LIV golfers were playing practice rounds at the JCB course in England, news broke that the Asian Tour was partnering with LIV’s rivals, the DP World Tour and the PGA Tour. A new three-tour partnership will see pathways created for players from Asia to the top two levels in Europe, as well as co-sanctioned tournaments. While LIV is in the market seeking investment for 2027, it was a significant hurdle to jump because the Asian Tour had been a vital stepping stone to LIV.



Originally, the Asian Tour had aligned with LIV in a $US300 million partnership ahead of its 2022 launch, and in turn created the cashed-up “International Series”, which LIV golfers frequently played in. As a feeder tour, the International Series had also been vital to the promotion and relegation aspect of LIV – its 2026 season featured the top two players from the series’ order of merit list. As a secondary circuit, the Asian Tour also helped provide LIV with an external pathway for player turnover – an issue that had long been scrutinised during the league’s original pursuit of Official World Golf Ranking recognition. LIV can still stage its own qualifying school, but building a credible promotion pathway without the Asian Tour now becomes considerably more complex. The Asian Tour was also important because some of its historic national opens were part of LIV’s future plans.



With LIV’s future under a cloud, Asian Tour chief executive Cho Minn Thant said he had to consider pathways for his member players. “I think the timing is just right now; it’s all about timing,” Thant said this week. “We’d kept in touch [with the DP World Tour] over all these years. [In 2022], it was right for us to do a partnership with LIV Golf, but given the circumstances now, we’ve had to look at other options. Pathways to different tours are very important for our members.” Cho Minn Thant with LIV Golf’s Greg Norman in 2022. Getty Images After the Asian Tour news, the obstacles mounted for LIV. A report surfaced on Wednesday quoting two-time major winner Martin Kaymer, who captains the Cleeks GC team on LIV, saying that it was “highly unlikely” the $US40 million Team Championships finale in Michigan would go ahead. Then, on Thursday, the popular social media account Flushing It Golf – which has cultivated considerable access to tour players – published a post after speaking to a host of players at the JCB course.



Flushing It detailed how seven players told the account they plan to exit LIV after the 2026 season, “regardless of whether LIV Golf finds funding”. A clear pathway back to the PGA Tour was forged this year by former LIV golfers, American Patrick Reed and Eugenio Chacarra from Spain, who departed the league for the DP World Tour. American golfer Patrick Reed. Getty Images Reed and Chacarra, who have won multiple times on the DP World Tour this year, are ranked within the top three on its points list and are in line to receive two of the 10 cards on the PGA Tour for 2027 awarded to Europe’s best season-long points earners. This was followed by revelations that the volume of players from LIV seeking assurances from the DP World Tour about individual playing opportunities for 2027 had increased “significantly” in the past few weeks.



LIV has two more individual tournaments after England, including stops in New Jersey and Indianapolis. Related Article British Open ‘All hell broke loose’: Herbert reveals toll of LIV Golf uncertainty, says he considered quitting Sports fans now watch on to see what the future holds for a league that was reported to have received $US5 billion from the PIF since its creation in 2022. LIV disrupted the entire ecosystem of professional golf, luring massive stars such as Bryson DeChambeau, Australia’s own Cameron Smith, Dustin Johnson, Jon Rahm and others. The league’s enormous tournament purses and guaranteed roster forced the PGA Tour to keep up via supercharging prizemoney. There were positive outcomes for fans, including LIV pushing the PGA Tour to streamline its competition structure to entice top players to compete together more often and develop a more innovative TV broadcast. Australia also benefited in receiving the world-class LIV Adelaide tournament. But ultimately, a league that initially promised “golf, but louder” is struggling to be heard. The next few months will determine whether LIV Golf survives, is radically reinvented, or quietly fades away.

World.title: Despite everything FIFA threw at it, football really was the winner
World.content:
SportSoccerFIFA World Cup Opinion Despite everything FIFA threw at it, football really was the winner Malcolm Knox Journalist, author and columnist July 25, 2026 — 9:30am

July 25, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

“So it’s over – the few weeks every four years when you pretend you know something about football.” Cutting words to hear, at the end of an all-absorbing FIFA World Cup. My son spoke with his hand over his mouth, so I appealed to the referee (his mother) to get him sent off, but she was busy watching video replays. Soccer unites the world in sore-loserism. Illustration: Letch Having lost the point, I went down screaming in agony, ankle in one hand, eye socket in the other, rolling downhill on a flat floor. This earnt a red card for “blatant simulation”, so I called the President of the United States to get it overturned. But he was busy taking a call from Bryson DeChambeau whining at him to impose Mar-a-Lago rules on the British Open. Under the Mar-a-Lago rules of golf, it’s OK for a “winner” to stomp down the grass around your ball. Hell, it’s OK to throw your ball back onto the fairway. Mar-a-Lago rules had already been invoked to rig the World Cup, so why not the Open? But the President couldn’t take my call. As the final loser, I claimed there was a conspiracy against me. Don’t tell me I don’t know something about soccer. Soccer unites the world in sore-loserism.



The chaotic scenes after the World Cup final – Argentine players trying to punch on and earning posthumous red cards, doddering US Presidents trying to muscle into the winner’s celebration, the eruption of conspiracy theories about the game being rigged – turned out to be completely consistent with the philosophy now embedded into global professional sport. Throughout the tournament, nobody got beaten by a better opponent. There had to be corruption or malfeasance or dark political fishiness. This great compelling carnival of sport, as it escalated to its conclusion, became more and more anti-sport. Donald Trump muscles in on Spain’s World Cup success. Getty Images “Show me a good loser, and I’ll show you a loser,” was one of the famous lines from football coach Vince Lombardi. It is a most American idea, and for the five weeks of the World Cup this American allergy to being a good loser infused the peak event of global sport. Australia was not immune, just a small-scale example. When the Socceroos lost in the round of 32 to Egypt, it was difficult to hear any credit given to the opposition or any good grace, any acknowledgement that Egypt, a soccer-mad country of 120 million, might just have a better team than Australia. Instead, commentators attacked coach Tony Popovic for his selections, the tactics of being overly defensive, and the “mentality” of lacking a killer instinct. This reaction did not show Australia to be a small soccer nation. To the contrary, it showed us to be a small version of the big soccer nations.



When England fell to Argentina, commentators attacked coach Thomas Tuchel for his selections, the tactics of being overly defensive, and the “mentality” of lacking a killer instinct. When France fell to Spain, ditto. When Argentina finally lost the decider, same again: coach’s selections, tactics, mentality, with the requisite addition of conspiracy theories. (Curiously, after four years of the global conspiracy theory that the World Cup was rigged for Argentina to win, the new conspiracy theory is that it was rigged for them to lose. Conspiracy theories themselves turn out to be sore losers.) Argentina and Spain players clash after full-time in the World Cup final. Getty Images Whether the sport is a billion-dollar industrial complex, a national obsessive-compulsive disorder or a third-tier, underfunded winter code, the response to defeat replicates itself: blame your own, hint at off-field shenanigans, and never, on any account, pay due credit to the other team for just being better than you on the day. Never admit that your team was forced to be “too defensive” because the other team would not let them get the ball. Never admit that the better team won. Or, if you’re Argentina, turn your backs and never even acknowledge that the other team exists. To do so might risk making you a good loser: that is, a loser. Under the hyper-magnification of the current American cultural climate, the World Cup produced this jarring, compelling mix of the very best and the very worst that sport has to offer: sublime skills and atrocious chicanery; passion so unbearable that it found its final expression in violence; the sweet purity of a 30-metre shot into the top corner against a backdrop of the filth and rot of phone calls between Donnie and Gianni. The higher the stakes, the sharper the juxtaposition.



If there was a game after the final, on the trajectory the World Cup was going, it would have been settled by gunfire. Maybe that’s where we’re headed in 2030, unless FIFA can break the circuit it has constructed during the past half-century. Rodri lifts the trophy as Spain celebrate their World Cup victory. Getty Images We journalists get criticised for paying too much attention to sports administrators, but the World Cup shows how administrators set the tone for the diseases that infect games. Only because of FIFA’s work over the decades does a World Cup become such fertile ground for sore-loserism: for accusations of cheating and corruption, for refusal to accept defeat, for everything that denies that a fair contest has taken place. FIFA’s naked and, under president Gianni Infantino, proud transactionalism – from ticket prices to “hydration breaks” to political favours – lays the ground for the ultimate dissatisfaction, the casting of doubt on results, the suspicion that this was not a game, it was just another transaction.



And yet … and yet ... Just as the de facto world championship of golf, the British Open, emerged from the DeChambeau muck to give us a winner in Ryan Fox – the most likeable and homespun individual and a deserved champion golfer of the year – the World Cup gave us Spain. Related Article Analysis

FIFA World Cup Spanish domination shows the limitations of ‘suffering’ in football What had Spain done? They’d overcome the embarrassment of their first match, when they were unable to put a goal past Cabo Verde. (Which ended up not such an embarrassment, with superhuman Cabo Verde goalkeeper Vozinha being named in the official team of the tournament despite playing just four games.) Spain had overcome the dreadful luck of a deranged draw that forced them to beat Portugal, Belgium and France before they even made it to the final. Spain had developed a brand of soccer that asphyxiated their opponents and was coldly systematic, and yet also hypnotic and, in its way, utterly pure. Spain played the best football, and then they shoved the silly old man out of their way. Football really was the winner in the end, in spite of everything FIFA could throw at it. What a dizzying month. I might not know much about football, but I know when the good guys and the best team win.

World.title: Want to learn how to forgive? First, consult Taylor Swift
World.content:
NationalGood Weekend Want to learn how to forgive? First, consult Taylor Swift Sharon Bradley July 25, 2026 — 9:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

This story is part of the July 25 edition of Good Weekend. See all stories .

Each week, Good Weekend’s how-to column shares expert advice on how to navigate some of modern life’s big – and small – challenges. This week: How to forgive. Photo: Simon Letch The first question might be, “Should I forgive?“, suggests Luke Russell, professor of philosophy at Sydney University and author of Real Forgiveness. Resentment, he explains, lies at the heart of every grudge, but it can be protective. “It prompts the person who’s been wronged to stand up for themselves and face their wrongdoer, who might say, ‘I’ve hurt you: I feel guilty and want to apologise.’ ” It can keep you safe from further harm and pave the way for moral reform. He reminds me that Taylor Swift, queen of the grudge banger, is famously cautious when it comes to forgiving her “haters”. “You don’t have to forgive and forget to move on,” she told CBS. “If something’s toxic, and it’s only ever been that, what are you gonna do?” Forgive an unrepentant transgressor, she’s saying, and you risk becoming a doormat. It’s an alternative view in a modern society shaped by Christianity, self-help gurus and media tsar Oprah Winfrey, who generally espouse a model of unconditional forgiveness (the victim forgives her offender, regardless of whether they’re repentant).



Related Article Pop culture Pop star, philosopher, poet: Taylor Swift is shaking up how we think “Importantly, Oprah justifies forgiveness, not by pointing to the benefits that flow to the person who’s been forgiven, but to the benefits that are gained by the victim herself,” says Russell. Science is certainly on her side: recent reports reveal that hard-baked anger is a significant physiological burden, flooding our nervous system with cortisol and raising our blood pressure. But let’s assume the wrongdoer is no longer a threat; maybe they’re even dead. How do we go about releasing the negative emotion around an unacknowledged hurt? One: try to understand the perspective of the person who’s hurt you, says Russell: “Maybe you’ll start to feel some sympathy for them.” Two: ask yourself, “What am I getting from this continued resentment?” “If the answer’s, ‘Nothing useful’, you might conclude that it’s just something to get rid of” – an excellent pathway, he adds, if your offender’s no longer alive.



Three: go high and simply bask in the warm benevolence of committing a good deed. “You might think, ‘I need to be the better person here’, ” says Russell; also, perhaps, “I’m sick of being in this hate rut.” Four: consider whether you’ve ever harmed someone in the same way. “Just maybe,” he suggests, “it’d be hypocritical for you to maintain the rage.” Ask yourself what you’d want from your victim: their unending rancour or their mercy? Unlike an apology, he says, forgiveness doesn’t need to be “received” by the wrongdoer in order to assuage years of pent-up ire and usher in a new era of peace. Get the best of Good Weekend delivered to your inbox every Saturday morning.

World.title: Why are teachers paying extra tax? - Ask Susan
World.content:
Got questions? RNZ has a podcast, 'No Stupid Questions', with Susan Edmunds.

We'd love to hear more of your questions about money and the economy. You can send through written questions, like these ones, but even better, you can drop us a voice memo to our email questions@rnz.co.nz.

You can also sign up to RNZ's new money newsletter, 'Money with Susan Edmunds'.

Many teachers in NZ currently have significant size tax bills due to being paid by the Ministry of Education over 27 fortnights instead of the usual 26 fortnights for the financial year 1 April 2025 to 31 March 2026. My understanding is the PAYE tables can't cope or aren't designed for 27 weeks which causes the debt. If an extra pay period (eg 27 fortnightly or 53 weekly pays) causes a small tax bill, IRD may automatically write off the amount, provided your income is under $180,000. The maximum automatic write-off is $420 for fortnightly pays and $250 for weekly pays. If however you owe say $445 then you still need to pay the entire amount rather than the difference between $420 and $445.

This is an issue that I've looked at in the past because it can come up any time there is an extra pay-day for people in a year.

Robyn Walker, a tax partner at Deloitte, said Inland Revenue would usually write off the debt as long as there wasn't another source of income that wasn't correctly taxed.

You can't have it written off if you were entitled to Working for Families during the year, you used a tailored tax code, your tax code was wrong or you were not employed by the same employer for the full 12 months.

And you're right, Inland Revenue has restrictions on the amount that can be written off due to extra pay periods.

In this situation, there's not a lot you can do. You won't be paying more tax than you are meant to - it's just the surprise factor of having a bill you weren't expecting. IR may allow you to pay what you owe off over a period of time if you get in touch.

What if you don't want a slice of the AI hype? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 13m

Is there any connection between GDP and a nation's level of debt? Globally, New Zealand seems to be okay compared to Japan or the United States.

Gareth Kiernan, chief forecaster at Infometrics, said debt was typically expressed for countries as a percentage of GDP, reflecting that the larger an economy was, the more debt it should be able to service.

"Put another way, the higher a household's income, the larger mortgage they will be able to borrow and meet the repayments on.

"We also typically see that larger and/or more well-performing economies are given more latitude by financial markets about debt levels. Thus the likes of the US, Japan, and Germany can typically have higher debt levels (as a percentage of GDP) than New Zealand or Ireland before financial markets get concerned about the riskiness and start to demand significantly higher interest rates on that debt.

"These larger countries are seen as being more stable and able to withstand external shocks.

"Similarly, the interest rates required on debt for countries like Brazil or Indonesia will typically be higher than for the US or Japan because their economies and/or political environments are judged to be less stable and therefore riskier for lenders."

He said that was evident in the fact that US bond rates were about the same as in New Zealand but US government debt was 124 percent of GDP compared to 57 percent in New Zealand.

"It's also worth noting that discussions about a country's debt can include both public and private sector debt.

"NZ's government debt looks fine by global standards, but our private sector or household debt has long been a source of concern… household debt to GDP is relatively high, reflecting concerns sometimes raised by ratings agencies that, as a country, we have a lot of debt, and our assets tend to be quite highly concentrated in the housing market."

I have an overdraft with the ASB bank I want to pay off, I am on a low income after being made redundant. The issue I have is they won't allow me to pay it off each week to reduce it. Even if I want to pay a small chunk of it or the whole amount I need to leave it in my account for anywhere from two to seven days before they'll process it due to short staffing, they say, which isn't really practical when money is tight. Is there anything I can do? Or is there a bank I can transfer it to and arrange to pay it off? And every time I want to pay it off I need to go into a branch or phone the call centre.

It sounds like you're wanting to reduce your overdraft limit in a structured way.

Any time you put money into your overdraft, you'll be reducing the balance but unless the limit is also reduced, you'll be able to pull it out and spend it again.

You might find it easier to clear it as a personal loan with set repayments - it would be worth getting some advice on the best way to structure this and how the interest rate might compare to what you're currently being charged.

Christine Liggins, at DebtFix, said you could try a financial mentor who might be able to help you get it resolved.

ASB said following changes introduced under the CCCFA reforms, it had processes to follow when reducing overdraft limits.

"For example to ensure we meet our disclosure obligations to the customer. We'd like to better understand what has happened and see how we can help... As the customer has indicated they have recently been made redundant, we can also talk through the options available to help customers experiencing financial hardship."

The bank's spokesperson suggested you could get in touch or I could pass on your contact details.

World.title: Thunderstorm warning lifted after monsoon-like rains sweep Wellington
World.content:
A MetService severe thunderstorm warning for Wellington has been lifted as residents report torrential rain engulfing parked cars and causing flooding.

Fire and Emergency said it had no weather-related callouts from Saturday morning's downpours.

Wellington woman Rebekah Ward said she watched floodwaters rise around parked cars during the monsoon-like rain.

The health coach and tour guide watched floodwaters surge down Wellington's Tinakori Road while having breakfast in Thorndon.

The water rose to the bottom of parked cars and even knocked over a scooter, prompting fears her own vehicle could be swept away, she said.

The timing of the downpour was an "ironic" reminder of the monsoon she would soon experience on a trip to India, Ward said.

MetService issued the severe thunderstorm warning at 9.20am Saturday, valid until just before 11am.

It said its weather radar had detected severe thunderstorms moving east-northeast.

World.title: 12 bodies recovered in PNG maritime disasters as searches continue
World.content:
Papua New Guinea authorities are managing several separate cases of missing people due to boating incidents in recent days.

East New Britain disaster officials continue to search for up to 27 people missing since last Saturday after their two boats capsized while travelling from the Duke of York group to Kokopo.

As of late Friday, 12 bodies had been found, on the south west coast of neighbouring New Ireland province.

In another incident, off New Ireland's north, a search was underway on Friday for six people missing after their boat capsized.

And the Post Courier reports that closer to PNG's mainland, a search was underway on Friday for about 8 passengers missing after a dinghy carrying a casket capsized off Makamaka in Alotau District on Thursday.

Bad weather in Bougainville hampers search

Search and rescue efforts for a missing vessel travelling from Nissan Island to Buka have been temporarily suspended at sea due to deteriorating weather conditions across the Bougainville region.

The Autonomous Bougainville Government's Directorate of Disaster and Emergency said the National Weather Service and the Maritime Rescue Co-ordination Centre have issued warnings of strong winds, making sea-based search operations unsafe until conditions improve.

The missing vessel left Nissan Island for Buka on Saturday, 18 July, carrying three people on board.

NBC Bougainville reports the missing persons are skipper Mitchell Tokiapron, crew member Darrell, and passenger Horen Kapiatu.

Despite the suspension of sea searches, the Maritime Rescue Co-ordination Centre and the Joint Rescue Coordination Centre continue to broadcast alerts to all vessels operating in New Ireland waters.

However, no confirmed sightings of the missing boat have been reported.

World.title: 'Severe' magnitude 5.9 quake hits North Island
World.content:
A strong earthquake jolted the central North Island early on Saturday.

GeoNet said the 'severe' magnitude 5.9 quake happened around five kilometres southwest of Taumarunui at 4.51am.

The earthquake was nine kilometres deep and the intensity was severe.

The quake was reportedly felt across much of the North Island, including Auckland, and as far as the top of the South.

By 6am, nearly 23,000 'felt reports' had been filed to GeoNet. At least 11 aftershocks, ranging between magnitudes 2.2 and 3.7, followed.

Fire and Emergency (FENZ) said there were no quake-related callouts at all.

Aftershocks could go on for a week or longer - seismologist

A seismologist told RNZ the earthquake was the first ever recorded in that spot.

While Earth Sciences New Zealand duty seismologist Sam Taylor-Offord said it was a normal faulting earthquake, so not unexpected, and could have occurred on one of the few mapped faults in the area. It was the first to strike since records began in the early 1800s.

Taylor-Offord said larger earthquakes were not common in the wider area.

"The nearest earthquake in the country was in 1946, south of Te Kūiti, magnitude 5.4.

"But I would remind people who might have felt them, there was an earthquake in 2023 in Te Aroha, magnitude 5.1, which is very similar to this, smaller. There was also a deep earthquake in the region in October 2018, which was a 6.2, and that was felt down to Otago.

"So they do happen in the region. They're just much less frequent than other parts of the country."

Taylor-Offord said there had been more than 50 aftershocks, up to 3.7 in magnitude, within three hours.

"It could go on for a week, more or less, regularly... and then we expect things would taper off. But we could still be seeing earthquakes here in years to come that are associated with this one, just much, much smaller."

While nearly 23,000 'felt reports' had been filed to GeoNet, Taylor-Offord said it only recorded the first five minutes.

"So that 23,000 is the people that woke up and reported it, and I could not tell you how many more have been reporting it in the hours since, so it could be in the high tens of thousands."

Minor damage in Taumarunui

The mayor of the Ruapehu District confirmed there had been some minor damage in Taumarunui.

Weston Kirton told Saturday Morning one or two commercial buildings had been affected, "glass broken and the like".

There had also been minor slips on the roading network, including one blockage where someone could not get out.

Quake Update - Weston Kirton Saturday Morning Download MP3 4m

Kirton, who lived just three kilometres south of the epicentre, described the earthquake as traumatic.

"My bedroom has got lights that were shaking, and I thought things were going to start falling over. We did have photos, and what have you, fall over, but it was one of those moments where you don't know whether it's going to get worse, but as it turned out, it was five or 10 seconds of, just, trauma, and then of course it quietened down.

"It certainly was traumatic. I've lived here all my life and it certainly was the largest I've experienced in my lifetime."

Minor slips reported

Manawatū-Whanganui Emergency Management Group urged motorists to take care while driving after minor slips were reported in the area.

"Emergency services and roading crews are assessing the situation, but a fuller view of any impacts is unlikely to be available until daylight," it said.

No injuries or other damage had been reported.

The Emergency Management Group expected aftershocks to continue throughout the morning.

"If people feel them, they should drop, cover, and hold. If you are in bed, the best thing to do is to stay there and cover your head and neck with a pillow."

Broken glass, smashed vases at Taumarunui Reuse Shop

An opportunity shop in Taumarunui was picking up damaged stock on Saturday morning.

Emily Jasmine from Taumarunui Resource Recovery Centre on Golf Rd, part of a Ruapehu Transfer Station, came in to find broken glass scattered across the floor.

Jasmine was around a quarter of the way through the clean-up at 11.15am, having found about 10 smashed vases so far.

"We got off very lightly," she said. "It looks worse than it is.

"In fact, you know what, the ugly ornaments didn't even crack."

'Strong and long' in the lower North Island

The earthquake felt like it would not end in Whanganui, according to a resident in the suburb of Springvale.

Cushela Robson described the tremor as a very strong, prolonged rolling motion.

"I thought, should I get out of bed? And if I did, could I stand? So I thought, no, probably, because I grew up in Wellington, I thought, no, I think it's probably better to stay in bed."

World.title: Lewis  Clareburt celebrates in and out of Commonwealth Games pool
World.content:
Fresh off winning a Commonwealth Games silver medal, Lewis Clareburt says meeting his baby nephew for the first time made the moment even sweeter.

Clareburt, alongside Erika Fairweather, claimed the country's first podium finishes with a pair of silver medals on the opening night of finals in Glasgow.

Delivering one of the races of the night, Clareburt stormed home in a thrilling men's 200m individual medley to claim silver in 1m 56.77s, half a second behind crowd favourite Scotland's Duncan Scott.

"To be able to do a personal best on this stage is such a good feeling. I've been on the 1.57 mark for eight years, so to dip under that today and to get a silver on top is a cool feeling," Clareburt told reporters following the race.

The 27-year-old was the fourth fastest qualifier during the earlier heats.

Clutching his silver medal after the medal ceremony, Clareburt was asked whether a silver medal or a personal best was more important to him.

Lewis Clareburt (L) celebrates with winner Duncan Scott (SCO) after claiming silver in the men's 200m Individual Medley Swimming at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games. Photosport

It turns out another special moment meant most.

"A PB (personal best), actually meeting my nephew for the first time, not going to lie, that was better than all of that. That was pretty cool," he said.

"My sister has had a child since the last time I saw her, seven weeks old and got to see the little man for the first time. I think he was asleep.

"It was a pretty special feeling. I'm pretty proud of my sister."

Although a first meeting was accompanied by a Commonwealth Games medal, the new uncle chuckled that his nephew probably would not remember the occasion.

The silver was Clareburt's fifth Commonwealth Games medal, adding to the two gold medals and bronze he won in Birmingham in 2022, as well as bronze on the Gold Coast in 2018.

Clareburt also claimed bragging rights over his training partner Australian William Petrick who touched fourth, 1.1 seconds behind the Kiwi.

The pair train together at the Nunawading Swimming Club in Melbourne.

"One-nil so far. We're versing each other once more so hopefully I can double that."

World.title: Country Life: "Why not llamas?"
World.content:
Already addicted to llamas' yarn, Janette Buckingham thought she'd give farming the animals a spin.

That was over 30 years ago and in that time her herd of camelids has grown to include a few ovine cousins - Gotland sheep - also raised for their fibre which she spins and sells from her home studio in Southland's Waikawa Valley.

"For me, I like just being able to turn fibres over to people who will use them, and certainly the money's good too," she told Country Life.

It was a high school friend who first got her wheels spinning - literally.

Addicted to yarn: Llama herd follows love of fibre Country Life Download MP3 13m

Follow Country Life on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, iHeart or wherever you get your podcasts.

Buckingham has been spinning since 1973 when she was first introduced to the craft.

"I was terribly uncoordinated, but I just stuck with it," she said.

"Nobody showed me what to do. I just felt my way sitting up 'til God knows what time at night, trying too hard, but eventually ... I got the hang of it and could even spin a lumpy yarn. Anyone will tell you that's the breakthrough."

Since then she's taught a few people to spin herself. The trick is in knowing how to coordinate one's hands and feet.

Janette Buckingham at her home in the Waikawa Valley. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

It was a high school friend that got her interested in spinning in the 1970s. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

She looked quite at ease, tucked up by the fire on a squally afternoon, working away on her electric spinning wheel - a massive timesaver which helps when she's trying to rapidly replenish her stock of yarns.

Her love of spinning is what got her started on the llama farming. She'd bought a packet of caramel-coloured alpaca fibre in the 1980s which she "fell in love with".

"It was absolutely beautiful, like nothing I'd ever spun before, just sort of buttery smooth. I became addicted to it."

It was a time when many farmers were looking to diversify their farming operations, and the llama's cousin, the alpaca, was starting to become more well-known.

A love of fibres saw a Southland woman build her own herd of llama, Guanaco and Gotland sheep. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

However, it was a herd off llamas near Canterbury that caught her eye.

"We managed to get three, and one was a guanaco male. The fine-fibred guanaco is also a cousin to the llama.

"They weren't as popular then because people just wanted alpacas or llamas. The guanaco was something else again."

The Gotland sheep came later, a breed popular for their dark and grey-toned wool. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

Crossed with a llama, she said they can produce "very fine fibre".

"They're a bit more of a challenge to handle, but they're something that perhaps make my business a little bit different from a lot of other people's."

Today she has about 40 llama and guanaco which she runs alongside the Gotland sheep on her 25-acres in the Catlins.

The Gotland sheep came later, a breed popular for their dark and grey-toned wool and originally from the Gotland Islands off the coast of Sweden.

"There seemed to be a lot of interest in the Gotland wool because of its lustre, its colour, not much crimp in it, but it's just got certain characteristics that appeal to people."

The studio is stocked with a range of finished products. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

She sells the skeins from her home studio. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

World.title: Country Life: Celery, butterflies and Travis the goat
World.content:
Please publish to Country page and Country Life page (CLI) by ****** Saturday 8AM *********

"Six days a week, rain or shine, hail, sideways, wind, lightning ... put a raincoat on and carry on."

That's Luke Franklin, standing in a field of celery on a grey winter's day, describing the almost daily harvest which has been going on in the Franklin family for 120 years.

The present owner of Franklin Farm is the fifth generation in the business and the third at this 28-hectare site near Waimauku, north-east of Auckland.

It was 1906 when Sid Roskill first planted celery in Mount Roskill. Fifty six years later, Luke's grandfather Graham moved the Franklin legacy to Waimauku. He and wife Lucy started off with just 2.4ha before gradually buying up neighbouring farms.

Graham Franklin RNZ/Sally Round

Celery has been harvested by the Franklins for 120 years Supplied

The 85-year-old is still on the tools, driving the forklift and helping around the packing shed.

Big celery bunches are out these days, neatly trimmed and packed stalks are in, Graham told Country Life. And of course there's no horse and cart to take the crop to market.

"Things have changed, but not a hang of a lot. We still cut by hand, we still bring it all up, pack it much the same."

Celery, butterflies and Travis the goat Country Life Download MP3 18m

Follow Country Life on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, iHeart or wherever you get your podcasts.

Graham's son Alan is standing at one of the benches packing, alongside workers from the Philippines and Tuvalu.

"I think with the amount of hard work that we do and the long hours that we do, it makes it sustainable. I think there's no member of the family that's a shirker," Alan said.

Solokiala Manulele in the packhouse RNZ/Sally Round

The Franklin family have been growing celery for 120 years RNZ/Sally Round

"There's times where there's more competition comes into the market and there's times when you're having weather events or disease events.

"It can wipe out the crop, but you've just got to see past it and just enjoy the job and hopefully your bank account lasts long enough to come out the other side."

Alan's been out in the celery fields since he was a baby, when his mother Lucy would be out helping her husband Graham.

"Oh, my goodness me, you get up and it's freezing cold or it's pouring with rain, you still had to go out there," Lucy said.

Lucy RNZ/Sally Round

"No babysitters in those days. The children come out with you. Yes, one in a pushchair, one in a pram.

"They were raised on slugs and snails," she laughed. "It doesn't really hurt children to be out in the soil."

Peak celery season is October until Christmas and when that winds down, the visitor experience winds up.

Families can visit from Boxing Day during the summer to visit the Franklin's butterfly house and experience the release of thousands of butterflies, wander through sunflower fields and visit a farmyard of small animals.

When she's not in the packing shed, Alan's wife Monique can be found in the paddocks with small goats, a flock of chickens laying different coloured eggs and a "micro miniature" cow called Bubba Gump.

"I find the little children really can connect with them because they're a nice size."

She said many children are surprised to find eggs are laid by chickens and don't just come in cartons at the supermarket.

Travis, an energetic pygmy goat, was one of the stars last summer, "Chewing people's bags, their flowers, he's hopping in kids' prams, chewing ladies' dresses. He was just getting into everything, and everyone just loved it."

Jasmine Franklin with Sarge and Travis RNZ/Sally Round

sign RNZ/Sally Round

Opening Franklin Farm to visitors is a great way to connect farming with the public, Luke's wife Jasmine said.

"People enjoy the raw, honest truth. So sharing crop failures or sharing animals that we can't contain, people love that because it's genuine and real, and they find it quite entertaining, and people like to come along and see, for example, our goat Travis that we struggle to contain.

"In a way, sharing our problems and failures keeps us real and relatable, and people like to come along and check that out as well."

"They're entertained, they're getting lots of exercise, just connecting back to nature and our roots. Yeah, it's like a big YouTube."

Four generations of the Franklin family in the sunflower field at Franklin Farm Supplied

World.title: Country Life: What NZ can learn from a US farmer who coped with H5N1
World.content:
Disbelief and a sense of failure swirled through Georgie Cartanza's mind as she found more and more dead birds at her broiler chicken farm on the eastern coast of the United States last year.

In January 2025, the Delmarva Peninsula - where many migratory birds converge - had already had seven cases of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) and her "angst" was building.

"Over the 20 years that I've grown chickens, I'd never observed a dead snow goose on my property, but [...] I found eight dead snow geese in close proximity to the poultry houses," she told Country Life.

What New Zealand can learn from a farmer who lived through H5N1 Country Life Download MP3 11m

Follow Country Life on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, iHeart or wherever you get your podcasts.

Cartanza is not only an experienced chicken farmer, she also educates poultry farmers on good practice as extension agent for the University of Delaware's Cooperative Extension programme.

She had noticed water and feed levels were a little off in one of her four chicken houses, each housing 37,000 birds.

"My mortality started to pick up, but it wasn't tremendous. It wasn't anything that would have been earth shattering, but I really started feeling uneasy on a Friday evening."

By 2 o'clock on Saturday afternoon HPAI was confirmed.

"I think it's, it's a little bit of disbelief. I think it's a little bit of, 'you know, I've done everything I can. I've done everything I know to do.' It's an overwhelming feeling because it's a sense of failure."

All farms within a three kilometre radius were quarantined.

"You're thinking, 'what did I do wrong? This is impacting me, but it's now impacting my neighbour as well.' It's a pretty traumatic experience to go through and so it's changed me as a human being."

The houses were then "depopulated" - the chickens euthanised in situ via "ventilation shutdown plus heat" overseen by state agricultural authorities and a vet.

"They actually didn't expect me to be present during the process itself, and that's good because you've invested yourself into a flock of chickens and it's hard regardless."

The hardest time for Cartanza was going in the next day to deal with the remaining feed, surrounded by dead chickens.

"It's a really bad feeling to have to do that. I wouldn't wish it on anybody for certain."

Then came the composting process - the bedding, chickens and other material decomposing within the chicken houses for 14 days to contain the virus, subjected to heat with the temperature monitored, deemed virus free after 28 days.

"Then the cleaning process starts - to get the house cleaned up and disinfected."

Changing the way she farms

After the initial shock, Cartanza wanted to figure out where the virus had come in.

"So I kind of put my extension hat on and really started trying to think about that as far as what could I do to help somebody else."

Still poultry farming, she said she has changed a number of things, aside from maintaining a line of separation between clean and dirty.

"Anything outside of where the chickens are is considered dirty. And then once you come into the area where you cross that threshold where the chickens are present, that's now your clean area."

Aside from footbaths, dedicated footwear, hand sanitizer and signs, each chicken house now has its own tool box and other equipment.

"There's no reason you're going to bring something from the outside into this house. It's all about touch points and opportunities where, whether it's your feet, your hands, or an inanimate object, that virus could be carried into your house."

Snow geese Wikimedia Commons, credit: Bruce Hallman, BLM

Cartanza grows organic broilers and said certifiers had allowed them to keep them indoors when they deem the risk is greatest - during peak wild bird migration times.

"What tends to happen is people almost get burned out and they're like, 'well, nothing's happened, you know, it's no big deal', and they let their guard down."

It was an "odds game," she said, and a clearly defined high level biosecurity plan implemented consistently was key to lowering the odds of getting the virus, noting New Zealand's "phenomenal biosecurity system".

"I've been to New Zealand, I went through the airport, I saw what they did to my shoes, but the (wild migratory) birds, they're not going through that.

"So we have to do whatever we can to prevent that from getting into our poultry houses."

World.title: Quick hits: Aussie's dash to glory, Englishman drops his lollies
World.content:
A broken lane rope holds up the swimming program, an Australian wins gold after a mad dash from the medal podium and an Englishman drops his lollies.

Here are the quick hits from day one of the Commonwealth Games.

1. Broken lane rope

A broken lane rope delayed a heat of the men's 100m breaststroke. (Getty Images: PA Images/Owen Humphreys)

There is a whole host of things you probably do not want to see when you are about to dive into the pool ahead of a major championship.

One of them faced Zac Stubblety-Cook ahead of the 100-metre breaststroke heat, when he saw the lane rope had popped out of its holder.

"I was a bit worried, and nobody noticed. It was in my lane," Stubblety-Cook told the Seven Network.

Stubblety-Cook backed away from his block and alerted the authorities, who initially seemed to make things worse, with part of the rope falling into the pool as an official precariously reached for it pool side.

His attempts were unsuccessful at first, as the swimmers sat back down for what felt like an indeterminable wait (ultimately about 15 minutes).

"I've never had a delay that long," Stubblety-Cook said.

"That's just sport. You have to roll with it."

Easily done, perhaps, for a 27-year-old four-time Olympic medallist and former world champion, but what about if you are 23-years-old and making your major championship debut?

"I think it's expected to expect the unexpected," Bailey Lello said.

Well said young man, and well swam too. He made it to the semifinals alongside Stubblety-Cook and Sam Williamson.

2. All in a day's (or hour's) work

Jenna Forrester shows off her gold medal after winning the women's 200m backstroke final. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

In the space of an hour, Australia's Jenna Forrester mastered multi-tasking.

After finishing third behind fellow Australian Lani Pallister in the women's 400m freestyle final, Forrester took part in the medal ceremony and the photo opportunities that come with that ritual.

She then raced to the call room, needing to back up for the women's 200m backstroke final.

Forrester could be forgiven if she was out of breath but managed to win gold in astonishing fashion.

What made her victory even more remarkable was the fact she initially missed qualifying for the event after placing fourth at last month's selection trials in Sydney.

She only got a berth in the 200m backstroke when Australia's backstroke great Kaylee McKeown withdrew from the Games with glandular fever.

"I don't know what to say and didn't expect it to happen," Forrester told the Seven Network.

"I gave it my all and I'm so proud of myself. I am shocked."

3. Englishman drops his lollies

The pause button was hit on Australia's clash with England in the men's 3x3 wheelchair basketball competition for an unusual reason: one of the England players dropped his lollies.

Play was halted after lollies fell from the pocket of England captain Peter Cusack.

Officials asked staff for some assistance clearing the court surface, but Cusack waved them away.

He politely scooped up the fallen cargo and took them to the side of court before re-joining the game.

4. Sister rivalry either side of Hadrian's wall

Astrid Carroll (left) represents Scotland, while younger sister Ursula Carroll represents England. (Getty Images)

The single heat of the women's 100m S13 freestyle event had something of an unusual quirk in it.

Teenage sisters Ursula and Astrid Carroll were both making their international debuts, but for different countries.

The reason is not quite as spicy as one might hope, even with the countries at stake being Auld Enemies England and Scotland.

Astrid, 17, was born in Edinburgh, so she swims for Scotland, while her 14-year-old sister Ursula was born in Halifax, the people's republic of Yorkshire, so she swims for England.

The pair both live with Stargardt disease, a rare, inherited eye condition that causes progressive, central vision loss, "basically like seeing through a doughnut" Astrid told the BBC.

"It'll be nice walking out and just seeing you," Astrid added in that same interview.

Ursula simply responded the only way she could have, as an Englishwoman: "Scottish, unbelievable."

In the heats, Ursula got the win over her big sister, swimming 1:05.25 to Astrid's 1:05.84.

5. It's all in a name

De Niro Pao (right) took on Pooana Khoahli in the men's 65kg class. (Getty Images: Lintao Zhang)

Did Niue's De Niro Pao chose boxing or did boxing choose De Niro Pao?

If you are wondering where we are going here, let's hear from Pao himself.

"Robert De Niro is my mum's favourite actor, so she named me after him," Pao said.

"That's my grandad's favourite actor too."

Of course, De Niro won an Oscar for his portrayal of boxer Jake LaMotta in the 1980 film Raging Bull.

Given Pao competed in the men's boxing in Glasgow, perhaps he psyched himself up with a viewing of Martin Scorsese's classic?

Perhaps not.

"My grandad always tells me about Raging Bull, but I've never seen it," Pao admits.

For the record, Pao was eliminated via a points decision in the men's 65kg class, going down to Lesotho's Pooana Khoahli.

World.title: Fifteen minutes after celebrating bronze, Forrester stuns with gold
World.content:
Jenna Forrester wasn't even supposed to be there.

The 23-year-old travelled to Glasgow as a 400m freestyle and individual medley swimmer.

Then, when backstroke queen Kaylee McKeown succumbed to illness on the eve of the Commonwealth Games, selectors decided to throw Forrester in the 200m back too.

Such is the depth in Australian swimming, that's usually a pretty solid tactic to nab a podium double or even the vaunted sweep.

But usually it's not the afterthought climbing the top step.

"I really just went into tonight with a positive attitude," she said.

Swimmers spark medal rush on day one Lani Pallister wins Australia's first gold of these Commonwealth Games in the women's 400m freestyle, with more Aussies scooping up medals in the pool on the first full day of competition.

"I felt like I had nothing to lose and my family would have been really proud of me no matter what the result was. I feel like I really just took that in my stride."

At the trials in June, it was 20-year-old Iona Anderson who announced herself as a potential heir to McKeown's throne when she bettered her qualifying time.

McKeown, in the depths of glandular fever, responded in the final with a dominant victory, besting Anderson by almost four seconds in the final.

Hannah Fredericks was third and Forrester was more than five seconds behind McKeown in fourth.

For much of Saturday morning's final, it appeared something similar would repeat, albeit without the knowledge that everyone is racing for silver behind McKeown.

Fredericks was out fastest, while Forrester sat sixth at the first turn.

In fact, Fredericks led for the first three quarters of the race, before slowing in the last lap with only a 34-second split of the top six.

Meanwhile, Forrester was only getting stronger, saving her second-fastest 50 metres for last as she mowed down her compatriot, Scotland's Katie Shanahan, and Canadian Madison Kryger.

Forrester was a surprise gold medallist on night one. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

A veteran of three world championships, a Commonwealth Games and an Olympics before arriving in Glasgow, this marks her first gold medal at a major meet.

The stamina on display was remarkable for a woman who, only 15 minutes earlier, was standing on the podium celebrating her 400m freestyle bronze alongside champion teammate Lani Pallister.

Exactly how she managed to pull that off remains a mystery even to her.

"I honestly couldn't tell you, I am as shocked as you are," she said.

"I think my training this year has been really consistent and I have all of Swimming Australia and my coaches to thank for that.

"Honestly, I couldn't have done it without the help of a lot of others."

And on a night when 15 of her fellow Dolphins also won medals, there's plenty of help around.

World.title: Pogačar claims stunning victory in stage 19 of the Tour de France
World.content:
Tadej Pogačar launched a stunning solo attack from the foot of the iconic Alpe d'Huez to win the 19th stage of the Tour de France and extend his overall lead overnight.

Even by the four-time Tour champion's lofty standards, it was up there with his best wins as he was more than 3 minutes behind with 12km remaining.

Riding without a teammate for the last section, he caught Ecuadorian rider Richard Carapaz and Frenchman Lenny Martinez with 1.5km left and then surged ahead for his fifth stage win of this year's race and 26th overall.

"It's very cool to win up here," Pogačar said. "I'm super happy to take the win."

Martinez finished six seconds behind and Carapaz — who won the 18th stage with a brilliant breakaway win of his own — nine seconds back. American Sepp Kuss, who faded in the closing stages, was 1 minute, 14 seconds adrift.

With a lead of 7 minutes, 11 seconds over Remco Evenepoel in the overall standings, and two stages remaining, Pogačar is on the brink of joining Eddy Merckx, Miguel Indurain, Jacques Anquetil and Bernard Hinault as the only men to win five Tours.

Barring mishap or accident, the Slovenian star will be crowned when the race ends on Sunday on the Champs-Élysées in Paris.

Rated as an HC mountain pass, the hardest category in the race, Alpe d'Huez is arguably the most famed climb in cycling and has near-mythical status on the Tour. Swarms of fans, many camping overnight and carrying flags of several nations, screamed encouragement on each of the 21 hairpins.

"It was a crazy atmosphere on the whole climb," Pogačar said.

He kept his focus as the public got perilously close to his face and, at one stage, he had limited visibility due to smoke from flares being lit by spectators.

But as impressive as Pogačar's win was, it also came about because Carapaz, Kuss and Martinez did not work together properly to distance Pogačar when he was lower down.

"I had to fight against super good riders," Pogačar said. "But they were playing against each other a bit so it helped me to catch up."

Perhaps thinking he could benefit from others fading and get the stage win, Martinez kept sitting on Carapaz's wheel, which was very much to Carapaz's annoyance and meant the veteran had too much work to do alone.

He kept trying to accelerate while Martinez — 10 years his junior — did less work and a tired-looking Kuss generally sat back too much before drifting away.

With 900m left, Carapaz was showing phenomenal stamina to stay with Pogačar, but he was finally undone by a brutal acceleration and could not follow as the yellow jersey rolled past him.

Saturday's mammoth 171m Alpine stage could be epic.

It features three HC climbs — Col de la Croix de Fer, Col du Galibier and Col de Sarenne — and one Category 1 climb up Col du Télégraphe before a hilly finish to Alpe d'Huez.

Pogačar does not need to go for victory and can safely hang back and protect his lead.

But will he?

There are 66m of pure climbing, and that may be too much for him to resist.

"Tomorrow is the Queen stage of the Tour," Pogačar said. "[It] is the hardest day of the Tour. We'll follow our own plan, our own rhythm. We don't care about anything else."

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

World.title: How Hani harnessed mum and mana to go 'balls out' for bronze
World.content:
There is a two-minute countdown clock when para powerlifters enter the arena.

In that time they have to settle on the bench, most get their legs strapped down, align their back and shoulders under the bar, get their grip perfect, then lift.

Eventually, the pump-up music fades out when the lifter is finally ready, usually about halfway through the time.

Not Australia's Hani Watson, though.

For the first 30-40 seconds of her time on the bench, Watson, an effusive and effervescent athlete who loves a chat, takes a moment of supreme stillness.

As trusted coach Simon Bergner hurriedly organises straps and chalk with arena staff, he at no point rushes his charge.

As the crowd nervously watches the seconds tick down, Watson sits, eyes closed, breath steady, mind awash with the words of her late mum.

"You got this darlin'."

Hani Watson manages rogue bones and a body on fire When Hani Watson settles under the barbell at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games, she will be lifting more than just the plates on the bar.

Watson credits mother Laurita June "Bub" Rayward, who died in 2023, for "creating the strong woman" she has become.

"I believe in having that spirit, that energy, that mana, my culture that's within me, the Australian spirit and just sitting there and calming myself down and listening to that internal voice," she said after winning a second straight women's heavyweight Commonwealth Games bronze medal.

"As kids we don't listen to our parents, but I'm listening to them now. And they told me, 'This is your superpower, this is what you can do, this is what you need to focus on.'"

She was plenty strong enough in 2022 to win bronze with a best lift of 127 kilograms, and shattered that number with a final re-rack of 147kg in Glasgow on Saturday morning AEST.

"I didn't actually think I was going to hit the numbers coach was gonna ask me to hit," she said.

"But I just blocked it out, I didn't wanna know. I just went balls out and just hit it."

A "wild" crowd at Glasgow's Armadillo was enraptured by the ease with which she completed her lifts — although the third took some shifting.

But the loudest moments were reserved for the Nigerians, who collected silver through Rita Ferdinard and gold courtesy of the all-conquering Folashade Oluwafemiayo, who shattered the 86kg+ world record with a final lift of 175kg for a second straight Commonwealth gold.

Folashade Oluwafemiayo (centre) is seemingly untouchable, but Watson is chasing. (Getty Images: Mattia Ozbot)

Watson is chasing her, and is hoping to have closed the gap by the time the 2028 Los Angeles Paralympics roll around.

"It's nice to have someone to chase and I keep chasing her, I keep looking up to her," she said.

"I think it's important to have mentors in the game. She's been doing it since she was a teenager so she's got a lot of years on me — maybe about 30 years in the game — and I've been doing it for five, so I've got a lot to learn from her."

Oluwafemiayo also broke her own Games record score of 134.8 points despite weighing 15kg less than Watson (Commonwealth Games scores are calculated by comparing body weight to weight on the bar).

Swimmers spark medal rush on day one Lani Pallister wins Australia's first gold of these Commonwealth Games in the women's 400m freestyle, with more Aussies scooping up medals in the pool on the first full day of competition.

Both athletes had added 20kg of apparently pure muscle since Birmingham.

"Every time I see her it's like she's become this big chunky cow that she's eaten or something. It's muscle upon muscle on that woman," Watson said with pure admiration.

"I just watch her in awe. I ask her what's changed, what do you bench, what are you eating, and she tells me everything.

"I need someone to look up to because the sport's always changing, the goalposts are always changing.

"As long as she's there I've gotta keep watching her and she's watching me too. She knows I'm on her tail."

World.title: What it feels like to have your sport dumped from the Comm Games
World.content:
As the Commonwealth Games kicked off on its first full day of competition, plenty more sat at at home, many wishing it could be them.

Organisers in 2026 ditched badminton, hockey, wrestling, road cycling, mountain biking, rhythmic gymnastics, rugby sevens, squash, table tennis, triathlon, beach volleyball, cricket and, the most storied of all, diving.

It has been held at every edition since the first Empire Games in 1930, until this year.

Of the 22 Commonwealth Games diving events, Anabelle Smith went to the past four, including Glasgow 2014.

Twelve years ago she won bronze in the women's synchronised 3m springboard with Maddison Keeney, but not in Glasgow like the rest of her team.

This dive for Smith (left) and Keeney was at Glasgow 2014 in name only. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

The Scottish capital did not have a facility to allow for diving, so Smith, Keeney and Co were shipped to Edinburgh, the site of the 1970 and 1986 Games.

"[There was] obvious disappointment from the divers … but also an understanding," Smith told ABC Sport.

"It made sense they weren't just gonna ship the divers up to Edinburgh, disappointing but they'll power on and look ahead now."

The 33-year-old had not been planning to defend her 3m synchro gold medal from Birmingham 2022, but is instead attending her fifth Games as a spectator and part of the Australian team's connection and belonging squad.

How we got to Glasgow 2026 The bumpy road to Glasgow 2026 has produced a Commonwealth Games that will look a little different than the ones that came before.

She's joined by other athletes who have seen their sports axed, including beach volleyballer Chris McHugh and Melissa 'Milly' Tapper.

Her sport of table tennis was also axed after being included in six straight Games from 2002 to 2022.

Tapper, an Olympian and Paralympian, embodies the inclusive and integrated nature of the Games perhaps better than anyone.

She won team bronze at Glasgow 2014 and singles gold on home soil on the Gold Coast in 2018, and is still getting the chance to flash her skills in the team lounge at the decked-out Glasgow Argyle Hotel.

Loading Instagram content

"I've got a little bit of a call-up having the table tennis table in there," she said.

"We've had plenty of athletes and even some staff come through and challenge. Being around athletes everyone's competitive. It's a lot of fun.

"So even though table tennis isn't technically in the Games, it's still a part of the Games."

Table tennis was a "core sport" for the Commonwealth Games and falls into the category of many of the 2026 events, in that it could be held in existing halls.

Melissa Tapper has represented Australia at the Olympics, Paralympics and Commonwealth Games. (Getty Images: Matt Roberts)

Field hockey, however, requires a bit more space and bespoke facilities. Its history in the Commonwealth Games is not quite as long as diving's, but it had an elevated status as a "core sport".

In 2014, it was held at the Glasgow National Hockey Centre, which remains operational and is located along the River Clyde, within the 13-kilometre corridor of the pared-back 2026 Games.

When cuts were being made for 2026, the International Hockey Federation (FIH) and Commonwealth member nations lobbied for the sport's inclusion, but they missed out as organisers opted largely for indoor sports with athletics the only outdoor event.

Glasgow 2026 events 3x3 basketball/wheelchair basketball

Artistic gymnastics

Athletics

Bowls

Boxing

Judo

Netball

Para powerlifting and weightlifting

Swimming

Track cycling

The Kookaburras have won all seven men's gold medals since 1998, while the Hockeyroos have also never missed the podium, boasting four gold, two silver and a bronze.

Kookaburras captain Eddie Ockenden carried the flag in the Birmingham 2022 opening ceremony, as evidence of the sport's standing in Australia's Commonwealth Games movement, so Hockey Australia was "naturally disappointed" to miss out in 2026.

"Our national teams only play a finite number of international tournaments, making every opportunity to compete in one incredibly valuable," high performance director Bernard Savage said.

"The Commonwealth Games have always been one of those opportunities that our teams have genuinely looked forward to. Beyond the competition itself, the Commonwealth Games provide a unique multi-sport environment that our athletes look forward to and aspire to be a part of.

"The broader interest in the Games has provided an opportunity for our athletes and teams to inspire the next generation of hockey players across Australia and the Commonwealth.

"While this has been disappointing news, our focus remains firmly on our preparation for the 2026 FIH Hockey World Cup."

The World Cup will be played in Belgium and The Netherlands from August 15-30, shortly after the end of the Glasgow Games.

World.title: Cats down Dees, Dockers flex muscle against Eagles in derby
World.content:
Jye Amiss has kicked five goals and Murphy Reid produced a third-quarter clinic as Fremantle continued their western derby dominance with a 70-point win over West Coast at Perth Stadium.

The Dockers led by just eight points at half-time of Friday night's match before kicking 11 goals to one in the second half to race out easy 16.16 (112) to 6.6 (42) winners.

(Getty Images)

Amiss took seven marks inside 50m on the way to 5.1, while last year's Rising Star winner Murphy Reid (26 disposals, one goal) snared the Glendinning-Allan medal as best afield after turning the contest on its head with a mesmerising nine-possession third quarter.

Matthew Johnson (29 disposals, six clearances) and Caleb Serong (26 disposals, seven clearances) also had big games in front of 56,616 fans — a record home crowd for a Fremantle regular-season game.

There was late concern for West Coast mid-season recruit Oliver Francou when his right knee was gashed open after sliding over the studs of Andrew Brayshaw during a tackle.

Eagles players immediately signalled to the bench for help as Francou lay on his back and lifted his leg high in the air to stop blood from gushing out.

Star West Coast midfielder Harley Reid battled hard on the way to 30 disposals, 12 clearances, while Tim Kelly (31 disposals, 603m gained) and defender Marcus Herbert (36 disposals) were prominent.

The Dockers have now won five derbies on the trot — and 10 of the past 11 — to close to within three in the overall head-to-head ledger (33-30).

The result means Fremantle (17-2) will finish the round at least three wins clear on top of the table with just four rounds remaining, putting them in an excellent position to snare just their second minor premiership.

AAP

World.title: Australia claims six gold on Commonwealth Games opening day
World.content:
Lani Pallister dominated as expected and Jenna Forrester was a shock winner as Australia made a golden start in the pool at the Commonwealth Games.

Pallister consigned years of struggle and setbacks to history, opening Australia's medal tally at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games with the first of six gold medals in the pool.

The daughter of three-time Commonwealth Games medallist Janelle Elford, Pallister was outside the Games record of 3:58.06, set by Australian great Ariarne Titmus in Birmingham.

It was also notably short of her 3:58.87 personal best, later admitting she wasn't happy with the time.

Lani Pallister claimed Australia's first gold medal of the 2026 Commonwealth Games. (Getty: Quinn Rooney)

But it represented a breakthrough win given COVID-19 cruelled her Paris Olympics campaign. Pallister qualified for the three distance freestyle events, but could only race in the 800m.

The god-daughter of Australian sporting great Dawn Fraser also had a succession of health problems in 2021, including heart surgery and an eating disorder.

"Without all the ups and downs I wouldn't be the person or the athlete that I am today, and I think that's really special," she said after the win.

" I'm proud of the journey that I've been on and I wouldn't change it for the world. "

Pallister is also favourite to win the 800m and 1500m freestyle, and will also contest the 200m freestyle and the 4x200m freestyle relay.

Mollie O'Callaghan later spearheaded a comfortable win in the women's 4x100 freestyle relay, while the men's 4x100 freestyle team rounded out the session by ruthlessly capturing Australia's sixth gold medal.

Kyle Chalmers closed clinically to ensure Australia smashed their Games record from Birmingham 2022, winning in three minutes 9.49 seconds.

But there was nothing predictable about Jenna Forrester's shock gold medal in the 200m backstroke.

Hannah Fredericks (left) and Jenna Forrester celebrate after winning the bronze and gold medals in the 200m backstroke. (Getty: Quinn Rooney)

Forrester claimed bronze in the 400m freestyle, stood on the podium alongside Pallister, then had to quickly prepare for her next final.

Fifth at halfway and still fourth at the start of the last lap, Forrester stormed home.

Forrester finished fourth in the event at the June trials and was only brought in when backstroke queen Kaylee McKeown had to pull out with glandular fever.

Like Pallister, it is her first Commonwealth Games gold medal.

"I did not expect that to happen tonight — I am so over the moon," Forrester said.

"I didn't really have much expectation going into the 400 free or the 200 backstroke, so I'm really happy with how that went."

Australian William Petric qualified fastest in the 200m medley, but was fourth in the final as Scottish legend Duncan Scott had the crowd roaring with the host nation's first gold.

Alex Perkins was the fastest semi-finalist in the 50m butterfly, while fellow Australians Sam Williamson and Zac Stubblety-Cook reached their day-two 100m breaststroke final.

Para swimmer Jenna Jones claimed Australia's second gold, taking out the S13 100m freestyle on Saturday morning (AEST), before Forrester's big upset.

Gymnasts, powerlifters add to day one medal haul

Hani Watson (right) claimed bronze for Australia in the women's para powerlifting. (Getty Images: Mattia Ozbot)

As Australia dominated in the pool, para powerlifter Hani Watson shattered her previous best lift of 127kg from 2022 with a final re-rack of 147kg to claim bronze.

Nigerians Rita Ferdinard and Folashade Oluwafemiayo claimed silver and gold respectively, with Oluwafemiayo smashing the 86kg+ world record with a final lift of 175kg for a second straight Commonwealth gold.

Watson credits mother Laurita June "Bub" Rayward, who died in 2023, for "creating the strong woman" she has become.

"I believe in having that spirit, that energy, that mana, my culture that's within me, the Australian spirit and just sitting there and calming myself down and listening to that internal voice," she said after winning a second straight women's heavyweight Commonwealth Games bronze medal.

Australia's gymnasts also added to the medal tally on day one, with the men's artistic gymnastics team claiming bronze.

Of the five team members, Ritam Malik, Ben Foster, James Hardy and Tru Hagens were competing at their first Commonwealth Games, while Jesse Moore claimed his first medal at his second Games appearance.

Catch up on how the day unfolded in our blog below.
